claim: President Barack Obama "is the first president to keep a dog-trainer on retainer for $102,000 a year at taxpayer expense."
rationale: False. There is no reliable evidence that Barack Obama was the first U.S. president to retain a paid dog trainer, and the specific $102,000/year figure is unsubstantiated and likely conflates different personnel or security-related costs. White House pets have long been cared for by staff or contractors, so the claim that Obama uniquely kept a trainer on retainer at that exact taxpayer cost is unsupported.

claim: "Trudeau's foundation owns 40% of Acuitas Therapeutics which makes mechanic lipids for Pfizer."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that any Trudeau-linked foundation owns 40% of Acuitas Therapeutics. The Pierre Elliott Trudeau Foundation is a charitable organization and is not known to hold large equity stakes in private biotech firms; Acuitas is privately owned by its founders and investors. Additionally, the phrase “mechanic lipids” is inaccurate — Acuitas develops lipid nanoparticle delivery technology and has had collaborations in the LNP space, but the ownership and description in the claim are incorrect or misleading.

claim: Brewpubs can't sell growlers of their beer to customers.
rationale: The claim is presented as a universal prohibition but is jurisdiction-dependent. In many places brewpubs are allowed to sell growlers or other to-go containers if they hold the appropriate license, while other states or countries restrict or prohibit such off‑premise sales. Thus it is not true that brewpubs categorically can't sell growlers.

claim: "Surveys show that many of our citizens think we devote a full quarter or even a third of our federal budget to foreign aid."
rationale: Multiple reputable public-opinion surveys have consistently found that a substantial share of Americans greatly overestimate U.S. foreign aid, with typical median or modal estimates around 20–30% of the federal budget — i.e., roughly a quarter or sometimes a third. Those polling results substantiate the statement that many citizens think we devote a full quarter or even a third of the federal budget to foreign aid.

claim: "Walmart rewards everyone with $75 coupon to celebrate its 125th Anniversary"
rationale: This claim is false. Walmart was founded in 1962 (so a 125th anniversary is impossible now), and there is no credible evidence Walmart issued a universal $75 coupon for such an anniversary. Broad, unsolicited claims of blanket high-value coupons are commonly scam/phishing tactics rather than verified corporate promotions.

claim: Property taxes "are now 18% higher than when (Mark Sharpe) first took office."
rationale: The claim cannot be confirmed as stated because it lacks a specific jurisdiction and timeframe tied to 'when Mark Sharpe first took office.' Property tax levels are set and reported by local governments (counties/municipalities) and vary widely; without identifying the office, county, or years, the 18% figure is unverified. Given the missing specifics and absent corroborating public fiscal data, the statement is treated as not supported.

claim: Says "massive floods" led to Legionnaires’ disease outbreaks at the Quincy Veterans’ Home.
rationale: There is no evidence that “massive floods” caused the Legionnaires’ disease outbreaks at the Quincy Veterans’ Home. Legionnaires’ outbreaks are typically traced to contaminated building water systems, cooling towers, or plumbing problems, and public health investigations of such outbreaks identify those sources rather than flooding. The claim therefore misattributes the recognized environmental source of Legionella to an unsupported cause.

claim: Says President John F. Kennedy released a star Green Bay Packer from military reserve duty so that he could play in the 1961 NFL Championship Game.
rationale: There is no reliable historical record that President John F. Kennedy intervened to release a Green Bay Packer from military reserve duty to play in the 1961 NFL Championship. Contemporary team histories and presidential archives do not document such an action, and notable Packers players of that era (e.g., Bart Starr, Paul Hornung, Jim Taylor) are not recorded as being released from reserve duty by JFK for that game. The claim appears to be a conflation or myth rather than a documented fact.

claim: Thanks to the Trans-Pacific Partnership, "Vietnam is drafting and presenting unprecedented labor reforms, changing their Constitution to recognize worker organizations in Vietnam for the first time."
rationale: This overstates the case. While TPP negotiations did push Vietnam to commit to labor-law reforms and greater freedom of association, Vietnam already had state-sanctioned unions (the VGCL) and the changes were mainly legal and regulatory commitments rather than a first-ever constitutional amendment recognizing worker organizations. Independent unions remain restricted and reforms have been incremental and contested rather than a clear one-time constitutional recognition.

claim: "Reporters rehearse questions with White House press (secretary)."
rationale: This is not a standard or accurate description of how White House press interactions work. The White House press secretary holds briefings and may have off‑the‑record or background sessions with select reporters, but reporters generally prepare their own questions and do not "rehearse" questions with the press secretary. Occasional coordinated interviews or friendly exchanges can occur, but they are exceptions, not routine rehearsal of questions with the press secretary.

claim: "With 40 billion dollars, Elon Musk could have given each of the 330M people living in America a million dollars and still had $7B left over."
rationale: The claim is mathematically impossible: 330,000,000 people × $1,000,000 each = $330,000,000,000,000 ($330 trillion), far larger than $40 billion, so you could not give each a million and still have $7B left. The numbers match if the per‑person amount were $100 (330M × $100 = $33B; $40B − $33B = $7B), so the statement appears to confuse $1,000,000 with $100.

claim: Says Julie Parrish "voted to divert $160 million from public schools to private for-profit schools."
rationale: There is no clear record that Rep. Julie Parrish cast a single vote to “divert $160 million from public schools to private for‑profit schools.” While she has voted on bills expanding school‑choice programs, the claim ties a specific dollar amount and destination (private for‑profit schools) to one vote in a way that public legislative records do not support. The $160 million figure and the characterization of recipient schools as for‑profit are unsupported and misleading without additional context.

claim: "I opposed the only multilateral trade deal that came before the Senate while I was there."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because no speaker, years, or definition of “multilateral trade deal” are given; without that context it cannot be confirmed. Moreover, over recent decades multiple multilateral trade-related agreements or implementing measures (for example Uruguay Round/WTO legislation, NAFTA-related implementing actions, CAFTA discussions) have come before Congress, so the absolute claim that only one did during a given senator’s tenure is unlikely. Because of the missing specifics, I treat the statement as not supported.

claim: Says a photo shows a man wearing a "government issue Saint Laurent hazardous materials suit."
rationale: The claim is misleading: governments do not issue luxury-brand clothing such as Saint Laurent, and certified hazardous‑materials (hazmat) suits are made by specialized PPE manufacturers rather than couture houses. A photo could show a person in a suit styled to look like a hazmat suit or a fashion item with Saint Laurent branding, but that would not be a genuine "government issue Saint Laurent hazardous materials suit."

claim: Says Donald Trump "doesn't make a thing in America."
rationale: The absolute claim that Donald Trump "doesn't make a thing in America" is incorrect. Trump owns and operates U.S.-based businesses and properties (hotels, real estate, golf courses) that produce goods and services domestically, even though many Trump-branded consumer products have been manufactured abroad. The blanket statement therefore overgeneralizes and is false.

claim: Says an appointed board created under Obamacare "will have the ability to come between you and your doctor in determining the best treatment options for you!"
rationale: The claim is misleading. The Affordable Care Act created the Independent Payment Advisory Board (IPAB) to propose Medicare cost‑saving measures, but statute explicitly barred it from recommending actions that would ration care, restrict benefits, change eligibility, or interfere with the doctor‑patient relationship. While system‑level payment rules could indirectly affect access over time, the board did not have authority to make individual treatment decisions or directly ‘come between you and your doctor.’

claim: "Same little boy died of COVID-19 in three different countries. Still don’t believe the media is #fakenews?"
rationale: The claim is false: one person cannot die in three different countries. This allegation conflates image reuse or miscaptioning with actual deaths; fact-checks during the pandemic found photos and stories were sometimes reused or misattributed, but that is not the same as the same child having died three times. The correct interpretation is media errors or recycled images, not multiple deaths of the same child in different countries.

claim: Says raising the state income tax rate on millionaires to offset property taxes for other residents is "not a tax increase. It's a tax shift."
rationale: The statement is misleading: raising the income tax rate on millionaires is, by definition, a tax increase for those taxpayers even if the revenue is used to cut property taxes for others. It could be characterized as a tax shift only if the overall net tax burden on the state and on most taxpayers remains revenue‑neutral, but the claim’s blanket "not a tax increase" is incorrect without that context.

claim: Hillary Clinton "agreed with (John McCain) on voting for the war in Iraq."
rationale: Both Hillary Clinton and John McCain cast affirmative votes on the 2002 congressional authorization that led to the Iraq War. Saying Clinton "agreed with McCain on voting for the war" is accurate in the sense that both senators voted for the 2002 AUMF.

claim: "According to ATF data, 70 percent of firearms recovered and traced in drug cartel crimes in Mexico originated from the United States."
rationale: This statement is misleading as a blanket claim. ATF trace data have shown a large share of firearms recovered in Mexico were originally sold in the U.S. in some years and subsets, but the percentage varies by year, category (e.g., cartel-related vs all recoveries), and whether guns could be successfully traced; ATF reports do not consistently state a single 70% figure for 'drug cartel crimes' across years. Without specifying the year and exact ATF dataset/methodology, the precise 70% claim is not reliably supported.

claim: "Our most important work has been creating and retaining almost 55,000 Ohio jobs."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it gives no speaker, timeframe, or source for the figure. While Ohio agencies and economic development groups have reported job creation/retention numbers in that range at various times, those totals depend heavily on attribution and counting methods and cannot be confirmed from the claim alone. Without a cited program, period, or independent audit, the assertion that "our most important work" produced or retained "almost 55,000 Ohio jobs" is not provable.

claim: Says rejecting federal aid to expand Medicaid in Texas will "send $9 billion in federal taxes paid by Texans to other states to insure their working poor."
rationale: The claim misstates how federal funding works and uses a specific $9 billion figure without context. While Texas would forgo billions in federal Medicaid matching funds by not expanding coverage, federal taxes are pooled and not directly 'sent' as Texans' taxes to other states; the $9 billion number is unsubstantiated without a specified time frame or source.

claim: "Making public colleges and universities tuition-free, that exists in countries all over the world, used to exist in the United States."
rationale: The claim combines two points that are true in broad terms: many countries (e.g., several European and Nordic states) offer tuition-free public higher education, and the U.S. has had periods and programs where public college was effectively tuition-free for residents or groups. Examples include GI Bill funding for veterans and state/local policies (notably many community colleges and some state programs mid-20th century) that provided free or nominal-cost tuition, though this was not a permanent, nationwide policy.

claim: "We have pay equity. When you think about that wage gap, we all know it's 78 cents to the dollar. Well, in New York state it's 90 cents to the dollar."
rationale: The claim mixes a commonly cited aggregate statistic with an incomplete interpretation. The “78 cents” figure is a frequently quoted unadjusted national median earnings ratio for women versus men in certain years, but the exact number varies by year and definition; it does not imply pay equity. New York’s female-to-male median earnings ratio has in some years been closer to ~0.88–0.92, but even ~90 cents is far from full pay equity (1.00) and depends on the year and whether adjustments (hours, occupation, experience) are made.

claim: "98 percent of small businesses make less than $250,000" and would not see a tax increase under Barack Obama's plan.
rationale: Contemporaneous IRS data and independent fact-checkers found that about 98% of businesses reporting business income on individual tax returns (sole proprietorships, S‑corps, partnerships) had net income below $250,000, and President Obama’s proposal to preserve tax cuts for households under $250,000 would not raise marginal rates for those pass‑through businesses. This conclusion depends on the common definition of “small businesses” as pass‑through entities taxed on individual returns and the use of taxable/net business income, not gross receipts or other measures. There are caveats (see safety notes) that mean the statement needs context but is accurate as typically stated in the 2012 debate.

claim: "Only Reuters" reported that the doctor who detected the omicron variant said its symptoms are "very mild."
rationale: The claim is false because multiple news organizations besides Reuters reported that the South African doctor who first flagged omicron (Dr. Angelique Coetzee) described the patients she saw as having mild or atypical symptoms. Major outlets including the BBC, AP, The Guardian and others carried her comments, so it is incorrect to say only Reuters reported this.

claim: Military spending cuts, known as the sequester, were President Barack Obama’s idea.
rationale: The automatic, across-the-board military (and domestic) cuts known as the 2013 sequester were created by the 2011 Budget Control Act as part of a debt-ceiling compromise negotiated by President Obama and congressional leaders — not solely Obama’s idea. The sequester was agreed to as a bipartisan enforcement mechanism to force deficit reduction after negotiations between the White House and Republican congressional leaders.

claim: "There's one (study) that came out of Pew in 2008 that showed 14 percent of people who voted were noncitizens."
rationale: This claim misstates and misattributes the data. Pew did not conclude that 14% of people who voted in 2008 were noncitizens; the 14% figure comes from a small subset of survey respondents who self-identified as noncitizens and said they voted, a result experts attribute largely to respondent error and tiny sample sizes. Multiple fact-checks and analysts say there is no credible evidence that 14% of 2008 voters were noncitizens.

claim: Says the "only valid reason to oppose voter ID is that you plan to cheat," and "every Democrat in Congress opposes voter ID."
rationale: This claim is false. Saying the 'only valid reason' to oppose voter ID is intending to cheat is a normative overreach—scholars, advocates, and courts have identified non-fraud reasons to oppose strict ID laws (e.g., disproportionate burdens on low-income, elderly, and minority voters, administrative barriers, and lack of evidence of widespread impersonation fraud). The universal claim that 'every Democrat in Congress opposes voter ID' is also incorrect because Democrats hold varied positions and some have supported limited or particular ID measures; the absolute word 'every' makes the statement factually implausible.

claim: A photo shows a helicopter rescue mission in Afghanistan where wounded men were loaded onboard.
rationale: There is insufficient information to verify that the photo actually depicts a helicopter rescue in Afghanistan with wounded men aboard. Without the image, metadata, geolocation, or independent reporting, visual claims about location and the condition of people in a photo are frequently miscaptioned or recycled, so the claim cannot be confirmed and is treated as false.

claim: Says Texas is "last in mental health expenditures."
rationale: The claim as stated is too broad and typically false: rankings of “mental health expenditures” depend on the metric (total dollars, per-capita spending, percent of budget) and the year. Texas is often among the lower-spending states on a per-capita basis, but it is not consistently ranked dead last across metrics and years. Without a specified year and spending measure the absolute claim that Texas is “last” is unsupported.

claim: "I’m proud to say that under my administration, as you just heard, we will be building the first new heavy icebreakers the United States has seen in over 40 years."
rationale: The United States' last heavy polar icebreakers (the Polar-class ships) were built and commissioned in the 1970s, and no new U.S. heavy icebreakers were constructed for decades. In the late 2010s/early 2020s the Polar Security Cutter program began contracting and construction to build new heavy icebreakers, so saying the administration will be building the first new heavy icebreakers in over 40 years is accurate.

claim: Says he "sued Obama’s EPA seven times."
rationale: The claim as written is unverifiable because it does not identify who “he” refers to. Multiple officials and organizations sued the Obama EPA on different rules and the number of suits attributed to any one person varies by source, so without a named individual or citation the statement cannot be confirmed.

claim: The proposed Gogebic mine in northern Wisconsin "could be extended as long as 21 miles."
rationale: Public materials and reporting about the Gogebic (Gogebic Taconite) proposal describe an iron-bearing formation that runs roughly 21 miles and note the company’s stated possibility of expanding mining operations along that strike. The statement that the project "could be extended as long as 21 miles" reflects documented discussion of a potential future expansion rather than an immediate footprint.

claim: Ken Mercer "wants Sean Hannity and James Dobson included in social studies texts."
rationale: I find no reliable, specific evidence that Ken Mercer explicitly proposed that Sean Hannity and James Dobson be named in social studies textbooks. Mercer was involved in Texas curriculum debates and promoted conservative perspectives, but credible reporting and records do not substantiate this precise claim as stated. Given the lack of primary-source documentation or direct quotes attributing this request to him, the statement appears to be an unsupported or mischaracterized assertion.

claim: "Education Secretary Betsy DeVos owes Ohio $5.3 million for campaign finance violations and Mike DeWine's office refuses to collect the fine."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Betsy DeVos personally owes Ohio a $5.3 million campaign-finance fine, nor verified reporting that Governor Mike DeWine’s office has refused to collect such a judgment. Major fact-checks and news outlets have not documented a $5.3 million debt owed by DeVos to the state of Ohio, and enforcement of Ohio campaign-finance penalties typically involves the Secretary of State or the Attorney General rather than the governor’s office.

claim: "At the Democratic convention, the Pledge of Allegiance was read with the words 'under God' removed."
rationale: This broad claim is not supported by available evidence. Viral posts alleging the Democratic convention edited out “under God” were investigated by news fact-checkers and recordings of convention proceedings show the phrase was not omitted when the Pledge was recited. There is no reliable documentation that the national convention deliberately removed those words.

claim: Says he got "support all over Raleigh"
rationale: The claim provides no speaker, time, or source, so there is no way to verify that any particular person actually said they got “support all over Raleigh.” Claims about someone’s statements require a verifiable quote or reliable reporting; absent that, the assertion cannot be confirmed. Under uncertainty I mark it false pending evidence.

claim: "We borrow $4 billion every single day, much of it from China."
rationale: The U.S. federal government’s net borrowing fluctuates by year but recent deficits translate to roughly $3–5 billion per day on average, so "$4 billion every single day" is an oversimplification. The claim that much of that borrowing comes from China is incorrect: China holds on the order of about $800 billion–$1.3 trillion in Treasuries (a small share of total U.S. debt) and is not the primary purchaser of daily new issuance, which is largely bought by domestic investors, the Federal Reserve, and government trust funds.

claim: Says Rick Scott’s "hospital company stole millions, defrauding the military’s health care program."
rationale: Rick Scott was CEO of Columbia/HCA, a hospital chain that in the late 1990s and early 2000s was the subject of federal investigations and paid large settlements (totaling roughly $1.7 billion) over fraudulent billing and related schemes involving federal health programs. Department of Justice actions and civil suits alleged false claims submitted to federal programs; some investigations encompassed federal military health benefits administered through defense health programs. Scott himself was not criminally charged, and exact allegations and settlements varied by program and year.

claim: The federal government "has $3 trillion in cash flow, so we can pay our bills" and won’t default.
rationale: The statement is misleading. While the U.S. federal government receives trillions in annual receipts, it does not typically hold $3 trillion in immediately available cash, and legal constraints (like the debt ceiling) and timing mismatches between receipts and obligations can still produce a default risk even if projected receipts are large.

claim: Federal spending is "the highest it's been as a share of our economy in 60 years (and) revenue is the lowest it's been as a share of our economy in 60 years."
rationale: The first half (federal spending as a share of GDP) is broadly correct insofar as federal outlays spiked during the COVID era to levels not seen since World War II, so spending was unusually high compared with the past 60 years. The second half (revenue being the lowest in 60 years) is not clearly true: receipts did fall sharply in 2009 and were very low in some recent years, and depending on exact year/fiscal definition 2020/2021 revenues were not uniquely the lowest in a 60‑year span. Different fiscal measures and time windows change the conclusion.

claim: An election worker in Georgia threw away a ballot.
rationale: The claim is unverified and lacks corroboration from credible sources. Social-media posts alleging Georgia election workers discarded ballots have repeatedly been debunked or shown to be misinterpreted, and official post-election reviews did not substantiate widespread or confirmed instances of ballots being thrown away. Given the vagueness (no time/place/person) there is insufficient reliable evidence to treat this as fact.

claim: "In 1986, President Ronald Reagan" cut the business tax rate to 34 percent and "it worked -- our economy boomed, the middle class thrived and median family income increased."
rationale: The statement mixes a correct factual element with an inaccurate causal claim. It is true that the Tax Reform Act of 1986 (signed by Reagan) lowered the top corporate tax rate to 34% (effective in the late 1980s). However, saying “it worked” and attributing a booming economy, a broadly thriving middle class, and clear increases in median family income solely to that cut is misleading: late-1980s growth reflected multiple factors (monetary policy, post-recession recovery, other tax changes), gains were uneven, deficits rose, and middle-class income growth was modest and concentrated for some groups.

claim: The United States is "#1 in oil consumption" in the world.
rationale: Contemporary international energy statistics (from agencies such as the U.S. EIA, IEA and BP) consistently show the United States consumes more crude oil and petroleum products in total than any other single country, typically on the order of ~18–21 million barrels per day in recent pre-pandemic years. Thus the claim that the U.S. is '#1 in oil consumption' (meaning total national consumption) is correct.

claim: "Some patients who are on transplant lists for kidney or other organs are being dropped from the list simply because they are shown as a licensed card holder" for medical marijuana.
rationale: Transplant centers have varied policies and there are documented cases and news reports of patients being denied listing or removed because they use medical cannabis or hold a medical-cannabis card. Professional transplant guidance urges individualized assessment, but in practice some programs have treated card-holding or ongoing cannabis use as a disqualifier.

claim: Sotomayor "ruled against the white firefighter — Ricci and other white firefighters — just on the basis that she thought women and minorities should be given a preference because of their skin color and because of the history of discrimination in the past. The law was totally disregarded."
rationale: This claim is false. In Ricci v. DeStefano (2009) the Supreme Court's majority (opinion by Justice Alito) ruled for the white and Hispanic firefighters; Justice Sonia Sotomayor was in the dissent supporting the city’s decision to discard the exam results to avoid disparate-impact discrimination. Her dissent argued the city faced genuine legal and practical risks of discrimination and did not assert she simply favored minorities "because of their skin color" nor that the law was entirely disregarded.

claim: "Grandparents must pickup up all their grandchildren every weekend no matter what or they will be fined $5,000."
rationale: There is no general federal or state law that universally requires grandparents to pick up all grandchildren every weekend under threat of a $5,000 fine. Childcare and visitation are private matters decided by parents or by courts in custody/guardianship cases, and courts can issue orders in specific cases but not a universal mandate as described. The specific monetary fine and absolute wording (“no matter what”) are implausible and not supported by general legal practice.

claim: Say Oregon Reps. Peter DeFazio and Earl Blumenauer are "socialists who are openly serving in the U.S. Congress."
rationale: Both Peter DeFazio and Earl Blumenauer are longtime members of the Democratic Party and are not known to publicly identify as socialists or be members of the Democratic Socialists of America; only a few House members self-identify as democratic socialists. Additionally, Peter DeFazio retired and left Congress in January 2023, so he is not currently serving. Thus the claim that they are "socialists who are openly serving in the U.S. Congress" is inaccurate.

claim: "I remember one of [Curt Schilling's] teammates said he painted his sock, the bloody sock."
rationale: There is no credible contemporary record of a Red Sox teammate publicly saying Curt Schilling “painted” the famous bloody sock. Contemporary news reports, teammates’ accounts, Schilling’s own statements and photographic/medical evidence describe an actual wound and blood on the sock, and while rumors circulated, they were not substantiated by named teammates or reliable sources.

claim: "As Ohio treasurer, Josh Mandel loaned your money to Chinese business interests, and Mandel opposed a bill holding Communist China accountable when they cheated and stole American jobs."
rationale: The claim combines two assertions that are not supported by clear public evidence. As Ohio treasurer Mandel oversaw state investments that could have included funds with foreign exposure, but that is not the same as directly "loaning your money to Chinese business interests," and I found no definitive record that he made direct loans to Chinese companies. Likewise, saying he "opposed a bill holding Communist China accountable" is vague — without citing a specific bill or vote it reads like a political characterization rather than a verifiable fact.

claim: "Within the three miles surrounding the University Circle area, infant mortality exceeds some Third World countries."
rationale: Multiple local public-health reports and news investigations have documented very high neighborhood-level infant mortality rates on the east side of Cleveland near University Circle (within a few miles) that are comparable to or higher than the infant mortality rates reported for some low- and middle-income countries. Because the claim compares a localized, high neighborhood rate to country-level averages, the statement that infant mortality "exceeds some Third World countries" is supported, though it depends on which countries and what year are compared.

claim: Says GOP recall challenger Kim Simac "was delinquent paying her property taxes eight of the last nine years."
rationale: I cannot verify this specific claim with the information available to me. Property tax delinquency is a matter of local public records and the assertion that Simac was delinquent 'eight of the last nine years' would require checking county tax records for the exact parcel(s) and years; I did not find corroborating, reliable reporting or accessible records in my data to confirm the claim. Absent that verification, the claim should be treated as unproven and thus classified as false for fact-checking purposes.

claim: "Ten retired nuns were barred from voting in the 2008 Indiana Democratic primary."
rationale: Contemporaneous news reporting and later fact-checks do not support a verified incident in which ten retired nuns were barred from voting in the 2008 Indiana Democratic primary. While there were some voting disputes and provisional-ballot issues in that primary, no credible sources document this specific claim as stated.

claim: "A Gallup report recently said that nearly 50 percent of small business owners aren't hiring because of what they call ‘regulatory uncertainty.’"
rationale: I could not find a recent Gallup report that states nearly 50% of small business owners are not hiring because of 'regulatory uncertainty.' Gallup's small-business and economic polls typically highlight labor supply, demand, costs, and taxes as leading hiring constraints and do not show a near-50% figure tied specifically to regulatory uncertainty; the claim appears to misattribute or exaggerate findings from other surveys or different questions.

claim: "The violent crime rate has risen, and the homicide rate has risen by more than 20 percent in just two years, really after 30 years of decline in violent crime."
rationale: U.S. violent crime rates rose notably in 2020–2021 after roughly three decades of decline from the early 1990s through the 2010s. National data sources (FBI Uniform Crime Reporting and CDC homicide estimates) show homicides jumped sharply in 2020 and remained elevated in 2021, amounting to an increase of over 20% across that two‑year span compared with 2019.

claim: Says the Steele dossier "was—according to (James Comey's) June 2017 testimony—'salacious and unverified.' "
rationale: In his June 2017 Senate Intelligence Committee testimony, then-FBI Director James Comey described the Steele dossier as containing “salacious and unverified” allegations and said the FBI had not verified its contents at that time. Multiple contemporaneous transcripts and news reports quote him using that exact wording when discussing the dossier.

claim: "2008 was the deadliest year of the war (in Afghanistan) for American forces."
rationale: This claim is incorrect. U.S. military fatalities in Afghanistan peaked after 2008, with 2010 widely reported as the deadliest calendar year for American forces during the Afghan war (substantially more U.S. deaths than in 2008). 2008 had a much lower annual U.S. death toll than the 2010 peak.

claim: Says the U.S. Constitution provides for just compensation when land is taken under eminent domain.
rationale: This is correct. The Fifth Amendment contains the Takings Clause, which provides that private property shall not be taken for public use without just compensation; the Supreme Court has applied this to eminent domain proceedings.

claim: Data show that more white people than Black people are shot and killed by police.
rationale: In raw counts for the United States, multiple datasets (e.g., Washington Post 'Fatal Force', Mapping Police Violence) routinely record more white people than Black people shot and killed by police in recent years. However, this statement omits that Black people are killed at a higher rate per capita, so absolute counts do not capture the disparity in risk.

claim: "Kyle Rittenhouse files $400 million suit against CNN!"
rationale: There are no widely reported or verifiable records that Kyle Rittenhouse filed a $400 million lawsuit specifically against CNN. While Rittenhouse and his lawyers have pursued defamation suits and legal claims against various individuals and entities after his trial, major news coverage and court filings do not support the specific $400 million claim against CNN. The claim appears to be a mischaracterization or amplification of other legal actions.

claim: Quotes incoming U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez as saying "under capitalism, man oppresses man. Under socialism, it’s the other way around."
rationale: The line is a long-standing satirical aphorism about capitalism vs. socialism that predates Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and has been widely misattributed to various figures. There is no reliable evidence or reporting showing Ocasio-Cortez uttered this specific quip, so attributing it to her is incorrect.

claim: The Atlanta Beltline paid nearly $3.5 million for less than a quarter-acre.
rationale: Contemporaneous local reporting and public property records show the Atlanta BeltLine purchased a very small parcel—reported at under a quarter-acre—for roughly $3.5 million. The figure and the parcel size were widely cited in news coverage of BeltLine acquisitions and drew controversy for the high per‑square‑foot cost.

claim: Under the new health care law, the elderly will be denied care when they have "passed the age limit for treatment."
rationale: There is no provision in the U.S. Affordable Care Act or similar recent major health reforms that creates an age cutoff requiring denial of care to the elderly. Claims that seniors will be refused treatment after reaching an "age limit" stem from misinformation (e.g., "death panel" myths) and misinterpretations of advance-care planning or triage discussions, not from enacted law. Routine Medicare and anti-discrimination rules remain in place and do not mandate blanket age-based denial of treatment.

claim: Says "99 percent of the time police officers aren't charged when they kill young people of color."
rationale: The assertion that officers aren’t charged 99% of the time is an overstatement not supported by available evidence. Public datasets and academic analyses show prosecutions of officers after deadly encounters are relatively uncommon but vary by jurisdiction and dataset; charging rates are typically higher than 1% and not uniformly 99% non-charging. The claim also lacks crucial definitions (time period, age cutoff, and what counts as 'charged').

claim: Says President Donald Trump "put out a $297 million contract to a vendor to show him how to hire Border Patrol. So, the first payment they made was $14.8 million. You know how many Border Patrol they hired with $14.8 million? Two."
rationale: I find no credible evidence that the Trump administration issued a $297 million contract specifically to “show him how to hire Border Patrol,” or that a first $14.8 million payment resulted in only two Border Patrol hires. Large DHS/CBP contracts do exist, but reporting and contract records do not support the specific figures and outcome claimed, and the claim conflates contract service payments with personnel hires. The asserted direct link between a single up-front payment of $14.8 million and hiring only two agents is implausible given how federal hiring contracts and training budgets are structured.

claim: Photos show Ukrainian citizens destroying two Russian tanks with Molotov cocktails in Kyiv.
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that the specific photos show Ukrainian civilians destroying two Russian tanks in Kyiv with Molotov cocktails. Independent reporting and image verifications have found viral images of burning or damaged Russian vehicles were miscaptioned or showed damage consistent with anti-tank weapons or from other locations/times; Molotovs are also generally ineffective against modern tank armor. Therefore the claim as stated is false.

claim: Chris "Sununu supported Obama’s Common Core agenda, taking away local control of our schools."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate. Chris Sununu has generally positioned himself against federal overreach on education and emphasized local/state control rather than endorsing Obama’s Common Core agenda; he did not advocate for a federal takeover of schools. Moreover, Common Core was a state-led standards initiative with federal incentives, so saying it "took away local control" is misleading.

claim: The Convention Center "was sold as a building that would never cost taxpayers a dime."
rationale: The claim is presented as an absolute guarantee but lacks any specific context (which convention center, who made the promise, or the contract terms). In practice municipal sales or public-private deals are rarely able to guarantee that a facility will "never cost taxpayers a dime," and many such agreements include subsidies, tax abatements, bonds, or contingent liabilities that can create taxpayer costs later. Without a specific, verifiable contractual promise showing an unconditional lifetime guarantee, the categorical statement is not supported.

claim: Says over 90 percent of Travis County’s eligible residents have registered to vote.
rationale: Publicly reported voter-registration and census-derived calculations for Travis County have historically shown registration shares well below 90% (more commonly in the 70s–80s percentile range). I found no authoritative evidence that over 90% of the county’s eligible residents are registered, so the claim is likely incorrect without a very recent and specific data source to back it up.

claim: Says Jill McCabe "supports late term abortions. Larger baby parts are more profitable."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reputable reporting that Jill McCabe made the quoted statement. Such an inflammatory quote would be widely reported and sourced; instead this allegation resembles fabricated or misattributed rhetoric tied to debunked 'selling baby parts' stories. Without a verifiable primary source, the claim should be treated as false.

claim: Photo shows "people coming from California to Washington DC" to protest election results.
rationale: The claim asserts a specific origin and intent for people in a photo but provides no provenance, metadata, or corroborating reporting to establish they traveled from California to Washington, D.C. Without geolocation, timestamps, captions from reliable sources, or travel records, the photo’s claimed origin and purpose cannot be verified. Because the claim makes a specific factual assertion that is unsupported, it is judged false absent evidence.

claim: "CNN reports DemDebate had 2.3 million viewers. Trump rally had 6.7 million last night!"
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because it gives no date or source for either figure and mixes two separate viewership measurements. CNN publishes specific Nielsen figures for particular debates and nights; without the exact debate date and which metric (overnight, Live+SameDay, total across platforms) this 2.3M figure can’t be confirmed. Likewise, the 6.7M rally number is not corroborated here and could reflect a different metric or aggregation, so the paired assertion is unreliable.

claim: "The permission to engage was given before the word RPG was ever used."
rationale: The claim asserts a specific temporal ordering but provides no context or documentary evidence (timestamps, recordings, or authoritative logs) to verify that permission preceded the utterance of the word “RPG.” Without such objective records the assertion is unproven and cannot be treated as established fact.

claim: On Syria, "a lot of the allies signed on. At the last minute, Obama backed off."
rationale: The statement is misleading. In 2013 after the Ghouta chemical attacks the U.S. did prepare strikes, but many key allies did not commit to a strike (notably the UK parliament voted against participation) and several others were reluctant; Obama ultimately accepted a Russian-brokered diplomatic deal and deferred immediate military action rather than leading a broad allied strike. Saying “a lot of the allies signed on” and that he “backed off at the last minute” oversimplifies and mischaracterizes the actual lack of a willing coalition and the diplomatic resolution that followed.

claim: "We’re seeing now 30 straight months of private-sector job growth, 4.6 million jobs created."
rationale: The statement gives a concrete run length and cumulative job total but omits a date, so it cannot be confirmed as universally true. U.S. private‑sector job gains are reported month‑by‑month by the BLS and the length of any consecutive growth streak and the cumulative jobs added depend on the reference month; reported streaks and totals around 30 months and 4.6 million vary by the snapshot used. Without a specific time point this claim is not verifiable as presented.

claim: "The Florida Legislature has not filed a lawsuit to fight Amendments 5 and 6."
rationale: I cannot confirm that the Florida Legislature filed a lawsuit to challenge Amendments 5 and 6; through my last update there were no widely reported cases brought by the Legislature itself against those amendments. Because I lack a specific date or year for which “Amendments 5 and 6” are meant, and because lawsuits could be brought after my cutoff, the statement as absolute is likely incorrect or at least unverifiable.

claim: Says five studies show his tax plan can cut rates and still bring the same revenue without raising taxes on the middle class.
rationale: The statement is not supported by the public record: there is no consensus of five credible studies showing a tax-cut plan can maintain the same revenue without raising middle-class taxes. Analyses that claim revenue neutrality typically rely on optimistic growth assumptions or unspecified modeling choices, while independent budget analysts generally find comparable rate cuts would lower revenue or require offsetting base-broadening that can affect middle‑class taxpayers. Because the claim lacks named, peer‑reviewed studies and contradicts standard independent estimates, it is not validated.

claim: "Georgia’s civil forfeiture laws are among the worst in the country and the very worst in the South."
rationale: This statement overgeneralizes. Georgia has been criticized for permissive civil forfeiture practices and has ranked poorly in some advocacy-group reports, but rankings vary by source and year and several other Southern states have statutory features that are as bad or worse. There is no consistent, authoritative consensus that Georgia is definitively the single worst in the South across all metrics and timeframes.

claim: "Just 400 Americans -- 400 -- have more wealth than half of all Americans combined."
rationale: Multiple independent analyses comparing the combined net worth of the Forbes 400 (the 400 richest Americans) to the bottom 50% of U.S. households have found the Forbes 400’s wealth exceeds that of the bottom half of Americans. This comparison, using Forbes’ estimates for the richest 400 and Federal Reserve/Survey of Consumer Finances data for the distribution of household wealth, has been reported repeatedly in recent years and was widely documented around 2016–2020.

claim: "The Cleveland police has issued a stand down order to officers."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or official statement from the Cleveland Division of Police or major news outlets indicating the department issued a blanket “stand down” order to officers. Claims like this have circulated on social media in the past but were not substantiated by press releases or local reporting. Without a specific time or source the assertion appears to be unverified and likely false.

claim: "Foster children are disproportionately victims of identity theft."
rationale: Multiple investigative reports, state child-welfare audits, and research by child-welfare advocates indicate foster children face higher rates of identity misuse than the general child population. Factors such as frequent placement changes, multiple caregivers, weak recordkeeping, and delayed credit monitoring create elevated vulnerability, though precise national prevalence estimates are limited.

claim: Says with his guilty impeachment vote, Senator Mitt Romney "could be removed from office."
rationale: A senator voting “guilty” in an impeachment trial does not trigger removal of that senator. The Senate can expel one of its own members only by a two‑thirds vote, and removal via impeachment applies to the person who was impeached and convicted, not to senators who vote. Expelling a senator solely for how they voted would be unprecedented and would raise serious constitutional and legal protections for legislative acts.

claim: "You've seen where we're now going from a $700 million surplus to getting into the next biennium with almost a $750 million deficit."
rationale: The claim gives specific budget figures but provides no jurisdiction, fiscal year, or source, so the numbers cannot be independently verified as stated. Budget surpluses/deficits are highly specific to a particular government and biennium; without that context the statement is not a verifiable fact. Because of the missing details, I treat the assertion as unsubstantiated.

claim: "We spend less than 2 percent more every year. That is the lowest increase in spending since they have been keeping numbers."
rationale: The claim is too vague and likely incorrect as stated: it does not identify which entity (“we”), what spending (total government spending, discretionary, defense, etc.), or the time period, and historical spending increases have varied widely and often exceeded 2%. Without precise definition and supporting data, the assertion that annual spending growth is under 2% and is the lowest since records began cannot be verified and is unlikely to be true.

claim: "The Democrat(ic) position on abortion is now so extreme that they don’t mind executing babies AFTER birth."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Democratic Party or mainstream Democratic officials endorse killing infants after they are born. Democratic platforms and officials support legal access to abortion (terminating pregnancies) within laws and medical guidelines, but U.S. law and medical ethics prohibit infanticide and homicide of born children. Claims that Democrats ‘don’t mind executing babies after birth’ misrepresent abortion policy and conflate fetal termination with post-birth killing.

claim: "Moscow was engulfed in flames" after a giant explosion.
rationale: There are no credible reports that the entire city of Moscow was "engulfed in flames" after any recent explosion; major news outlets and emergency services would document a city‑wide conflagration. Past large explosions in Moscow have produced localized damage and fires, not the entire metropolis being ablaze, so the claim is hyperbolic or misleading without specific corroboration.

claim: The effort to recall California Gov. Gavin Newsom is "a coup."
rationale: Calling the recall effort "a coup" is inaccurate as a factual description. The California recall is a constitutionally authorized, legal electoral process that requires collecting validated signatures and a statewide vote, not an extra-legal seizure of government power; while critics may describe its political intent as illegitimate, that is an opinion, not a literal coup.

claim: "I have no financial interests in Saudi Arabia."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because the speaker is unnamed and financial ties can be indirect (e.g., investments, trusts, pension funds, or corporate holdings) and typically require documentary evidence to disprove. Without access to the individual's financial disclosures, tax records, or other authoritative attestations, one cannot confirm the absence of any Saudi-related financial interests. Therefore the claim should not be accepted as factual without supporting evidence.

claim: "Over 130 legislators in this chamber have endorsed legislation that would bankrupt our nation by providing free taxpayer-funded health care to millions of illegal aliens, forcing taxpayers to subsidize free care for anyone in the world who unlawfully crosses our borders."
rationale: The claim mixes several unsupported assertions and hyperbole. There is no verifiable, specific bill widely endorsed by over 130 members of a chamber that universally provides free, unlimited taxpayer-funded health care to “millions of illegal aliens” and has been scored as bankrupting the nation; most immigrant-health proposals are limited in scope (e.g., emergency care, certain children or pregnant women) and require CBO scoring to estimate costs. The statement appears to conflate endorsements, broad media rhetoric, and inflammatory language rather than documented legislative text and budget analyses.

claim: Microsoft and Bill Gates created a 1999 video game called "Omikron."
rationale: The 1999 game Omikron (full title Omikron: The Nomad Soul) was developed by the French studio Quantic Dream and directed by David Cage, and published by companies such as Eidos; it was not created by Microsoft or Bill Gates. While Microsoft has published or distributed many PC titles, neither Bill Gates nor Microsoft are credited as the creators of Omikron.

claim: "Actor Tom Hanks has passed away age 63."
rationale: This claim is false. Tom Hanks is alive; he was born July 9, 1956 (making him older than 63) and there have been no credible reports of his death. The assertion that he 'has passed away age 63' contradicts widely available biographical and news information.

claim: Says Novak Djokovic said of Simone Biles: "Pressure is a privilege, my friend. ...If you are aiming to be at the top of the game you better start learning how to deal with pressure…"
rationale: There is no reliable public record or reputable news coverage showing Novak Djokovic saying this line about Simone Biles. Coverage of Biles' withdrawal from competition in 2021 documents many public reactions and Djokovic's comments were generally supportive/neutral; the specific quoted admonition appears fabricated or misattributed. Given lack of sourcing, the claim is not supported.

claim: When President Barack Obama said ISIS, or ISIL, was contained, he "was responding very specifically to the geographic expansion of ISIL in Iraq and Syria."
rationale: Contemporaneous transcripts and fact-checks show Obama used the word “contained” in the context of ISIL’s territorial expansion, noting U.S.-led coalition action had halted further geographic gains in Iraq and Syria. His remark was about stopping the group’s territorial growth, not a claim that ISIL was defeated or wholly neutralized.

claim: Olive Garden employees are allowed to wear Black Lives Matter masks "but NOT the American flag."
rationale: There is no verifiable corporate-wide Olive Garden (Darden) policy showing employees were explicitly allowed to wear Black Lives Matter masks while being forbidden from wearing American-flag masks. Reporting and fact-checks around this claim found no official memo that singled out BLM as permitted and the American flag as prohibited; mask and dress-code rules have varied by location and over time. The claim appears to conflate or misrepresent local franchise decisions or social-media anecdotes as a blanket company policy.

claim: Bernie Sanders’s plan is "to raise your taxes to 90 percent."
rationale: Bernie Sanders has not advocated raising people’s taxes to 90%. His proposals raise taxes on high-income households and corporations to fund programs like Medicare for All, but even proposed marginal or effective rates were far below 90% and targeted at top earners, not the general public.

claim: Schools stopped teaching children cursive so they wouldn’t be able to read the U.S. Constitution and other historical documents.
rationale: There is no evidence that schools stopped teaching cursive as a deliberate effort to prevent students from reading the U.S. Constitution or other historical documents. The decline of cursive instruction is better explained by shifts in curriculum priorities (e.g., emphasis on keyboarding and standardized-testable skills), adoption of Common Core standards that did not require cursive, and practical classroom time constraints. Many districts still teach cursive, and historical documents are commonly provided as printed transcriptions or taught alongside handwriting lessons.

claim: Dan Patrick "changed his name from Danny Goeb to hide from" his "debts."
rationale: This is false. Public biographical records show Dan Patrick was born Dannie/Dannie Goeb and later adopted the name “Dan Patrick” as a professional/branding name for his broadcasting career; there is no credible evidence that he changed his name to evade debts or creditors. Reporting and his own biographies link the name change to his media career rather than to hiding financial obligations.

claim: Republicans extended unemployment insurance under President Bush "when he asked to extend unemployment insurance."
rationale: The claim is too broad and ambiguous. While Republican-controlled Congresses did approve some extensions of unemployment benefits during George W. Bush’s presidency, those votes were case-by-case, often bipartisan, and depended on the specific program and year; presenting it as a simple rule that “Republicans extended unemployment insurance when he asked” is misleading without a specific date or bill.

claim: "The unemployment rate for Wisconsin workers has reached historic lows. It’s never been this low before, ever, ever, ever."
rationale: This absolute claim is incorrect: Wisconsin's state unemployment rate has hit similarly low levels in earlier periods. Historical BLS state-level data show prior troughs (for example in the late 1990s and around 2018–2019), so saying it has 'never been this low ever' is inaccurate without a specific numeric and historical qualifier.

claim: Says Oregon’s highest income tax bracket included anyone making more than $250,000 in 2012 before the state expanded its upper bracket to include "anyone making more than $125,000."
rationale: False — the statement misstates Oregon’s 2012 bracket structure. Oregon’s top marginal rate in that period did not simply start only above $250,000 and then was later expanded to >$125,000; thresholds and rates have differed by filing status and specific legislative changes adjusted brackets and rates rather than a single one-time switch from $250k to $125k.

claim: "In 2009, Jim Doyle and the Democrats rushed through a budget repair bill with billions in tax increases and held no public hearings."
rationale: This statement is inaccurate. The highly publicized rushed "budget repair bill" controversy (with claims about limited hearings) involved Governor Scott Walker in 2011, not Jim Doyle in 2009. Doyle's 2009 budget proposals went through the regular legislative process and were not a single, no-hearing "budget repair bill" imposing billions in new taxes as described.

claim: European allies "pay us $2.5 billion a year to keep our forces there. It would cost us more money to bring the troops home than to keep them in Europe."
rationale: Public accounting does not support the precise claim that European allies pay the U.S. $2.5 billion annually specifically to keep U.S. forces in Europe; allies do provide some host-nation support and NATO common funding, but these reimbursements are limited and recorded differently. The assertion that it would cost more to bring troops home than to keep them in Europe is also unproven—the one-time relocation and base-closure costs can be substantial, but long-term savings from redeployment and reduced forward-stationing expenses could outweigh those costs depending on assumptions. Because the statement bundles different funding lines and presents a decisive cost-comparison without documented evidence, it is not supported as stated.

claim: John McCain says he never supported the privatization of Social Security, even though video shows he did.
rationale: During the 2008 campaign McCain publicly insisted he had not supported privatizing Social Security, yet archival video and interviews from earlier years show him endorsing private personal retirement accounts and allowing younger workers to invest part of payroll taxes in private accounts. That contrast between his later denials and prior recorded statements supports the claim.

claim: "Bikers show up to The Walter Reed Hospital to pray for President Trump."
rationale: Multiple contemporary news reports documented supporters — including motorcyclists/bikers — gathering outside Walter Reed National Military Medical Center to show support and pray for President Trump during his October 2020 hospitalization for COVID-19. While not every individual there may have been praying, the presence of bikers participating in prayers or vigils at the site was reported.

claim: Joe Biden’s 100-day approval rating "is the lowest in American history."
rationale: This claim is false. While Joe Biden’s 100-day approval was low relative to some recent presidents, historical polling (Gallup and other national trackers dating back to the 1930s–1940s) shows earlier presidents—e.g., Harry Truman—had lower measured approval levels at comparable early points in their terms. Approval estimates also vary by pollster and precise timing, so a blanket “lowest in American history” assertion is not supported by the available polling record.

claim: Says Section 1325 of U.S. immigration law was "put into place in 1929, by a segregationist."
rationale: The misdemeanor unlawful-entry provision now codified at 8 U.S.C. § 1325 has roots in federal immigration penalties enacted in 1929, so the date claim has some basis. However, it was enacted by Congress as part of broader immigration legislation and cannot be reliably attributed as having been “put into place by a segregationist” — there is no clear evidence that a single named segregationist authored or uniquely drove that statutory provision. The attribution to a specific segregationist is therefore misleading.

claim: "In fact, the data coming in from some states that have legalized marijuana is that they actually see a decrease in use over time, particularly among young people."
rationale: Multiple peer-reviewed state-level analyses and national youth surveys have reported stable or declining marijuana use among adolescents in several states after legalization, so the statement that some states see decreases—particularly among young people—is supported. However, effects are heterogeneous across states, time periods, and measures, and causation is not uniformly established.

claim: "Heidi Cruz, Ted’s wife, is managing director of Goldman Sachs. They oversee the Texas utilities."
rationale: The claim mixes a partial truth with a falsehood. Heidi Cruz has held senior roles at Goldman Sachs (including a managing-director title in the past), but neither she nor Ted Cruz — nor Goldman Sachs as an institution — “oversee the Texas utilities.” Regulation and oversight of Texas electric utilities is handled by state regulators and grid operators, not by the Cruzes or a private bank.

claim: "A new poll shows 62 percent support the president's plan to reform health care. That means ... letting you choose between keeping the private insurance you have and a public health insurance plan."
rationale: The statement combines an unattributed poll result with an asserted policy consequence without verifiable sourcing. Poll percentages depend on the specific survey and question wording, and multiple presidential health‑care proposals differ in whether they include a public option or allow keeping existing private coverage. Because the claim provides no source and conflates separate factual claims, it cannot be treated as true as stated.

claim: North Korea’s missiles are "not going to have a capability to reach the United States anytime real soon."
rationale: This claim is incorrect because North Korea has tested intercontinental-range missiles (e.g., Hwasong-14 and Hwasong-15 in 2017 and larger ICBM-class tests thereafter) that analysts judge can reach parts of the continental United States in principle. While uncertainties remain about operational reliability, re-entry vehicle survivability, and deployed operational forces, the country already demonstrated the basic range capability, so saying it will "not" have the capability anytime soon is false.

claim: "When President Obama landed in Cuba on Air Force One, no leader was there, nobody, to greet him -- perhaps an incident without precedent in the long and prestigious history of Air Force One."
rationale: This is inaccurate: when President Obama arrived in Havana in March 2016 he was met at the airport by Cuban officials (including Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez), though Cuban President Raúl Castro did not personally meet him on the tarmac and instead hosted a later meeting. Furthermore, it is not unprecedented for a head of state to not meet a visiting leader at the plane — so the claim that “nobody” greeted him and that it was without precedent is false.

claim: Georgia has "a dropout rate that’s higher" than Alabama's.
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because high-school "dropout rate" can mean different measures and varies by year. Recent federal and state education statistics do not consistently show Georgia with a higher dropout rate than Alabama; in many common measures Alabama's rate is equal or higher. Without a specified year and definition the assertion is unsupported.

claim: Says NASCAR "bans the confederate flag but FORCES all their drivers to do Muslim prayer."
rationale: NASCAR did prohibit display of the Confederate flag at its events in June 2020, but there is no evidence that NASCAR forces drivers to perform Muslim prayers. Drivers are independent contractors and there is no published policy or credible reporting indicating NASCAR requires any religious observance. The claim conflates a factual ban with an unsupported and implausible allegation about forced religious practice.

claim: Says "we brought crime rate down by 30 percent" when he was mayor of Dallas.
rationale: The claim as framed is unverifiable because it does not name which mayor or the time period; no clear evidence that any recent Dallas mayor publicly achieved and documented a 30% overall crime-rate reduction attributable to their tenure. Dallas crime statistics have fluctuated year to year and vary by category (violent vs. property), and major declines of 30% would be notable and sourced. Without a specific person, date range, and data source, the assertion cannot be confirmed and is therefore treated as false.

claim: "Half of all hospitalized seniors are suffering from malnutrition so severe that it either caused their illness or it prevents them from getting better."
rationale: This statement overreaches. While malnutrition or risk of malnutrition is common among hospitalized older adults, prevalence estimates vary widely by setting and screening method and are generally not established as "half" universally, nor is it routinely proven that malnutrition was the cause of admission or definitively prevents recovery in 50% of cases. The claim conflates prevalence, severity, and causation in a way not supported by typical clinical evidence.

claim: Says Donald Trump’s "Make America Great Again" hats were made in China.
rationale: Contemporaneous reporting showed that at least some of Donald Trump’s early 'Make America Great Again' hats were manufactured in China (and in some cases Mexico). However, production was later shifted for many batches to U.S. manufacturers, so the claim is true for some hats but not universally for all time periods or batches.

claim: Says condoms "used to be tax-exempt here in Texas."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that condoms were broadly tax‑exempt under Texas sales tax law; Texas generally exempts prescription drugs and certain medical devices, while over‑the‑counter items like condoms have typically been taxable. While some states or programs have provided free or untaxed contraceptives, Texas’s routine sales tax rules have not historically listed condoms as a statewide exempt category.

claim: "Governor Carcieri has not been campaigning with me."
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as written because it provides no timeframe, context, or identity for “me.” Public records show former Governor Don Carcieri has made campaign appearances and endorsements for other Republicans during and after his tenure, so a blanket claim that he has never campaigned with a particular person cannot be confirmed and is likely false without more detail. Given the missing specifics, treating the claim as false is the conservative assessment.

claim: Opening the schools "is a local determination, but it’s not a state determination."
rationale: The statement is incorrect as an absolute: authority over school openings varies by jurisdiction. In the U.S. states typically have legal authority over public education and governors or state education agencies can issue binding statewide orders, while local school boards/districts retain operational control in many areas. Therefore opening schools is sometimes a state determination and sometimes a local one, not exclusively local.

claim: Says COVID-19 has killed more North Carolinians in a year than the flu has in 10 years.
rationale: I could not find reliable evidence that one year of COVID-19 deaths in North Carolina exceeded the total influenza deaths for that state over the prior ten years. Typical US flu mortality (12,000–61,000 annually) scaled to North Carolina’s population yields a multi-year flu death total comparable to or larger than the several-thousand COVID deaths North Carolina recorded in a single early pandemic year. The claim therefore lacks support without specific year ranges and verified state counts.

claim: Says the new coronavirus vaccines contain toxic ingredients and are more dangerous than getting COVID-19.
rationale: This claim is false. Authorized COVID-19 vaccines contain ingredients (mRNA or viral vector, lipid nanoparticles, salts, sugars, and in some vaccines approved adjuvants) that are not toxic at the doses used and were shown safe in large clinical trials and extensive post‑authorization surveillance. While very rare adverse events (e.g., myocarditis, VITT) have been documented, the risk of severe outcomes, hospitalization, long COVID, and death from SARS‑CoV‑2 infection is higher for most people than the risk from vaccination.

claim: Says "Claire McCaskill receives the second-most contributions from insurance companies in the entire Senate."
rationale: Campaign finance records and industry contribution summaries (e.g., OpenSecrets/FEC compilations) do not list Claire McCaskill as the single second-largest recipient of insurance-industry donations across the entire Senate. While McCaskill received substantial contributions from insurance companies at times—particularly given her committee assignments—multiple other senators received larger totals, and rankings vary by election cycle and category. The blanket statement that she "receives the second-most" in the entire Senate is not supported without a specific year or dataset.

claim: Mitt Romney previously believed "that abortion should be safe and legal in this country." Now he is "prolife."
rationale: Mitt Romney has publicly shifted on abortion: in earlier campaigns he described himself as supporting legal abortion (including saying it should be 'safe and legal'), while in later years he has identified as pro‑life and campaigned on restricting abortion. The change in his stated position is well documented across multiple election cycles.

claim: "1 in 4 Rhode Islanders under the age of 65 does not have health insurance."
rationale: A 25% uninsured rate for Rhode Islanders under 65 is much higher than official estimates. Census Bureau/ACS and state health data show Rhode Island's uninsured share among nonelderly residents has been in the single digits in recent years, not one in four. Medicaid expansion and ACA marketplace coverage have kept the state's under‑65 uninsured rate well below 25%.

claim: There are nanoparticles in the COVID-19 vaccine that will help people "locate you" via 5G networks.
rationale: Authorized COVID-19 vaccines do not contain tracking nanoparticles designed to be located by 5G networks. Vaccine ingredient lists and regulatory filings show components such as mRNA or viral proteins, lipids, salts and sugars, not radio-responsive tracking particles, and there is no plausible physics or infrastructure by which passive particles in a body could be tracked by 5G cellular networks. Independent scientific and regulatory sources have repeatedly debunked claims that vaccines enable geolocation via 5G.

claim: The United States' southern border is "basically open" and is "a super spreader event."
rationale: The claim mixes a subjective characterization with an epidemiological assertion that is not supported by available evidence. The U.S. southern border has substantial controls, processing, and expulsions (apprehensions, Title 42/other policies, deportations) and is not objectively "open" in the sense of unrestricted entry; migration flows have varied over time. Public-health data and CDC reporting did not identify border crossings or migrants as a primary driver of nationwide COVID-19 surges or as a documented "super spreader event."

claim: "Update: van full of illegals caught voting at multiple Alabama polling locations."
rationale: There is no credible, independently verified evidence that a van full of noncitizens was caught voting at multiple Alabama polling locations. Local election officials, law enforcement, and contemporary fact-checking organizations found no records or prosecutions supporting the viral claim, which appears to be a social-media rumor. Mass noncitizen voting would have produced verifiable official documentation and reports, which are absent.

claim: Says "Ruth Bader Ginsburg was nominated and confirmed 43 days before an election."
rationale: False. Ruth Bader Ginsburg was nominated by President Bill Clinton on June 14, 1993 and confirmed by the Senate on August 3, 1993 — dates that are not 43 days before any federal general election (the next major federal election was November 1994). The claim likely confuses different timing (for example, Ginsburg’s death in 2020 was 46 days before that year’s election) or conflates other justices’ timelines.

claim: "Expanding Medicaid, which if we had done at the beginning of the Abbott administration, would have brought in $100 billion to this state's economy."
rationale: The statement is a specific counterfactual claiming a $100 billion economic gain from expanding Medicaid at the start of the Abbott administration; no authoritative source confirms that exact figure as a guaranteed outcome. Estimates of Medicaid expansion’s fiscal and economic impact vary widely depending on the time period, whether one counts gross federal dollars or net state economic activity, and assumptions about crowd-out and state costs, so the claim as a definitive fact is unsupported.

claim: Says Steve Chabot "voted to strip insurance protections for pre-existing conditions."
rationale: Steve Chabot voted in favor of Republican measures (notably the 2017 House American Health Care Act) that would have allowed states to waive key Affordable Care Act rules and permit insurers to charge or deny coverage based on preexisting condition-related criteria in many circumstances. Those votes were widely characterized as removing or weakening federal protections for people with preexisting conditions.

claim: Says Facebook is now a "public entity" that will be able to "use your photos" and "information" unless you post a statement declining your permission.
rationale: This is false. Facebook (now Meta) being a publicly traded company does not make it a 'public entity' that can automatically take rights to use your photos; use of content is governed by the platform's Terms of Service and Privacy Policy and by the consent you gave when signing up. Posting a status saying you decline permission does not supersede those agreements or change the legal relationship, and such 'post to retain rights' warnings are a long-running hoax.

claim: "Oklahoma 100% coronavirus test rate after Trump Tulsa rally."
rationale: The claim that Oklahoma had a 100% coronavirus test rate after the Trump Tulsa rally is false. No credible public-health data or state reporting showed that every test came back positive; reported COVID-19 positivity in Oklahoma remained far below 100% and while cases rose in some areas after the event, they were not universal. Such an absolute claim would have been widely reported by health authorities and media but was not.

claim: "We adopted the modern Social Security system at a time when the average person died before they were old enough to get Social Security."
rationale: The Social Security Act establishing retirement benefits at age 65 was adopted in 1935, and U.S. life expectancy at birth in the 1930s was below 65 (roughly around 60–63 years), so the average person by that measure would not live to 65. However, this statement is commonly misleading because life expectancy at birth is lowered by high infant and early-childhood mortality; conditional life expectancy for adults who survived to older ages was higher and many did reach 65.

claim: Former President Donald Trump "is fluent in Japanese."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Donald Trump speaks Japanese fluently. Public records, news coverage, and his diplomatic interactions show he speaks English as his native language, has used interpreters with Japanese leaders, and at most uses a few Japanese words or greetings in public — which does not constitute fluency.

claim: Says Rep. Justin Amash "votes more with the Democrats than with the Republicans."
rationale: Overall roll-call records and party-alignment metrics show Justin Amash voted with House Republicans more often than with Democrats during his Congressional tenure. He did sometimes side with Democrats on particular issues (civil liberties, oversight), but those exceptions do not make his overall voting record 'more with the Democrats than with the Republicans.'

claim: Says when he was governor, "most of the Democrats" voted for his billion-dollar property-tax cuts, but U.S. Senate rival Tammy Baldwin "voted against it."
rationale: The claim is incorrect or misleading. Tammy Baldwin, as a U.S. Representative (1999–2013) and then U.S. Senator (2013– ), does not vote on Wisconsin state legislation, so she could not have cast a vote on a governor’s state property‑tax cut. In addition, major state property‑tax cuts in Wisconsin were driven primarily by Republican majorities and were not passed with “most” Democrats voting in favor; Democratic state legislators typically opposed Walker-era tax changes.

claim: "They voted for (a border wall) in 2006. Then-Senator Obama voted for it. Sen. Schumer voted for it. Sen. Clinton voted for it."
rationale: The statement refers to the 2006 Secure Fence Act (H.R.6061), which authorized construction of hundreds of miles of border fencing. Senators Hillary Clinton and Charles Schumer voted for the measure, and then-Senator Barack Obama also supported the bill. While the law funded physical barriers, it was for fence construction and related enforcement measures rather than the continuous concrete 'Trump-style' wall often implied.

claim: "The average student will be spending $1,700 to $1,800 more during the life of their loan because of this surcharge."
rationale: The statement lacks critical context (the specific surcharge rate, which loan program, and assumptions about average loan balance, interest rate and repayment term), so it cannot be universally true that the average student will pay exactly $1,700–$1,800 more. The lifetime extra cost from a surcharge depends on principal, interest, term, and whether the charge compounds; under some specific assumptions that range might be plausible, but it is not a general fact for all students.

claim: "If you printed a $1 bill for the entirety of the $14.1 trillion national debt, the resulting pile of money would weigh more than 136 aircraft carriers."
rationale: A US banknote weighs about 1 gram, so $14.1 trillion in $1 bills would weigh roughly 14.1 billion kilograms. A Nimitz‑class aircraft carrier’s full-load displacement is about 100,000 long tons (~1.02×10^8 kg), so 14.1 billion kg is roughly 139 carriers — exceeding 136. Thus the claim is correct within those common assumptions.

claim: Says President Donald Trump is one of "only three people that won the Ellis Island Award for their work within the black community."
rationale: The claim is not supported by evidence. The Ellis Island Medal of Honor (Ellis Island Honors Society) has honored many individuals across diverse communities and the organization does not list only three winners 'for their work within the black community.' There is no credible record showing Donald Trump is uniquely one of three recipients honored specifically for work within the Black community, so the statement is misleading or false.

claim: "More than a million Californians" do not have "clean water to bathe in or drink."
