rationale: There are no credible contemporaneous news reports or official records documenting that any former North Carolina elections board chairman physically tried to remove a cancer-stricken woman from her hospital bed to force testimony. Such an extreme act would have generated clear public records and wide news coverage; reporting about contested board hearings has not substantiated this allegation. The claim appears to be a partisan or sensationalized assertion rather than a documented factual event.

claim: "Hair stylists are required to undergo more government scrutiny than foreclosure consultants."
rationale: Most U.S. states require hair stylists/cosmetologists to complete substantial mandated training hours, pass state exams, and hold licenses enforced by state cosmetology boards. Rules for 'foreclosure consultants' are uneven across jurisdictions and typically consist of consumer-protection restrictions, registration or bonding in some states rather than standardized training and licensure, so overall stylists face more consistent government scrutiny.

claim: Says that Minnesota Democratic congressional candidate Dean Phillips doesn’t offer health insurance for his employees.
rationale: False. Public reporting and fact-checks found that Dean Phillips’s company provided employer-sponsored health insurance to its full-time employees, so the blanket claim that he offered no health insurance is incorrect. The claim appears to conflate full-time and part-time staffing or refer to different time periods to create a misleading impression.

claim: "More than one in five of veterans aged 20 to 24 can’t find a job to support their family or to ease the transition to civilian life."
rationale: This specific claim is not supported by broadly reported labor statistics. BLS and other labor data show veteran unemployment for the 20–24 age group has generally been below 20% in most recent years, and the claim appears to conflate general unemployment with a subjective survey response about not finding a job that 'supports their family' or 'eases transition.' Without a timeframe or source, the statement overstates the typical measured rate.

claim: Says former Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan said that "if the workers are more insecure, that's very healthy for the society" because "they'll serve the masters gladly and passively."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reliable primary source showing Alan Greenspan ever made this statement; the line circulates on social media and partisan sites but cannot be traced to any Greenspan speech, interview, book or archived record. Fact-checking organizations and searches of contemporary news and transcript archives find no record of Greenspan uttering those words, making the attribution highly unlikely and essentially fabricated.

claim: "In South Dakota, I’m putting prayer back in our schools."
rationale: The claim implies that the state can reintroduce official, school‑sponsored prayer; under longstanding U.S. Supreme Court precedent public schools cannot lead or endorse prayer. While South Dakota lawmakers or the governor can protect or permit voluntary, student‑led prayer or invocations at certain events, there is no lawful mechanism for the state to constitutionally ‘put prayer back’ as an official, school‑led activity. The statement is therefore misleading as an absolute factual claim.

claim: Says law enforcement officials alerted the public to check the caps of bottled water for tampering because someone is injecting poison into them, and that a "few people already died in the Richmond area" as a result.
rationale: This claim is false. Local law enforcement agencies and news organizations in the Richmond area have not issued verified warnings that someone was injecting poison into bottled-water caps or that multiple people had died as a result; fact-checkers found the story to be a viral hoax and police denied such incidents. There is no credible evidence or official reports supporting the alleged deaths or public alert described.

claim: "Many of the countries in question (in Trump’s travel ban) don't even have a U.S. embassy there to help us vet."
rationale: The original Trump travel bans covered countries such as Iran, Syria, Libya, Yemen and Somalia — several of which did not have an operational U.S. embassy or consulate on the ground at the time (e.g., Iran and Syria have had no U.S. embassy for decades; Libya, Yemen and parts of Somalia had no functioning U.S. diplomatic missions post-conflict). Some listed countries (notably Iraq) did have U.S. embassies, so the statement that “many” lacked embassies is accurate but not universal. Embassy presence also changed over time and across later versions of the policy.

claim: "Embalmers finding ‘strange clots’ in jabbed people"
rationale: Reports that embalmers are routinely finding unique or vaccine-specific “strange clots” in vaccinated people are anecdotal and not supported by systematic pathology evidence. Forensic pathologists and coroners note that postmortem clots can look unusual and are commonly seen regardless of vaccination status, and no peer-reviewed studies have shown a distinct clotting pattern caused by COVID vaccines in embalmed bodies. Therefore the broad claim is not established as fact.

claim: "The only time government employment has gone down during a recession has been under me."
rationale: This is false. Historical data show government employment has declined in prior recessions — for example, the 2007–2009 Great Recession saw substantial state and local government job losses, and the 2020 COVID recession also produced declines in government payrolls — so it is not true that the only time government employment fell during a recession was under the speaker.

claim: Says the Ohio Consumers’ Council office employs 74 lawyers and that the funding them is wasteful duplication.
rationale: The claim is inaccurate: the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel (the state office that represents utility consumers) is a relatively small state agency and does not employ 74 in-house lawyers. The second part of the statement—that funding them is “wasteful duplication”—is a value judgment, not an objective fact, and depends on policy priorities and comparison to other legal resources.

claim: Says Michele Bachmann said on Fox News, "This country could use a president like Benjamin Franklin again."
rationale: I could not find reliable evidence that Michele Bachmann said that exact line on Fox News. While Bachmann has invoked founding-era figures in speeches and interviews, no credible transcript or major fact-checking outlet attributes the precise quote “This country could use a president like Benjamin Franklin again” to her on Fox News, suggesting the claim is a misattribution or paraphrase.

claim: Says Donald Trump's first 17 Cabinet appointments "have a net worth of more than a third of America."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and unsupported as stated: it gives no clear definition of “a third of America” (does that mean one-third of people, one-third of households, or one-third of national wealth?) and no verifiable source for the comparison. Public analyses at the time noted the combined wealth of Trump’s early cabinet was large, but whether it exceeds the combined net worth of a specified ‘third’ of Americans depends entirely on the metric and population slice chosen, so the blanket statement is misleading and not reliably true. Given the ambiguity and lack of precise evidence, the claim cannot be accepted as factual.

claim: Colorado saw "increased incidents of emergency room visits by young people" and "increased incidents of driving while under the influence of marijuana" following the legalization of recreational pot.
rationale: Multiple state reports and peer-reviewed studies documented increases in cannabis-related emergency department visits and pediatric poison-control exposures in Colorado after recreational legalization and commercialization. Traffic-safety data from Colorado also show increases in drivers testing positive for THC and in marijuana-involved fatal crashes during the post-legalization period, though testing positive does not always prove impairment.

claim: "Congressman Cicilline, when he was the mayor of Providence, espoused a sanctuary city."
rationale: There is no clear, widely reported evidence that David Cicilline formally advocated that Providence become a ‘sanctuary city’ while he was mayor (2003–2011). He pursued immigrant-friendly outreach and community policing, but Providence did not adopt a high-profile sanctuary-city designation tied directly to Cicilline’s mayoral actions. The claim conflates general pro-immigrant measures with an explicit sanctuary-city endorsement.

claim: Says unlike Tim Kaine, who "invested" in education, Indiana Gov. Mike Pence "slashed education funding."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Tim Kaine as Virginia governor did increase education spending and expanded pre‑K and teacher pay, but Indiana Gov. Mike Pence’s record is mixed — he supported budget and policy changes (including voucher expansion and some line‑item reductions) and faced cuts in certain programs, yet did not enact a single across‑the‑board ‘slashing’ of all education funding; K‑12 funding levels under Pence varied by year and program. Framing Pence as having simply ‘slashed education funding’ without context overstates and simplifies the budgetary record.

claim: "BREAKING: Trump family donates $1 billion to wall fund."
rationale: There are no credible reports, public filings, or major news sources confirming a $1 billion donation from the Trump family to any 'wall fund.' Such a large, high-profile donation would have been widely reported and documented; available information and past reporting do not support this claim. The phrasing 'BREAKING' and lack of specifics match patterns of a viral falsehood or hoax.

claim: "Statistics show one male cat can father 420,000 kittens in five years."
rationale: This is implausible. 420,000 kittens in five years equals 84,000 kittens per year; at ~4 kittens per litter that would require about 21,000 successful litters per year (~57 new litters per day), meaning a male would need to impregnate dozens of different females every single day. Female cats have ~63‑day gestation, limited estrus cycles, and population/logistical limits make that rate biologically and practically impossible.

claim: "Gavin Newsom reportedly intervened at the request of Nancy Pelosi and directly ordered the California Highway Patrol to drop all charges" against Paul Pelosi for his DUI arrest.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Gov. Gavin Newsom intervened at Nancy Pelosi’s request to order the California Highway Patrol to drop all charges against Paul Pelosi. Official statements and public reporting indicate the CHP and Newsom’s office denied any such intervention, and the handling of the incident followed routine law-enforcement investigation and prosecutor review.

claim: If sea levels rise six feet due to climate change, Waterplace Park in Providence and Wickford village would be swamped
rationale: Both Waterplace Park (a low‑lying riverside park in downtown Providence at roughly sea level) and Wickford village (a historic waterfront village on Narragansett Bay) sit at low elevations susceptible to sea level rise. A sustained 6‑foot rise would inundate many tidal and waterfront areas in Rhode Island, and coastal flood‑mapping by state planners shows these kinds of locations would be flooded or frequently overtopped under that scenario.

claim: "Biden took down Dr. Seuss and Mr. Potato Head."
rationale: The removals/changes were decisions by private companies, not actions taken by President Biden. In 2021 Dr. Seuss Enterprises ceased publication of six titles for racist imagery, and Hasbro rebranded Mr. Potato Head to 'Potato Head' — both corporate choices rather than directives from Biden or his administration.

claim: "In the last year, Wisconsin ranked third in Midwest job growth."
rationale: The claim is unverified because it does not specify the exact 12‑month period or whether it means percent growth or absolute job gains; state job‑growth rankings change month-to-month and year-to-year. Public labor data (BLS/state workforce reports) for recent years show varying placements for Wisconsin in Midwest job growth and do not consistently place it third across standard annual measures, so the blanket statement is unsupported without a precise timeframe and metric.

claim: Video shows helicopters in Ukraine "being picked off in ambush - Short range air-to-air missile"
rationale: The claim is unproven: a raw video alone cannot reliably show that helicopters in Ukraine were ‘picked off’ specifically by a short-range air-to-air missile. Visual footage typically cannot distinguish between air-to-air missiles and ground-launched MANPADS or other causes, and location/metadata and weapons-expert analysis are required to attribute weapon type and launch source. Absent that verification, the specific assertion is likely a misattribution.

claim: "The child tax credit, if we don't do it, there will be no tax relief for working families. How much tax relief working families get under tax reform is entirely dependent on whether or not we put in place an increase to the child tax credit."
rationale: The claim is false because tax relief for working families can come from many provisions besides the child tax credit (CTC). Changes to tax rates, the standard deduction, the earned income tax credit, payroll-tax rules, or other credits and deductions can all provide relief, so outcomes are not “entirely dependent” on an increase in the CTC. The CTC can be an important factor, but it is not the sole determinant of tax relief under reform.

claim: "Mitt Romney’s pledged to protect (oil companies') record profits – and their billions in special tax breaks, too."
rationale: This claim frames Romney as having explicitly pledged to ‘protect’ oil companies’ record profits and their ‘billions’ in tax breaks. Romney’s campaigns advocated pro‑energy policies—supporting domestic drilling, opposing tax hikes on corporations and resisting elimination of some fossil‑fuel tax preferences—but there is no clear, contemporaneous public pledge in which he promised to shield oil companies’ specific ‘record profits’ or characterized tax breaks in the quoted form. The statement thus overstates and politicizes his policy positions.

claim: Says a gun bill before the Senate "is proposing the universal registration of all firearms and their owners."
rationale: The statement is misleading: publicly discussed Senate gun proposals in recent years have focused on expanded background checks, purchaser licensing, reporting of certain sales, red‑flag measures, or funding for state programs, not creation of a federal, universal registry of every firearm and owner. Without the specific bill text, there is no evidence that a Senate bill currently on its face mandates universal registration of all firearms and their owners.

claim: "Barack Obama has consistently voted against tougher penalties for criminals."
rationale: This claim is false because Obama’s record on criminal penalties is mixed rather than uniformly oppositional. Early in his political career he supported some tougher law-and-order measures, while later as a U.S. senator and president he backed sentencing reforms, clemency actions, and legislation to reduce mandatory minimums. Therefore he did not 'consistently vote against tougher penalties.'

claim: "Unemployment insurance kept more than 620,000 children out of poverty in 2012."
rationale: Government and policy analyses (notably Census Bureau income/poverty tabulations reported and summarized by analysts such as the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities) estimated that unemployment insurance kept roughly 620,000–630,000 children out of poverty in 2012. The claim’s phrase “more than 620,000 children” aligns with those published estimates.

claim: Democratic candidate Jeff Greene "ran for Congress as a California Republican."
rationale: Jeff Greene is a Florida-based businessman who ran for U.S. Senate in Florida as a Democrat (not for Congress in California as a Republican). He has not been a California Republican congressional candidate, so the claim misstates both the office/state and party of his known campaigns.

claim: Says Peter DeFazio votes with Nancy Pelosi 86 percent of the time.
rationale: The claim gives a precise 86% figure but provides no timeframe or source; vote‑alignment percentages vary by year and by the method used to calculate them. Public roll‑call analyses (e.g., FiveThirtyEight/GovTrack style metrics) show DeFazio generally voted with House Democratic leaders frequently, but the exact percentage depends on the period examined and is not reliably demonstrated to be exactly 86% over his entire tenure. Because the claim lacks context and a verifiable source, it is judged false as stated.

claim: "Belarus declares war on Poland."
rationale: There are no credible reports or official announcements that Belarus has declared war on Poland; such an action would be major international news and widely reported. Available information indicates no formal declaration of war or open military conflict between Belarus and Poland.

claim: "There will be several thousand dollars in payments going to families with six-figure incomes who’ve had no income interruption whatsoever."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate as a general statement. Major federal relief programs (e.g., stimulus payments, advance child tax credits) included income thresholds or phaseouts that typically prevented families with six-figure incomes and no interruption from receiving “several thousand dollars,” although narrow exceptions (large numbers of dependents or tax-year mismatches) can produce payments for some higher-income households.

claim: Says Judge Amy Coney Barrett said that "gays have a right to be discriminated against because they are against God’s wishes" and that "white people are God’s chosen ones."
rationale: There is no credible record—transcripts, published writings, or major news reporting—showing Amy Coney Barrett ever said those exact statements endorsing discrimination against gay people or calling white people "God’s chosen ones." While Barrett is a conservative Catholic who has opposed legal recognition of same-sex marriage in some contexts, the explosive quotes in the claim are not documented and appear fabricated or misattributed.

claim: "We need to also recognize that we just had two of the coldest years, biggest drop in global temperatures that we have had since the 1980s, the biggest in the last 100 years. We don't talk about that."
rationale: The claim that the world "just had two of the coldest years" and the "biggest drop in global temperatures" since the 1980s is inconsistent with instrumental global temperature records. Multiple independent datasets show the last decade contains the warmest years on record and there has been no recent, large global-temperature drop of the magnitude described. While year-to-year variability and regional cold spells occur, they do not amount to the claimed global cooling trend.

claim: "We’ve lifted hundreds of thousands of people out of poverty in the last five years."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated because it omits which country or population, which poverty metric, and the exact five-year window, so it cannot be verified as stated. While some governments or programs have plausibly lifted 'hundreds of thousands' out of poverty in specific contexts, publicly reported poverty data (which vary by measure and period) do not universally support this broad, context-free assertion and the statement is therefore misleading as presented.

claim: "More than 27,000 Rhode Island jobs depend on trade with Canada."
rationale: I could not verify a reliable source that specifically states more than 27,000 Rhode Island jobs depend on trade with Canada. Estimates of jobs ‘dependent’ on trade vary widely by year and methodology (direct, indirect, induced effects), so the precise figure is ambiguous without a cited source. Given the lack of corroborating data, the claim cannot be confirmed.

claim: Says Dontre Hamilton, who was killed during a confrontation with a Milwaukee police officer, was "unarmed."
rationale: Reports and official accounts indicate Dontre Hamilton was carrying a small folding pocketknife at the time he was shot by Milwaukee officer Christopher Manney. Because he was in possession of a knife, the blanket statement that he was “unarmed” is incorrect.

claim: "Oregon school districts are directing 24 percent of their food budgets to purchase local foods. That’s the highest percentage in the country."
rationale: I could not verify a reliable source saying Oregon school districts direct 24% of their food budgets to local foods, and the phrasing appears to conflate different metrics (share of districts buying any local food versus share of total food dollars spent on local). National Farm to School surveys report varying measures (percent of districts that purchase local, number of local products) and do not clearly support the specific 24%-of-budget-and-highest-in-country claim without additional context or a year. Given lack of corroborating evidence and likely misinterpretation of available data, the claim is not supported as stated.

claim: Says Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Tammy Baldwin ranks "as the most liberal member of the House."
rationale: Tammy Baldwin was a reliably liberal House member, but historical ideological rankings (DW‑NOMINATE and interest‑group scores like ADA) do not consistently place her as the single most liberal member of the House. Other representatives (e.g., Barbara Lee, Pete Stark, Raúl Grijalva and others) typically score at the ideological extremes more than Baldwin. Thus the blanket claim that she "ranks as the most liberal member of the House" is inaccurate without a specific metric and date.

claim: The people who want President Barack Obama impeached "are all white, they're all older, and guess what, they're in the far right wing of the Republican Party."
rationale: The statement is an absolute generalization that is not true. While calls to impeach President Obama were concentrated among conservative and far-right Republican activists and tended to skew older and white, supporters were not literally all white, all older, nor universally limited to the far right of the GOP. Surveys and public records show variation in age, race, and partisan intensity among those who expressed support for impeachment.

claim: Says David Perdue wants to abolish the U.S. Department of Education, which would cost Georgia schools $1 billion a year and eliminate millions in student loans.
rationale: David Perdue has publicly supported eliminating the U.S. Department of Education, so the first part has a basis in his statements. However, claiming that abolishing the department "would cost Georgia schools $1 billion a year" is a misleading oversimplification because federal education funding is distributed through many programs (and totals vary by program and year), and abolishing the agency would not automatically erase or cancel millions in student loans—those loans are created and governed by federal law and would require Congressional action to cancel. Combining the accurate claim about Perdue's position with the inaccurate and unsupported fiscal and loan consequences makes the overall claim false.

claim: "As of today, no one has the right to film or photograph Mr. Biden as he climbs the flight of stairs. New White House spokesman orders!!?"
rationale: The claim is false. There is no evidence that a White House spokesman issued a blanket order stripping everyone of the right to film or photograph President Biden climbing stairs; U.S. press and public photography rights generally remain protected. While security or restricted-area rules can limit photography in specific locations or times, that is not the same as an across-the-board prohibition announced by the White House spokesman.

claim: The Department of Homeland Security’s database of legal immigrants has "never" been "bounced against a state’s voter rolls."
rationale: The absolute claim that DHS’s legal-immigrant database has "never" been compared to state voter rolls is not supported. DHS operates verification systems (notably the SAVE system) that state agencies can query to confirm immigration or citizenship status, and states have in limited cases used federal immigration checks when verifying voter eligibility. Saying "never" ignores documented mechanisms and instances where state officials have queried federal immigration records for eligibility purposes.

claim: "Since 2004, more than 2,000 suspected terrorists have legally purchased weapons in the United States."
rationale: This claim overstates and misrepresents available data. Independent fact-checkers and government reporting show the 2,000 figure stems from conflating different datasets (name matches to watchlists, queries, or investigative leads) rather than confirmed instances where known or legally adjudicated 'suspected terrorists' legally purchased firearms, and no reliable public data supports >2,000 confirmed legal purchases since 2004.

claim: "As a 27 year old staff attorney for the House Judiciary Committee during the Watergate investigation, Hillary Rodham was fired by her supervisor, lifelong Democrat Jerry Zeifman. When asked why Hillary Rodham was fired, Zeifman said in an interview, ‘Because she was a liar. She was an unethical, dishonest lawyer, she conspired to violate the Constitution, the rules of the House, the rules of the Committee, and the rules of confidentiality.’"
rationale: Multiple contemporary reports and later fact-checks confirm that Jerry Zeifman, a senior counsel associated with the House Judiciary Committee, said he fired Hillary Rodham when she was a 27-year-old committee staff attorney and publicly called her a liar and unethical, using language very similar to the quoted passage. Zeifman made these claims in interviews and letters decades later, and reputable fact-checkers have verified he made those statements. There is dispute about some contextual details and motivations, but the core quoted allegation is attributed to Zeifman himself.

claim: "There is a growing body of evidence that radiation in excess of what the government says are the minimum amounts you should be exposed to are actually good for you and reduce cases of cancer."
rationale: The claim misstates the scientific consensus. Major health and radiation protection bodies and the bulk of epidemiological evidence do not conclude that exposures above regulatory limits are beneficial or reduce cancer; the presumed benefit of low-dose 'hormesis' remains contested and unproven. While a few small or laboratory studies report hormetic responses, they are not sufficient to overturn the prevailing view that increased ionizing radiation generally raises cancer risk.

claim: Says health insurance premiums will rise under Obamacare.
rationale: The claim as stated is overly broad and therefore incorrect. The Affordable Care Act (Obamacare) produced mixed effects: gross premiums in the individual market rose in many places (partly due to guaranteed issue and required benefits), but federal premium tax credits offset costs for most exchange enrollees and employer-sponsored premiums did not uniformly rise because of the law. Empirical and CBO analyses showed varied impacts by market, state, and year rather than a universal premium increase for all people.

claim: "Since President (Donald Trump’s) election, 36,000 jobs have been created in WI."
rationale: The claim is misleading and not supported as stated: it gives a precise total (36,000) without specifying the end date or which employment series is meant. U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics state employment series (total nonfarm payrolls and private payrolls) do not unambiguously show an increase of exactly 36,000 jobs from the date of President Trump's election — reported gains vary by measure and cutoff month and are generally different from the claimed figure. Without a clear time window and job-definition the claim is not accurate.

claim: Says Mitt Romney "paid only 14 percent in taxes — probably less than you."
rationale: During the 2012 campaign Romney repeatedly said his effective federal tax rate was about 14 percent and in interviews and debates made remarks suggesting that was lower than many Americans’ rates. His released tax returns (around 2010–2011) showed an effective federal tax rate in the ~13.9–15% range, which matches the 14% figure he cited.

claim: Donald Trump would "engage in a risky scheme to privatize Social Security."
rationale: The claim is a predictive assertion about what Trump "would" do and there is no clear evidence he planned or attempted a wholesale privatization of Social Security. As president he publicly vowed not to cut Social Security and his administration did not enact a privatization scheme; while some Republicans have proposed partial privatization ideas, those were not enacted or explicitly driven by Trump. Therefore labeling the statement as a factual description of his actions or plans is unsupported.

claim: "Fox News went from 97% reporting to 94% in Virginia. The fraud is so blatant it's not funny anymore."
rationale: The claim offers no specific race, date, or evidence and appears to infer fraud from a change in a reported percentage. Broadcasters' “percent reporting” figures can change when vote tallies, precinct definitions, or denominators are corrected or updated; isolated changes in a displayed percentage do not by themselves prove fraud. I found no verified evidence that Fox News deliberately reduced reporting from 97% to 94% in a way that demonstrates election fraud.

claim: "U.S. military at the White House arresting Congress."
rationale: This claim is false. There are no credible reports or evidence that the U.S. military went to the White House to arrest members of Congress, and such an action would be unprecedented and largely unlawful under U.S. constitutional norms. Domestic use of the armed forces for civilian law enforcement is tightly restricted, and any arrests of federal legislators would have been widely reported by major news outlets.

claim: "When I become the nominee, the Democratic nominee, I will be the only pro-choice candidate on the ballot."
rationale: The statement claims no other pro‑choice candidates would appear on the general‑election ballot if this person is the Democratic nominee. That is unlikely and factually incorrect in general: third‑party and independent candidates (and occasionally major‑party candidates) who qualify for the ballot can and often do hold pro‑choice positions, so a Democratic nominee would not reliably be the only pro‑choice option.

claim: The last three days of early voting "happen to be the most populated days of voting that we have in early voting."
rationale: The claim is presented as a universal fact but voting patterns vary widely by jurisdiction and election. While many jurisdictions do see a surge in early voting in the final days, other places have peak turnout on weekends, specific early voting launch days, or more evenly distributed turnout, so the statement cannot be affirmed generally without locale- and election-specific data.

claim: "For four years, we balanced the budget and paid off $405 billion in debt."
rationale: The U.S. did run four consecutive unified-budget surpluses in FY1998–FY2001 and debt held by the public fell by roughly $400–$450 billion in that period, but the claim as phrased is misleading. It omits that the reduction applies to 'debt held by the public' and that total (gross) federal debt including intragovernmental holdings did not decline by that amount. Without specifying which debt measure is meant, the statement is inaccurate.

claim: The COVID-19 vaccine "will make the common cold/flu extremely lethal."
rationale: The claim is false. COVID-19 vaccines elicit immunity specific to SARS‑CoV‑2 and there is no credible biological mechanism or epidemiological evidence showing they make unrelated respiratory viruses (common cold coronaviruses or seasonal influenza) "extremely lethal." Large clinical trials and population surveillance have not observed increased flu or cold mortality attributable to COVID‑19 vaccination; theoretical concerns like antibody‑dependent enhancement were investigated and not supported by data.

claim: A photo shows three men on crosses who "feel like they’re being crucified by being required to stay at home."
rationale: The claim treats a photo of three people on crosses as evidence they were literally being crucified for staying at home, but there is no verifiable evidence that such a punishment occurred. Photos of people on crosses more commonly come from staged religious reenactments, symbolic protests, or altered/repurposed images rather than actual enforcement of lockdown orders, so the literal interpretation is unsupported.

claim: About 750,000 people die in China each year from auto emissions.
rationale: There is no strong evidence that 750,000 people in China die each year solely from auto (road-transport) emissions. Global Burden of Disease and WHO estimates put total outdoor/ambient PM2.5-related deaths in China on the order of about one to 1.5 million (varying by year and method), and peer-reviewed attribution studies typically assign only a fraction of that burden to road transport (tens to a few hundred thousand at most), not 750,000 by itself.

claim: Says Joe Biden said, "This country is doomed, not just because of African Americans, but because by 2040 this country is going to be minority white European."
rationale: There is no credible record of Joe Biden ever saying this quote; it is inflammatory and inconsistent with his documented public remarks about demographic change. Fact-checkers and public speech archives do not contain this statement, and similar claims have appeared as misattributions or manipulated clips.

claim: The planned expansion of Savannah’s port is a "jobs creating project."
rationale: Major port expansion projects like Savannah’s are routinely described as "jobs-creating" because they generate short-term construction employment and longer-term jobs in cargo handling, logistics, and related services. Official studies and statements from the Georgia Ports Authority and project proponents have projected thousands of construction and ongoing jobs tied to the Savannah harbor/port expansion. While the exact number and net long-term employment effects can be debated, the claim that it is a "jobs creating project" is supported by standard economic impact reasoning and the project's own analyses.

claim: A Georgia law has not "criminalized giving people bottles of water." It pertains to political organizations.
rationale: The Georgia voting law’s provisions that drew criticism restrict the distribution of food and drink by campaigns and organized third parties within specified distances of polling places and to voters in line, rather than creating a blanket criminal prohibition on any person handing a bottle of water to someone. Multiple fact‑checks and summaries of SB 202 noted the law targets organized, paid or coordinated electioneering activity and contains exemptions, rather than criminalizing casual individual assistance.

claim: "The fundraising numbers are in, and our grassroots support is unmatched!"
rationale: The statement is vague and comparative without providing data, timeframe, or competitors. Claims that "fundraising numbers are in" and that grassroots support is "unmatched" require verifiable finance reports and measurable metrics; absent those, the assertion cannot be confirmed and is therefore treated as false.

claim: "More businesses are closing than opening in Virginia today."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated because there is no publicly available real‑time statewide dataset showing that more businesses are closing than opening on a specific day in Virginia. Official statistics on business births and deaths are reported quarterly or annually (e.g., state registries, Census Business Dynamics), and net openings/closings vary by sector and locality, so the statement cannot be verified as true for "today."

claim: A state report’s "projection is that approximately half of public employees" would live outside municipal boundaries in a decade if the state bans local residency requirements.
rationale: The claim presents a specific projection but gives no state, report title, year, or source; I am not aware of any widely circulated state report projecting that about half of public employees would live outside municipal boundaries within a decade if local residency requirements were banned. Empirical studies of residency-rule changes typically show modest shifts in employee residence patterns, not a uniform half of workers leaving municipal limits, so the assertion appears unverified and likely exaggerated or misattributed.

claim: "Much more than 50 percent of parents out there are spankers."
rationale: The claim is too broad and unsupported as stated: prevalence of parents who spank varies widely by country, cohort, and how “spanking” is defined (ever vs currently). While some older surveys and certain populations show a majority have spanked children at some point, more recent national data in many countries show declines and rates not uniformly “much more than 50%.” Without specifying place, time, and definition the blanket assertion is not factually justified.

claim: "This is the first time since Roe was decided in 1973 that a court has granted personhood status to the preborn."
rationale: This is not the first time since Roe (1973) that courts or laws have treated the preborn as legal persons or conferred person-like protections. Since Roe, many state courts and legislatures have recognized fetuses as victims in homicide prosecutions and allowed wrongful-death or related civil claims for unborn children; Congress also passed the Unborn Victims of Violence Act in 2004 recognizing an unborn child as a crime victim. Roe addressed constitutional personhood under the Fourteenth Amendment, but statutory and many judicial rulings since 1973 have granted legal protections to the preborn in various contexts.

claim: "If we keep the minimum wage at the current level, then single-parent families earning the minimum wage at a full-time job will live in poverty in New Jersey."
rationale: As written the claim is overly broad and false in most plausible interpretations. A single parent working full time (about 2,080 hours/year) at New Jersey’s recent minimum-wage levels would typically earn more than the federal poverty guideline for a two-person household, so they would not automatically ‘‘live in poverty.’' Whether a minimum-wage earner falls below the poverty line depends on the exact hourly wage, hours worked, and number of dependents, so the universal if–then statement is incorrect.

claim: "The Obama-Clinton war on coal has cost Michigan over 50,000 jobs."
rationale: The claim greatly overstates Michigan coal employment and misattributes causes. Michigan historically had only a small number of coal-mining and coal-plant jobs (hundreds to low thousands), so a loss of over 50,000 coal-sector jobs in the state is implausible. Broad declines in coal employment nationally and regionally have been driven largely by market forces (cheap natural gas, automation) and long-term trends rather than a discrete "Obama‑Clinton war on coal."

claim: Says North Carolina’s "Democratic Secretary of State" controls the state's elections.
rationale: This is false. In North Carolina, elections are administered by the State Board of Elections and local county boards of elections; the Secretary of State’s office handles business registrations and other administrative matters and is not the agency that controls or runs state elections.

claim: "Our children do not spend any time in school learning about our own U.S. Constitution."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate: U.S. K–12 curricula commonly include instruction on the U.S. Constitution in U.S. history, civics, and government classes across elementary, middle, and high school levels. While the amount and depth of instruction vary by state, district, and school, it is not true that children universally spend no time learning about the Constitution.

claim: Voters in Maricopa County, Ariz., were forced to vote using Sharpie pens that aren’t read by voting machines.
rationale: This claim is false. Maricopa County did distribute Sharpie pens at many polling locations in 2020 but voters were not forced to use them, and county officials and election experts confirmed that optical ballot scanners can and did read ballots marked with Sharpie ink. Post-election audits and reviews in Arizona found no evidence that Sharpies caused widespread unreadable ballots or changed vote totals; a small number of ballots with bleed-through would be manually reviewed if needed.

claim: Says the state’s budget shortfall is "not that much different" than it was in 2003.
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because it fails to specify which state and whether the comparison is nominal or inflation‑adjusted. State budget shortfalls typically change over time due to inflation, population and revenue shifts, so saying they are "not that much different" from 2003 is likely misleading without explicit figures and adjustments.

claim: During Lyndon B. Johnson’s first 20 years in Congress, "he opposed every civil rights measure that came up for a vote."
rationale: The statement is incorrect. Lyndon B. Johnson had a mixed civil‑rights voting record early in his career—he opposed some measures but also supported and helped pass others, most notably playing a central role as Senate Majority Leader in enacting the 1957 Civil Rights Act. Thus he did not uniformly oppose every civil‑rights measure during his first 20 years in Congress.

claim: "This is the only state in the country that bypassed the General Assembly to authorize [in-state tuition for undocumented immigrants]."
rationale: The claim is incorrect as phrased: several states have implemented in-state tuition for undocumented immigrants through non-legislative routes (administrative boards, university regents, executive actions, or court rulings) rather than via their legislatures. It is therefore not true that a single state is uniquely the only one to have "bypassed the General Assembly."

claim: Georgia is the second-fastest growing state for international tourists.
rationale: The statement is presented without a time frame or data source, and there is no consistent evidence that the U.S. state of Georgia is universally ranked as the second-fastest growing state for international tourists. Rankings of states by international arrivals or growth change year to year and depend on the metric and source; some years Georgia saw notable growth but it is not consistently or clearly second across authoritative datasets. Because the claim lacks context and is not verifiable as a stable fact, it is false as stated.

claim: "The labor participation rate is at an all-time low."
rationale: The claim is false as stated because the labor force participation rate is not currently at a recorded all-time low. For example in the U.S. the rate fell sharply in 2020 to about 60% during the pandemic but recovered into the low‑60s by 2023–2024; historically the series contains lower values at other times depending on the start date. The statement also lacks a specified country and date, so it cannot be taken as a correct universal fact.

claim: When Honduran children came into this country, "Secretary Clinton said send them back."
rationale: There is no credible record of Secretary of State Hillary Clinton ever instructing U.S. authorities to “send [Honduran] children back.” Immigration enforcement and decisions about repatriation are handled by DHS/ICE/CBP, not the State Department, and Clinton’s public statements from her tenure emphasized humanitarian concerns and diplomatic coordination rather than a directive to return arriving children. The quoted line appears to be a misattribution or distortion of events.

claim: "For the first time in history, Wisconsin has more government jobs than manufacturing jobs."
rationale: This claim is not supported by historical employment data. Wisconsin has long had manufacturing as one of its largest employment sectors, and publicly available BLS and state labor reports through recent years show manufacturing employment remaining similar to or larger than total government employment; a claim of a first-ever crossover would require a specific year and authoritative source. The statement may reflect a temporary counting quirk or a misinterpretation of payroll vs. job counts, but as worded it is not accurate.

claim: "Senator Obama has, in fact, never had a serious Republican challenger."
rationale: The claim is false because Barack Obama did face Republican challengers in his 2004 Senate race — most notably Jack Ryan (who was a serious GOP nominee before withdrawing amid scandal) and Alan Keyes (who replaced Ryan as the general election Republican). Obama won the general election by a large margin, which may be why challengers are characterized as not "serious," but it is incorrect to say he "never" had Republican opponents or any initially serious GOP nominee.

claim: "In 2005, Dan Branch tried to expand third-trimester abortions in Texas."
rationale: This claim is inconsistent with Dan Branch’s record. As a Republican member of the Texas Legislature in 2005, Branch was known for sponsoring and supporting restrictions on abortion rather than efforts to expand third‑trimester abortion access; there are no credible reports that he attempted to expand late‑term abortions in Texas that year. The available evidence points to the opposite posture (pro‑life/restrictive) on abortion from Branch.

claim: In Europe, "church attendance rates (are) in the single digits" because churches are supported by taxes.
rationale: The claim is incorrect because it overgeneralizes both attendance levels and the cause. Weekly church attendance does fall to single digits in many Western and Northern European countries, but several European countries (notably Poland, Romania and parts of southern/eastern Europe) have substantially higher attendance. State or tax support for churches exists in some countries (e.g., church taxes in Germany, Austria, Nordic states) but is not universal, and there is no simple evidence that tax funding causes low attendance — secularization, cultural change and social modernization are better-supported explanations.

claim: Refugees are throwing rocks and trying "to kill you."
rationale: This is an alarmist generalization that is not supported by available evidence. While there have been isolated incidents in which some migrants or people at border crossings threw rocks during confrontations, there is no credible evidence that refugees as a group are routinely throwing rocks and attempting to kill civilians. The claim conflates occasional confrontations with a widespread, coordinated murderous intent.

claim: Says Virginia Republican "Scott Taylor has been convicted in at least four different courts across the country, at times failing to even appear, and having a warrant issued for his arrest."
rationale: Reporting and publicly available court records about Virginia Republican Scott Taylor show he faced a mix of civil judgments, traffic and misdemeanor matters and at least some missed court dates, but there is not reliable evidence that he was criminally convicted in “at least four different courts across the country” nor that multiple arrest warrants were issued as claimed. The statement appears to conflate civil judgments, unpaid fines or missed hearings with criminal convictions and overstates the number and nature of cases.

claim: "Instagram has been limiting our posts so that no more than 7% of our friends see our posts."
rationale: This is false: Instagram does not enforce a universal, fixed cap that limits posts to 7% of a user's friends. Visibility is determined by an algorithm (engagement, relevancy, recency, and other signals) and organic reach varies widely by account, content, and time; while some accounts may see low (~7%) reach, that is not a platform-declared hard limit.

claim: "No member of the American public has ever been killed by commercial nuclear power — a record unmatched by other fuels."
rationale: U.S. commercial nuclear power plants have not caused any verified deaths of members of the general public from radiological exposure; major U.S. incidents (Three Mile Island) produced no attributable public fatalities, and the SL-1 deaths were military personnel at an experimental reactor, not members of the public. By contrast other energy sources (coal, oil, natural gas, hydro in some historical cases) have caused public fatalities through accidents, air pollution, spills and dam failures, so the zero-public-death record for U.S. commercial nuclear power is unmatched.

claim: Dozens of artists, including Justin Timberlake, Jay Z and Rihanna, are canceling Florida shows like Stevie Wonder in protest of  "stand your ground."
rationale: This is inaccurate. While Stevie Wonder did publicly cancel Florida concert dates in 2012 citing concerns tied to the state's 'stand your ground' law, there was not a wave of dozens of cancellations by major artists — Justin Timberlake, Jay‑Z and Rihanna did not cancel Florida shows en masse; most high-profile acts continued performances despite petitions and calls for boycotts. The claim thus overstates and misattributes a broad coordinated cancellation.

claim: The Buffalo Billion is "still breaking every job promise"
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement that is not supported by evidence. Independent audits and news reporting show that while several high‑profile Buffalo Billion projects fell short of job targets (for example SolarCity/Tesla and others flagged in state reviews), other investments produced jobs or met at least some commitments, so outcomes are mixed rather than every promise being broken.

claim: "From 2000 to 2016, every major drug that was introduced came out of" National Institutes of Health funding.
rationale: The claim is implausible and unsupported: drug discovery and development from 2000–2016 involved a mix of private pharmaceutical/biotech R&D, venture funding, and some publicly funded basic research, but not every major new drug was directly produced from NIH funding. While NIH grants have contributed foundational basic science that underpins many therapies, many marketed drugs were discovered, developed, and funded primarily by industry or non-NIH sources. The absolute term "every" overstates the role of NIH.

claim: "We’re the seventh highest taxed state in America. And that’s not just state, it’s local as well."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because it omits which state and which tax measure/year are being referenced; rankings of “highest taxed” vary by metric (state-only vs. combined state and local, per-capita vs. share of income) and by year/source. Without that context the assertion cannot be confirmed and could be misleading—some states do rank near the top on combined state+local tax burden in certain years, but this blanket statement is unsubstantiated.

claim: "Scott Walker gave Wisconsin job creation money to his cronies: corporate friends who contributed to his campaigns" and got $570 million in job-development incentives
rationale: The statement mixes fact and an unproven inference. It is true that Wisconsin’s economic development programs awarded hundreds of millions in incentives during Scott Walker’s governorship and that some recipients had contributed to his campaigns, but there is no conclusive evidence that Walker personally directed payoffs as quid pro quo or that a discrete $570 million sum was knowingly given specifically to his “cronies.” The $570 million figure is an over-simplification without clear attribution to campaign contributors alone.

claim: "I went to the Olympics that was out of balance, and we got it on balance."
rationale: The claim is vague, first-person, and lacks verifiable specifics (who "I" refers to, which Olympics, what "out of balance" means, and what "got it on balance" entails). There is no corroborating public record or reporting that matches this exact statement or documents the asserted intervention, so it cannot be verified as factual. Given the ambiguity and absence of evidence, the claim is treated as unproven and thus judged false for fact-checking purposes.

claim: "The spillover violence (from Mexico) in Texas is real and it is escalating."
rationale: While there are documented, localized incidents of cartel-related violence crossing the U.S.–Mexico border into parts of Texas, authoritative crime statistics and law‑enforcement assessments do not show clear, sustained statewide escalation attributable to spillover. The claim bundles two assertions (that spillover exists and that it is escalating); the existence is supported in limited areas but the broader escalation claim is not consistently borne out by available data.

claim: A 13-year-old girl "is now in critical care in the hospital here in Halifax because her heart stopped right after she had a vaccine."
rationale: There is no credible public evidence that a 13-year-old in Halifax went into critical care with cardiac arrest and that this was caused by a vaccine. Health authorities and reliable news/fact‑checking outlets have not confirmed such a vaccine-caused cardiac arrest, and temporal proximity alone does not establish causation. Known rare adverse events (e.g., myocarditis) after mRNA vaccines have been reported but are uncommon and typically less severe than described.

claim: "The CBO says (the Build Back Better Act) is $3 trillion of deficit spending."
rationale: This is incorrect: the Congressional Budget Office did not state the Build Back Better Act was $3 trillion of deficit spending. CBO (and JCT) scored the pared-down reconciliation text Democrats ultimately advanced at roughly $1.7–1.8 trillion in projected costs over 10 years; the larger $3.5 trillion figure was an early party proposal price tag, not a CBO estimate of deficits. CBO also reports gross costs separately from deficit impact and includes offsets, so lumping a proposal’s headline price tag into a single “$3 trillion deficit” is misleading.

claim: "70 percent of the people who voted" on June 5, 2012, "just didn’t feel comfortable with the recall of the governor," weakening any idea that Wisconsin is "fully behind this Walker agenda."
rationale: The June 5, 2012 Wisconsin gubernatorial recall election resulted in Scott Walker winning reelection with roughly 53.8% of the vote to Tom Barrett’s ~46.2%, not a 70% margin. There is no evidence from the official returns or reputable exit polls that 70% of actual voters were "uncomfortable with the recall," so the numeric claim is inaccurate and misleading.

claim: Says "President Trump makes English the official language of the United States!"
rationale: There is no federal law or binding executive order from President Trump that made English the official language of the United States. The U.S. has no nationally established official language; while Trump and his administration promoted English in some rhetoric and policy preferences, they did not enact legislation or a definitive executive action creating English as the official national language.

claim: "There's been a 1,700 percent increase in asylum claims over the last 10 years."
rationale: The claim is implausible as stated because it gives no country or time baseline and a 1,700% rise (an 18‑fold increase) in asylum claims over a decade is not supported by widely reported national or global asylum data. Major data sources (UNHCR, national immigration agencies) show increases in some years and in some countries but typically by tens or a few hundred percent, not 1,700%, unless referring to a very small baseline or narrowly defined subgroup. Without a specific jurisdiction, timeframe, and data source the blanket 1,700% assertion is misleading and likely false.

claim: "The collective net worth of Americans has taken a $5.5 trillion hit ... mainly due to plummeting home values."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated as stated because it gives no timeframe or source; when U.S. household net worth has fallen by several trillion dollars (for example in late 2022), analysts attributed most of the decline to stock-market losses rather than a nationwide plunge in home values. National house-price indices generally did not ‘plummet’ in the same periods and in many cases remained flat or positive, so saying the hit was driven mainly by falling home values is misleading.

claim: "The higher the education level, the more likely they are to vote Democratic."
rationale: The statement is an oversimplification. In recent U.S. elections higher education (especially postgraduate degrees) has been associated with greater Democratic support, but the relationship varies by level of degree, race, and other demographics — for example, college-educated white voters have in some cycles leaned Republican. Patterns also differ across countries and change over time, so the blanket claim is inaccurate.

claim: "In the 18th Congressional District, 100% of electric generation comes from coal."
rationale: The claim that 100% of electric generation in any U.S. congressional district comes from coal is not supported by available energy data. Regional and EIA generation statistics show that even coal-heavy districts have at least some generation from natural gas, nuclear, hydro, wind, solar, or imported electricity, and coal’s share has declined over time.

claim: "Over 73% of all donations raised (from the ALS Ice Bucket Challenge) are going to fundraising, overhead, executive salaries, and external donations."
rationale: This claim is incorrect. Public financial statements, IRS Form 990s and charity watchdog analyses from the period after the Ice Bucket Challenge show that a substantial share of donations was used for research grants and program services rather than that more than 73% being consumed by fundraising, overhead, executive pay, and pass-through/external donations. While some administrative and fundraising costs existed, they were well below the 73% figure cited.

claim: Huckabee "was one of the highest taxing governors that we had in this country and rivaling Bill Clinton in terms of the Cato ratings."
rationale: The statement overstates the case. Cato Institute report cards did give Huckabee some low fiscal grades in certain years, but he was not consistently ranked as one of the very highest-taxing governors nationwide and a direct comparison to Bill Clinton across Cato’s metrics is not supported. Huckabee’s record included both tax increases (notably for education) and later tax cuts, so the blanket claim is misleading.

claim: "Due to the recent downturn in steel production, more than 13,600 Americans have been laid off and the steel industry is facing billions in losses."
rationale: The claim is unverified and likely false as stated: I am not aware of any authoritative industry, government, or major news report that documents a single recent downturn that directly caused more than 13,600 U.S. steelworker layoffs while quantifying "billions in losses." Public reporting around 2020–2024 mentions assorted plant idlings, localized layoffs and revenue hits, but not the specific nationwide figure cited, and the phrase "billions in losses" is vague and un-sourced.

claim: While in Congress, Nathan Deal was a leader when it came to protecting our borders.
rationale: The claim is an overstatement. While Nathan Deal (U.S. Representative 1993–2010) generally supported stricter immigration enforcement and border security measures, he was not widely recognized as a national Congressional leader on border protection or the sponsor of landmark federal border-security legislation—other members were more prominent in that role.

claim: Clean energy employs "more than half a million Californians. That’s nearly ten times more the number of coal mining jobs that exist in the entire nation."
rationale: Independent industry and state analyses have reported California clean‑energy employment above 500,000, while U.S. coal‑mining employment in recent years (BLS/industry data) has been on the order of roughly 40,000–60,000. Those figures make California’s clean‑energy workforce roughly ten times the size of the entire U.S. coal‑mining workforce.

claim: "Florida’s high school graduation rate falls well below the national average."
rationale: This is false in general: Florida’s on-time (4-year adjusted cohort) high school graduation rate has in recent years been at or above the national average, with the state reporting record-high rates and often ranking above the U.S. rate. Saying it “falls well below” the national average misstates the typical relationship unless a specific year or subgroup showing a decline is cited.

claim: Says Gerald Daugherty advocated lowering the penalty for crimes like strangulation in domestic violence cases because "they just ‘throw more people into the’" jail "‘system."
rationale: I could not find verifiable reporting or primary-source evidence that a person named Gerald Daugherty publicly advocated lowering penalties for strangulation in domestic violence cases using the quoted phrase about ‘throw[ing] more people into the…jail system.’ The claim appears to be an attribution without corroborating news articles, official statements, or transcripts. Given the absence of reliable sources tying that quote and policy position to Gerald Daugherty, the claim cannot be confirmed as true.

claim: Athletes are collapsing with heart-related issues due to the COVID-19 vaccines
rationale: The broad claim that athletes are collapsing with heart-related issues due to COVID‑19 vaccines is not supported by the evidence. While rare cases of myocarditis have been reported after mRNA vaccines—primarily mild and in young males—large surveillance studies and clinical reviews have not shown a population‑level increase in sudden cardiac collapses among athletes attributable to vaccination, and COVID‑19 infection itself carries a higher cardiac risk. Isolated temporal reports do not establish causation.

claim: "Our economy created over 6.5 million new jobs just last year, more jobs in one year than ever before in the history of the United States of America."
rationale: This matches official U.S. payroll data: the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported nonfarm payroll employment rose by about 6.7 million over 2021, which is the largest annual increase on record in the BLS series. Saying "over 6.5 million" and "more jobs in one year than ever before" is consistent with that measure and year.

claim: Says his plan to end the toll on Ga. 400 fulfills his campaign promise to commuters.
rationale: The claim as written is ambiguous and provides no named speaker, date, or sourcing to confirm that any specific person said their plan to end the Ga. 400 toll fulfills a campaign promise. Without identifying who “he” is and without a verifiable quote or source, the statement cannot be confirmed as true. Therefore I rate it false pending proper attribution and evidence.

claim: Says Pope Francis "was arrested Saturday in connection with an 80-count indictment of charges including possession of child pornography, human trafficking, incest, possession of drug paraphernalia and felony fraud."
rationale: This claim is false. There are no credible reports from major international news organizations or the Vatican that Pope Francis was arrested on any charges, and such an event would have been globally reported and officially confirmed. The wording and list of crimes match known hoax/satirical social-media fabrications rather than verified facts.

claim: Says Adam Schiff used taxpayer money to "reach a sexual harassment settlement with a 19-year-old male."
rationale: There is no credible public record or reporting showing Rep. Adam Schiff used taxpayer funds to settle a sexual‑harassment claim with a 19‑year‑old male. Major news organizations and House ethics/public disclosure records up to mid‑2024 do not document such a settlement, and the allegation appears to stem from unverified social media claims. Without reliable evidence, the assertion is unsupported.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton dressed up in blackface.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Hillary Clinton ever dressed in blackface. Claims alleging she did originated on social media and have been investigated by journalists and fact‑checkers, who found no authenticated photos or reliable eyewitness accounts to support the claim. Alleged images are misattributed or show other people or costume contexts rather than Clinton in blackface.

claim: Says Republican Gov. Phil Scott "just voted to impeach President Trump."
rationale: The claim is false because impeachment of a U.S. president is performed by the U.S. House of Representatives, and only members of that body cast impeachment votes. Phil Scott is the Republican governor of Vermont, not a member of the U.S. House, so he could not have "just voted" to impeach President Trump. While Scott has publicly criticized Trump at times, he did not cast an impeachment vote.

claim: New and proposed state laws on voting mean "if you are going to be standing in that line for all those hours, you can’t have any water or any food."
rationale: The claim overstates and universalizes. While a few recent or proposed state bills include narrow prohibitions on distributing gifts or campaign materials within a specified distance of polling places (and some language could be read to restrict handing out food or water in certain circumstances), this is not a blanket rule in all new or proposed voting laws and many statutes include exceptions or different definitions. Enforcement and scope vary widely by state and many states have no such restriction.

claim: Says a New York physician and his wife jumped to their deaths because they "can’t afford" Obamacare.
rationale: Reliable reporting and fact-checkers found no credible evidence that a New York physician and his wife jumped to their deaths because they “can’t afford” the Affordable Care Act. The claim appears to have originated on social media and is not supported by police statements, coroner findings, or reputable news coverage attributing their deaths to inability to pay for Obamacare. In short, the asserted causal connection is unverified and contradicted by available official reports.

claim: "Dr. Oz releases COPD gummies that help quit smoking, detox lungs and stop COPD."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Dr. Oz has released any scientifically validated “COPD gummies,” nor that any gummy can make people quit smoking, "detox" lungs, or stop COPD. COPD is a chronic, progressive disease treated with proven interventions (medications, pulmonary rehab, smoking cessation programs), and claims of a cure via gummies contradict medical consensus and lack clinical trials or regulatory approval.

claim: "The committee that advises @GovEvers and his department tasked with leading during this pandemic is recommending allowing prisoners to receive the vaccine before 65 year old grandma?"
rationale: The claim is misleading: while some advisory bodies and states recommended prioritizing people in high‑risk congregate settings (including some incarcerated populations) early in rollout, there is no clear, documented universal recommendation from the Wisconsin committee advising Gov. Evers to vaccinate prisoners broadly before all people aged 65+. State and federal guidance generally prioritized health care workers, long‑term care residents, and older adults, and prioritization decisions varied over time and by context.

claim: Tapping the Strategic Petroleum Reserve would immediately lower gasoline prices
rationale: Releasing oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve increases crude supply and can put downward pressure on crude prices, but that does not usually translate into an immediate drop in retail gasoline prices. Gasoline prices at the pump depend on refined-product markets, refinery capacity and blends, transportation and wholesale contract timing, and taxes, so any consumer-price effect is often delayed and can be modest. Historical SPR releases have tended to have limited or lagged effects on pump prices.

claim: Photos show Kamala Harris, Joe Biden, Gretchen Whitmer and Cory Booker violating COVID-19 safety precautions.
rationale: While some photos have shown individual politicians without masks at various times, images alone do not reliably demonstrate that Kamala Harris, Joe Biden, Gretchen Whitmer and Cory Booker were definitively violating COVID-19 safety rules. Whether masking or distancing was required depended on the date, location, local guidance, and whether people were vaccinated or outdoors, so the broad claim lacks verified, context-free support.

claim: Says Gov. Rick Scott's approval ratings are up.
rationale: The statement gives no timeframe or polling source, so it cannot be verified as true. Rick Scott’s approval has varied across different polls and periods; without a specified poll/date showing an upward trend, the claim that his approval ratings are "up" is unsubstantiated. Given the missing context, I treat the assertion as false until specific data is provided.

claim: Says Georgia ranks "near the bottom in per capita transportation spending."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and not consistently supported: rankings of state per‑capita transportation spending depend heavily on the year, data source, and whether capital, operating, and federal funds are included. Georgia's position in published state-by-state comparisons has varied and it is not uniformly or reliably ranked “near the bottom” across reputable datasets, so the blanket statement is misleading without specific context.

claim: "Two million more people just dropped out of Obamacare. It is in a death spiral."
rationale: This claim is not supported by available enrollment data or market analysis. There was no verified, sudden nationwide loss of two million marketplace enrollees “just” occurring; in recent years ACA marketplace enrollment has been roughly stable or rising overall after expanded subsidies, and insurer participation has continued, which contradicts an imminent “death spiral.” The term “death spiral” describes a specific adverse-selection collapse that independent analyses and CMS enrollment reports do not show happening across the exchanges.

claim: "Nobody suffered any lasting injuries" from the CIA interrogation program.
rationale: The claim is false. Multiple independent investigations, medical evaluations, human-rights organizations, and testimony from released detainees document enduring physical and psychological harm—including PTSD, chronic pain, cognitive and neurological complaints—associated with CIA interrogation techniques such as waterboarding and prolonged sleep deprivation. While some officials have contested the extent of lasting injury, the preponderance of evidence shows long-term effects for many detainees.

claim: "The average person who gets the minimum wage in America is 35 years old."
rationale: This claim is inconsistent with labor statistics and research showing minimum-wage workers are disproportionately young; analyses and BLS data typically find the typical (median or mean) minimum-wage worker is in their late teens or twenties, not 35. While some older workers earn minimum wage, they do not raise the central tendency to age 35 for the broad population of minimum-wage workers.

claim: "There was never a single shred of evidence presented to anyone" that the attacks in Benghazi, Libya, were "spontaneous, and in fact, the CIA themselves understood that early on."
rationale: This claim is false. Multiple official reviews and contemporaneous intelligence assessments indicated the Benghazi attacks were a coordinated terrorist assault (groups like Ansar al‑Sharia were implicated) rather than purely a spontaneous protest, and the CIA’s public talking points were changed over time — they did not uniformly assert early-on that the Benghazi compound attack was spontaneous. While some early intelligence and media references mentioned protests elsewhere in Libya linked to an anti‑Islam video, that is not the same as there being ‘no evidence’ or that the CIA uniformly understood the Benghazi attack to be spontaneous from the start.

claim: Dan McCready backed state legislation that raised consumers "$149 million a year in higher energy costs."
rationale: This claim is misleading. Dan McCready was a congressional candidate, not a member of the North Carolina legislature, and there is no public record that he sponsored or voted for state legislation that directly produced $149 million a year in higher energy costs; the specific dollar figure and attribution appear to come from political attacks rather than documented legislative action by McCready.

claim: Says Trump ties are made "in China, not Colorado. Trump suits in Mexico, not Michigan. Trump furniture in Turkey, not Ohio. Trump picture frames in India, not Wisconsin."
rationale: The claim asserts categorical, exclusive pairings of specific Trump-branded goods with single foreign countries. While it is true that many Trump-licensed consumer products have been manufactured overseas (including China, Mexico, India and others), production sources have varied by product line and over time and are not exclusively limited to the countries listed; some items (and some tailoring) have been produced in the U.S. or by multiple foreign suppliers. Because the statement overgeneralizes and assigns sole country origins, it is inaccurate.

claim: Multnomah County has faced "11 straight years" of cuts
rationale: The statement is unsubstantiated as presented. Multnomah County’s budget and staffing levels have not shown a verified, continuous 11-year decline across the board — municipal budgets frequently fluctuate, and in many years the county’s nominal budget and some program funding increased. Without a clear time frame and definition of what constitutes a "cut" (nominal dollars, inflation-adjusted dollars, specific departments, or staffing), the claim is misleading.

claim: Illegal immigration on the U.S.-Mexico border is "the lowest in 17 years."
rationale: The claim is misleading or incorrect based on publicly reported U.S. Border Patrol trends: encounters and apprehensions in recent years (particularly FY2021–FY2023) were not at a 17-year low and in many periods were near multi‑year highs. The statement likely cherry-picks a short timeframe or a specific month/metric (e.g., a COVID-related dip) rather than reflecting overall annual data.

claim: "There was a raid on the Biden residence yesterday by the military!"
rationale: There is no evidence in the record available through my training cutoff (June 2024) of any military raid on the Biden residence, and such an action would be an extraordinary, widely reported event. The presidential residences are protected by the Secret Service, and domestic military operations are tightly limited and highly publicized when they occur. Because I cannot access real-time news past my cutoff, I cannot confirm events that might have occurred after that date, so the claim lacks verifiable support here.

claim: Says the fluoride Austin is putting in its drinking water is "toxic waste."
rationale: Calling the fluoride Austin adds to drinking water 'toxic waste' is misleading. Municipal fluoridation chemicals (commonly hydrofluorosilicic acid or fluorides) are industrial byproducts but are used in very low, regulated concentrations (~0.7 mg/L) that public health authorities (CDC, WHO, ADA) consider safe and effective; they are not treated or managed as hazardous 'toxic waste' in standard water treatment practice. Toxicity depends on dose and form, and the amounts added for fluoridation are far below levels considered hazardous.

claim: "How is a misogynist bigot of epic proportions (like U.S. Rep. Steven Smith) allowed to serve?"
rationale: The claim is a subjective, pejorative characterization rather than a verifiable factual statement. Labeling someone a “misogynist bigot of epic proportions” requires citation of specific, documented statements or patterns of behavior; without those specifics the allegation is opinion and not objectively provable. Because the claim as presented offers no concrete evidence, it cannot be treated as a factual assertion.

claim: Says Brett Kavanaugh "refused to uphold key patient protections in the past."
rationale: The claim is a broad, absolute assertion that Kavanaugh "refused to uphold key patient protections," but it lacks specific laws or decisions to verify. Kavanaugh’s D.C. Circuit record includes opinions that favored insurers or plan administrators in some ERISA and coverage disputes, which critics say limited patient remedies, but that does not establish a general, documented refusal to uphold patient protections across the board. Without particular cases or a legal standard cited, the sweeping wording is unsupported.

claim: State "school funding per pupil is down 16 percent compared to 2009, after adjusting for inflation."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as written because it does not name which state or which inflation index/year is used; trends in inflation-adjusted per-pupil funding since 2009 vary considerably by state. Nationally and in many states K–12 spending rebounded after the 2009 recession and did not uniformly fall by 16% in real terms, so the blanket claim is misleading without specification. Some individual states may have experienced large declines, but the claim as stated is not supportable.

claim: The mobilization of the military in response to the storms in Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands "is the largest ever mobilization of our military in a naval and marine operation" and an Air Force carrier there "was the first-ever as well."
rationale: The assertion is false. Prior domestic and regional disaster responses (for example Hurricane Katrina in 2005 and the 2010 Haiti earthquake response) involved equal or larger naval and Marine deployments and use of aircraft carriers and large naval assets, so the Puerto Rico/USVI response was not uniquely the largest; additionally the speaker’s reference to an “Air Force carrier” is incorrect because aircraft carriers are Navy vessels. The claim conflates service roles and overstates uniqueness.

claim: "I campaigned on (the proposals in the budget repair bill for Wisconsin) all throughout the election. Anybody who says they are shocked on this has been asleep for the past two years."
rationale: The statement is substantially accurate: the Wisconsin governor (Scott Walker) and his campaign repeatedly emphasized fiscal reforms and curbing public-employee collective bargaining as central campaign themes in the lead-up to his 2010 election and the 2011 budget debates. While the phrasing “all throughout the election” and the rhetorical “anybody...asleep” are emphatic, public speeches, ads and campaign materials consistently raised those proposals beforehand.
