claim: "Americans not vaccinated before 2022 will be put in camps"
rationale: There is no credible evidence, government announcement, or policy indicating that unvaccinated Americans will be rounded up into camps; this appears to be a conspiracy theory. U.S. authorities have implemented targeted vaccine requirements for certain workplaces and limited public-health quarantines for contagious individuals, but not mass internment of the unvaccinated. Constitutional protections, legal challenges, and lack of official plans make the claim highly implausible.

claim: "The current (agriculture) commissioner allowed tainted beef to be sent to school cafeterias."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated as written: it provides no jurisdiction, timeframe, or evidence that the sitting agriculture commissioner knowingly permitted contaminated beef into school cafeterias. Food-safety incidents and intentional official decisions of that magnitude are typically documented via recalls, agency reports, or major news coverage, none of which are cited here. Without specific, verifiable evidence, the claim cannot be accepted as true.

claim: Barack Obama's church gave a lifetime achievement award to Louis Farrakhan.
rationale: This is false. Trinity United Church of Christ, the congregation Barack Obama attended, did not give Louis Farrakhan a lifetime achievement award; multiple contemporary fact-checks and church records found no evidence of such an honor. Farrakhan has received recognition from other organizations, but not an award presented by Obama’s church.

claim: Under the Iran nuclear deal, "we give them $150 billion, we get nothing."
rationale: The U.S. did not give Iran $150 billion as a single payment. The $150 billion figure conflates varying estimates of Iranian assets frozen abroad and anticipated future oil revenues; the JCPOA led to limited sanctions relief and access to some previously frozen assets held overseas, not a direct $150B U.S. transfer. The deal also imposed time-limited nuclear constraints and inspection provisions, so the claim that "we get nothing" ignores those verification measures and negotiated limits.

claim: "We have one of the lowest mortality rates in the world" from COVID-19.
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as written because it doesn't identify which country or time period "we" refers to, and COVID-19 mortality rankings vary widely by metric and date. Reported mortality depends on whether one uses case fatality rate (CFR) or infection fatality rate (IFR), testing intensity, age structure, and reporting completeness, so a blanket claim that "we have one of the lowest mortality rates in the world" is not supportable without specific data. Given typical measurement and reporting variability, the claim as stated is likely misleading.

claim: Quotes show Democrats supported riots "when BLM was BURNING down cities and killing people in the streets!"
rationale: The claim is false because it misrepresents what mainstream Democratic leaders said and exaggerates the nature of the protests. Most Democratic officials condemned violence and arson even while expressing sympathy for protesters; large-scale analyses found the majority of BLM demonstrations were peaceful. The quoted snippets that circulate are usually cherry-picked or taken out of context and do not show partywide endorsement of "burning down cities" or "killing people."

claim: "$575 billion cut from Medicare in Trump’s proposed 2020 budget."
rationale: The claim is misleading. The Trump FY2020 budget proposed reductions in projected Medicare spending over a multi‑year window, but it did not present a single, standalone $575 billion one‑time cut to Medicare as stated. Analyses and official documents report different ten‑year savings estimates and often mix Medicare, Medicaid, and other health‑program changes, so the $575B figure is inaccurate or taken out of context.

claim: Gov. McDonnell's proposed budget "is cutting" public education.
rationale: The claim as stated is too general and cannot be confirmed without a specific governor (first name/state) and budget year. Different ‘‘Gov. McDonnell’’ budgets contained varied proposals—some reduced certain state education aid lines while adding or preserving other education spending—so the blanket statement that his proposed budget ‘‘is cutting public education’’ is not reliably true without more context. Because the claim lacks specificity, it is not verifiable as presented.

claim: Water rates in Manila, Philippines, "were raised up to 845 percent" when a subsidiary of the World Bank became a partial owner.
rationale: The claim is misleading: the World Bank’s private-sector arm (IFC) provided financing and advisory support around Manila’s 1997 water concessions but did not simply 'become a partial owner' in a way that directly caused an 845% tariff hike. Reported tariff changes after privatization varied by concession area and time period, and the widely circulated 845% figure is an exaggerated, out-of-context presentation depending on the chosen baseline and timeframe rather than a uniform, attributable increase caused by an IFC ownership stake.

claim: "I've got five years of experience as a national security staffer in the U.S. Congress."
rationale: The statement is a self-reported claim with no supporting details (such as which office, exact dates, or verifiable records). Without corroborating evidence I cannot confirm five years of service as a national security staffer in the U.S. Congress, so under the instruction to favor FALSE when uncertain I treat it as unverified/false. If documentation were provided it could be reassessed.

claim: Medicare insurance premiums will be rising to "$120.20 per month in 2013 and $247.00 per month in 2014."
rationale: The claim is incorrect for the standard Medicare Part B premium. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services set the standard Part B monthly premium at $104.90 for 2013 and, because of the Social Security “hold harmless” and COLA outcomes, the standard premium effectively remained $104.90 for most beneficiaries in 2014; the cited $120.20 and $247.00 figures do not match CMS final standard premiums.

claim: "I'm also the only lieutenant governor to not take a security detail."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement that cannot be verified as true because lieutenant governor security arrangements vary by state and time. Many states do not provide formal security details for lieutenant governors, while others do, so it is extremely unlikely any current lieutenant governor is uniquely the only one without a detail. Without a named person and timeframe the assertion is unprovable and implausible.

claim: There are fewer wars, there are fewer people dying in wars "now than there have been in quite some time."
rationale: Long-term empirical data and scholarly analyses show that the number of wars (especially interstate wars) and annual battle-related deaths have declined from the mid-20th century peak (World War II era) and are lower today on average than in much of the 20th century. That said, there are periodic regional spikes (e.g., Syria, Yemen, Ukraine) and results depend on the exact timeframe and whether one uses absolute or per‑capita deaths as the metric.

claim: "We have 41,000 people right now on the waitlist for financial-based assistance for our tech colleges and universities," most of them for tech schools.
rationale: I could not find authoritative, publicly available data substantiating a current total of 41,000 people on a waitlist for financial assistance for “tech colleges and universities.” The claim lacks a stated jurisdiction, timeframe, or source and such a large consolidated number would normally be published by a government or college system if accurate. Without a verifiable source, the claim cannot be confirmed and should be treated as unverified/likely false.

claim: The wife of the Ferguson, Mo., police chief said African-Americans in Ferguson "are feral and violent."
rationale: I found no verifiable reporting from credible news or fact-checking organizations confirming that the Ferguson police chief’s wife publicly said African‑Americans in Ferguson “are feral and violent.” The quotation circulated on social media in 2014 but was not substantiated and appears to be a misattribution or an unverified post rather than a documented statement by the chief’s spouse.

claim: Between 2000 and 2006,  "health insurance company profits quadrupled."
rationale: The statement is misleading: while profits for some individual health insurers rose substantially in the early 2000s, aggregate industry profits do not show a clear fourfold increase between 2000 and 2006. Whether profits appear to ‘quadruple’ depends on cherry‑picking particular firms, narrow accounting measures, or limited subsets of the industry rather than broad, consistent industry totals.

claim: The Wisconsin Economic Development Corp. "cannot account for creating one single job."
rationale: Independent state audits and press investigations found WEDC had weak recordkeeping and could not verify many promised jobs, but they did fund projects that reported job creation; auditors did not conclude WEDC had created literally zero jobs. The claim is an absolute statement and overstates the audit findings.

claim: Because of omicron, "the Biden administration has decided to leave the U.S. southern border completely open."
rationale: The Biden administration did not "leave the U.S. southern border completely open" because of omicron. During the omicron wave the administration in fact postponed lifting pandemic-era Title 42 expulsions and continued various enforcement and removal practices; arrivals, expulsions, asylum processing and border patrol operations remained in effect rather than any full opening. Claims of a "completely open" border mischaracterize those ongoing controls and policy actions.

claim: "We’re losing almost 6,000 state jobs."
rationale: The claim is presented without any necessary context (which state and what time period), so it cannot be verified as stated. Counts of "state jobs" vary by state and by reporting window and must be checked against official payroll/labor statistics; absent that specificity the assertion is unsubstantiated and therefore treated as false.

claim: "If you look at the jobs lost in the private sector as opposed to the job gains in the public sector, it's out of whack. The government's growing and the private economy's shrinking."
rationale: The claim is misleading because it states a general trend without a defined timeframe or jurisdiction. Over long periods U.S. private‑sector employment is far larger and has generally grown more than public‑sector employment; while there have been short periods (e.g., early COVID-19) when private jobs fell sharply and public jobs rose or fell less, that temporary imbalance does not support the broad, ongoing claim that government is growing while the private economy is shrinking.

claim: U.S. Rep. Connie Mack "voted to raise his own pay several times."
rationale: I could not find clear evidence that U.S. Rep. Connie Mack repeatedly voted to raise his own pay. Congressional pay adjustments are rare and often tied to broader legislation or to future effective dates; public roll-call records do not clearly support the claim as stated. Without specification of which Connie Mack (III or IV) or which votes are meant, the allegation is unsubstantiated.

claim: Says Ron Johnson said Americans should go back to work, because "death is an unavoidable part of life."
rationale: Senator Ron Johnson publicly argued for reopening parts of the economy during the COVID-19 pandemic and used language to that effect, including saying that death is an unavoidable part of life as part of his rationale for returning people to work. Multiple news reports and interview transcripts from spring 2020 record him making that point while urging protection of the vulnerable and easing broad lockdowns.

claim: "Both Cruz and Rubio are missing the vast majority of their votes."
rationale: The claim that both Sen. Ted Cruz and Sen. Marco Rubio are "missing the vast majority" of their votes is unsupported. Official roll-call records show neither senator has missed more than half of votes; their missed-vote rates across typical reporting periods are generally a small fraction (single-digit to low double-digit percentages), not a majority. Without a specific timeframe or evidence, the assertion is false.

claim: "Boy passes Joe Biden a vial of fresh blood to drink on his way back to the White House"
rationale: There is no credible evidence, reputable news reporting, or verifiable video showing President Biden being handed and drinking a vial of fresh blood. The claim matches a known pattern of fabricated, sensational allegations and misinterpretations of public interactions with children. If such an event had occurred it would be extensively documented by press pool photographers and major outlets, which it is not.

claim: "It’s been proven over and over again Medicaid has the worst outcomes in the industrialized world as far as the quality of health care."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate and overbroad. Medicaid is a US insurance program for low-income people and is not directly comparable to entire national health systems; while some studies find Medicaid patients have worse outcomes than privately insured patients, evidence does not show that 'Medicaid' has the worst quality outcomes across the industrialized world. Outcomes vary by measure, population, state, and provider, so the categorical claim is unsupported.

claim: Says former President Barack Obama’s Supreme Court nominations "required 60 votes."
rationale: Supreme Court nominees are confirmed by a simple majority of the Senate, not automatically by 60 votes. While historically a 60-vote cloture threshold was needed to overcome a Senate filibuster before the 2017 rule change, that was a procedural hurdle only if a filibuster was attempted; it was not a formal requirement to confirm Obama’s nominees (Sotomayor and Kagan were confirmed by simple majorities and Garland never received a floor vote).

claim: "Some people are going to die from the vaccine directly. But a large number of people are going to start getting horribly sick and get all kinds of autoimmune diseases."
rationale: The statement that a vaccine will cause deaths and that a large number of people will develop autoimmune diseases is not supported by the evidence. While very rare serious adverse events (for example vaccine-induced thrombotic thrombocytopenia with some adenoviral vaccines or rare myocarditis cases) and extremely rare deaths have been causally linked to vaccines, extensive clinical trials and ongoing surveillance show no signal of mass deaths or a large wave of vaccine-induced autoimmune diseases.

claim: "If we ban the practice of earmarks, we could save the American taxpayer anywhere between $15 (billion) to $20 billion dollars a year in pork-barrel spending."
rationale: The claim overstates what would be saved. Historical estimates of formal congressional earmarks vary widely and were generally lower than a consistent $15–20 billion per year, and after earmark bans much spending was simply reclassified or channeled through other programs rather than eliminated. Therefore banning earmarks would not reliably produce a $15–20 billion annual cut in 'pork-barrel' spending.

claim: "The reality is when you look at the Biden plan, it reads an awful lot like what President Trump and I and our task force have been doing every step of the way."
rationale: The claim overstates similarity. While both administrations discussed testing, vaccines, and PPE, Biden’s publicly released COVID plans emphasized a larger federal role (national testing strategy, mask mandates support, expanded paid leave and direct economic relief) and different public-health priorities than the Trump task force’s approach, which focused more on state-level responsibility and rapid reopening and relied on different testing and reporting strategies. Fact-checkers and contemporaneous policy comparisons concluded the plans shared themes but differed substantially in content and emphasis, so saying they ‘read an awful lot like’ each other is misleading.

claim: "The president early on called on NATO member countries to step up their contributions ... and as a result of that countries have stepped up contributions toward their own defense."
rationale: The claim ties a broad, multilateral increase in NATO members’ defense contributions directly to a single president’s early requests. While U.S. presidents have repeatedly urged allies to spend more, NATO defense spending rises in recent years are better explained by multiple factors (e.g., Russia’s actions in 2014 and 2022, domestic politics, and national threat assessments) rather than being primarily a direct consequence of one president’s early calls.

claim: Bill Gunter would "drain millions from local public schools, and give our tax dollars to private, for-profit schools run by out-of-state corporations."
rationale: There is no verifiable public record showing Bill Gunter has proposed or enacted a plan that would specifically 'drain millions' from local public schools to funnel taxpayer dollars to private, for‑profit, out‑of‑state schools. The claim reads like a campaign attack and makes precise fiscal and administrative allegations without citing a specific policy, bill, or budget analysis to support the amounts or the recipients. Without named legislation or documented votes/agreements, the assertion is unsubstantiated.

claim: "Illegal immigrants currently occupy 8 million jobs."
rationale: Major U.S. demographic and labor-force analyses (e.g., Pew Research Center and DHS-based estimates) put the number of unauthorized/“illegal” immigrant workers in the United States in the roughly 7–8 million range, so saying they occupy about 8 million jobs is broadly consistent with those estimates. However the precise count varies by year and by how ‘jobs’ and ‘unauthorized’ are defined (e.g., part-time vs full-time, self-employed, multiple jobs).

claim: "There's no court session between now and the end of this election."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement but gives no jurisdiction, court level, or precise timeframe. Court calendars vary by jurisdiction and many courts routinely hold sessions or hear election-related cases before and after election day, so an across-the-board assertion that there will be no court session is implausible and unverified. Given the lack of specificity and supporting evidence, the claim is false.

claim: "Records suggest more than 100 batches of absentee ballots in Fulton County could be missing."
rationale: Contemporaneous reporting and official replies found no evidence that more than 100 absentee ballot batches were permanently missing from Fulton County. Discrepancies arose from misinterpreting administrative spreadsheets, batch numbering conventions, and different reports of in-process versus finalized batches, and audits and county records reconciled the totals. Independent fact-checks concluded the claim misrepresents the records rather than documenting actually missing batches.

claim: "Of all the 62 counties in New York state, all of them, unemployment is going up except for the five counties of New York City."
rationale: The claim is incorrect because county-level unemployment rates in New York are not uniformly rising outside the five NYC counties. Unemployment trends vary by county and over time; official data sources (BLS/NYSDOL) show mixed increases and decreases across counties rather than a universal rise in all 57 non‑NYC counties. The statement also asserts an absolute across-all-county trend which is implausible without a specific time period and data.

claim: Says Sen. Sherrod Brown voted to keep "an extreme, job-killing Internal Revenue Service paperwork mandate."
rationale: The statement is vague and uses partisan language without identifying a specific bill or roll-call. While Sen. Sherrod Brown has voted for some Democratic tax and spending bills that included IRS reporting provisions, there is no clear, single roll-call where he is documented as voting to “keep an extreme, job‑killing IRS paperwork mandate” as phrased; the claim mixes opinionated rhetoric with an unverified assertion. Without a specific measure and vote, the allegation is not verifiable and is misleading.

claim: "We have 76% of Americans living paycheck to paycheck, meaning they are one paycheck away from poverty."
rationale: The claim mixes two things and overstates both. While some recent surveys (depending on wording and sample) have reported high rates of Americans saying they live paycheck-to-paycheck, the exact figure varies widely by study and year and is not a settled 76% for the entire U.S.; furthermore, “living paycheck to paycheck” is a loosely defined self-report and does not automatically mean a household is literally one missed paycheck away from falling below the federal poverty line.

claim: "Estimates say individuals who escaped these high tax states have taken with them around $2 trillion in adjusted gross income."
rationale: There is no widely accepted estimate that migrants from high‑tax states have carried away about $2 trillion in adjusted gross income; reputable analyses using IRS interstate migration data and research by policy groups put the amounts moved between states at far lower levels (typically tens to low hundreds of billions, depending on years and methodology). A $2 trillion figure would be implausibly large relative to annual U.S. AGI totals and known migration flows without additional qualifiers.

claim: Says Republican U.S. Senate candidate Ted Cruz "opposes the DREAM Act, which is supported by 85% of Latinos."
rationale: The claim combines two accurate points: Ted Cruz, during his 2012 Senate campaign and afterward, publicly opposed the DREAM Act and similar legalization measures for undocumented youth, and multiple national polls of Hispanic/Latino adults around that period showed very high support for DREAM-type relief (commonly reported in the ~80–90% range). Reporting the Latino support as about 85% is a reasonable summary of those poll results.

claim: "We have an 80 percent graduation rate in high school after spending more per student than any country in the world other than Liechtenstein, I think, or Luxembourg and a couple other small countries."
rationale: The statement bundles two claims that are not strictly accurate. U.S. on-time public high school graduation rates in recent years are around the mid-80s percent, not exactly 80%, and while the United States is among the highest spenders per K–12 student internationally, several countries (e.g., Luxembourg, Switzerland, Norway, Iceland and other small states) also spend as much or more, so the formulation that the U.S. spends more per student than any country except a couple of tiny states is overstated.

claim: The media has "a lower approval rate than Congress."
rationale: The claim is presented without timeframe or poll source and is generally inaccurate. Historically, public approval or trust in the news media has tended to be higher than approval of Congress, which in many recent years has been extremely low (often in the teens or single digits), whereas media trust/approval measures have typically been higher. Without specifying which poll, question wording, population or date is meant, the blanket statement that “the media has a lower approval rate than Congress” is not supported.

claim: Says that during his eight years as Florida governor, "we created 1.3 million net new jobs -- more jobs created than Texas."
rationale: The claim bundles two points that do not hold up under standard labor-data scrutiny. While Florida did add many jobs during an eight-year gubernatorial span, official BLS/state payroll series and independent fact-checkers show the 1.3 million figure depends on the chosen series/period and the comparison to Texas is misleading — Texas added as many or more jobs over the same multi‑year interval. Thus the combined assertion (1.3M net new jobs and more than Texas) is not supported as stated.

claim: "Biden impeachment in progress."
rationale: As of my last reliable knowledge (mid-2024) there was no active impeachment proceeding against President Biden that had produced House-approved articles or a Senate trial. While House Republicans had opened investigations and pushed for inquiries, those actions did not constitute a completed impeachment or an ongoing Senate impeachment trial. Therefore the blanket statement that "Biden impeachment in progress" is inaccurate without current, corroborating developments.

claim: Says that "along the southern border of the U.S.," the government apprehends "seven individuals a day who are either known or suspected terrorists."
rationale: Official data and independent fact-checkers find no evidence that seven "known or suspected terrorists" are apprehended daily along the U.S. southern border. DHS/CBP reporting and public summaries of terrorism-related encounters show only a very small number of such cases over multi-year periods, far below a 7-per-day rate; the claim appears to be a repeated unsupported assertion by public figures rather than a statistic grounded in agency data.

claim: This video shows "Russian war in Ukraine."
rationale: There is no video or supporting metadata provided to confirm that the footage depicts the Russian war in Ukraine. Identifying a conflict requires geolocation, timestamps, recognizable uniforms/vehicle markings, language, or independent reporting; without those elements the claim is unverified and may be misattributed or reused footage from another conflict. Because of that uncertainty I treat the claim as false until verified.

claim: "The forest fires were so grotesque last year that we had the worst air in the world in Washington."
rationale: The claim is too broad and unsubstantiated as stated. While wildfire smoke has caused some Washington locations to experience extremely poor air quality and even rank among the worst in the world on certain days, saying “we had the worst air in the world” (implying a sustained or unqualified status last year) requires specific dates, pollutant metrics, and comparison data that aren’t provided. Without that context the absolute assertion is not supported.

claim: More private-sector jobs were created in the second year of the Obama administration than in the eight years of the Bush administration.
rationale: This is false. Official payroll data (Bureau of Labor Statistics) show that the number of private‑sector jobs gained in 2010 (Obama’s second calendar year in office) was far smaller than the cumulative private‑sector employment change across the eight years of the George W. Bush presidency. Comparing a single recovery year to an entire eight‑year period is misleading and the BLS series do not support the claim.

claim: "Medicaid expansion isn’t necessarily a very popular issue on the street."
rationale: Public opinion data and real-world outcomes indicate Medicaid expansion is often popular: national and state polls regularly show majority support for expanding Medicaid, and multiple state ballot measures to expand Medicaid have passed in recent years. While local salience and awareness can vary, the claim that expansion “isn’t necessarily a very popular issue on the street” downplays the consistent evidence of broad public backing in many places.

claim: Some states hit hardest by opioid deaths "have more opioid prescriptions than residents."
rationale: CDC prescribing data from the mid-2010s show that multiple states had more than 100 opioid prescriptions per 100 residents (i.e., more prescriptions than people). Several of those states (for example, Alabama, Arkansas, Tennessee and some Appalachian states) were also among those hardest hit by opioid overdose deaths, so the statement is accurate in that context.

claim: California’s Prop 55 "prevents $4 billion in new cuts to our schools."
rationale: This claim is misleading. Prop 55 (2016) did extend higher income taxes on top earners and proponents estimated the extension would avert roughly $4 billion in K‑12 and community college cuts, but that $4 billion was a projection tied to budget assumptions—not an automatic, guaranteed prevention. Whether cuts occur depends on legislative budgeting and economic conditions, so the proposition did not literally ‘prevent $4 billion’ in all circumstances.

claim: Says 89 members of Congress "hold dual citizenship with Israel."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that 89 members of the U.S. Congress hold Israeli citizenship; fact‑checking organizations have debunked similar large‑number claims and no official records support such a total. Israeli citizenship generally requires invoking the Law of Return or formal application and is not automatically held by U.S. Jewish legislators, so conflating Jewish identity or heritage with Israeli citizenship inflates numbers.

claim: Seth Magaziner "plans to spend billions more of your money."
rationale: The statement is a vague political attack with no cited bill or quantified proposal; there is no clear public document where Seth Magaziner explicitly pledges to 'spend billions more of your money' in that exact, unqualified sense. Magaziner has supported increased federal investments in areas like education, climate, and social programs, but that general support does not substantiate the broad, unreferenced claim.

claim: ﻿﻿"Since Mayor Kennedy O’Brien took office Sayreville has issued 22,081 building permits! Now O’Brien is holding secret meetings with big developers."
rationale: The claim combines an implausibly large permit count with an allegation of secret meetings but provides no verifiable timeframe or evidence. Sayreville is a small borough and issuing 22,081 building permits since a mayor took office would be extraordinarily unlikely; local permit records and council minutes — which are public — show no corroboration of that figure or documented secret meetings with developers. Without verifiable municipal records or credible reporting, the claim is not supported.

claim: "In her campaign for president, Hillary Clinton has received $100 million in contributions from Wall Street and hedge funds."
rationale: Campaign finance records and independent analyses do not support the claim that Hillary Clinton’s presidential campaign directly received $100 million from Wall Street and hedge funds. Data from FEC reporting and nonprofit trackers show the finance industry contributed tens of millions (not $100M) to Clinton’s campaign and allied groups, and totals vary depending on whether you include party committees, super PACs, bundlers, or foundation donations. The specific $100 million figure appears to be an overstatement or a conflation of different funding sources and time periods.

claim: "PPP on average probably provided a grant of around $11,000 per employee."
rationale: The statement is unlikely to be accurate as a general average. PPP loans were structured to cover roughly 2.5 months of payroll (later flexibilities changed the period), and empirical analyses of program disbursements and job coverage have generally found lower per-employee funding when calculated across all loans and employees rather than the maximum allowable amount. Reported averages vary widely by calculation method and cohort, but many estimates of PPP dollars per job saved are below $11,000.

claim: "Gene Green is the NRA’s favorite Democrat in Congress. ... "It’s no wonder the congressman has a lifetime A rating from the NRA."
rationale: Calling Gene Green "the NRA’s favorite Democrat in Congress" is a subjective, non‑verifiable claim; it asserts a singular preference rather than a factual rating. It is true that Green, a Texas Democrat, historically received high NRA grades and endorsements (including an A rating in NRA scorecards), but labeling him the NRA's single "favorite" is opinion rather than an objective fact.

claim: "Four balanced budgets in a row, with no new taxes for anyone. The best job growth in 12 years. Nearly 130,000 new private-sector jobs. Merit pay to reward New Jersey’s best teachers, and the most education funding ever."
rationale: The statement mixes verifiable actions with misleading or disputed claims. While New Jersey enacted teacher-evaluation reforms and pilot merit-pay programs, the fiscal and jobs assertions are contested: budgets were formally balanced but relied on accounting shifts and delayed pension payments, the ‘‘no new taxes for anyone’’ pledge omits fee increases and other revenue changes, and the jobs/education-funding claims depend on timeframe and inflation adjustments and do not unambiguously match official series. Because key phrases are vague or contradicted by common fiscal accounting and labor-data practices, the overall multi-part claim is misleading.

claim: Only "18 percent of jobs are accessible by transit for metro Atlanta residents. 33 percent for those living in the city."
rationale: The numbers match published transit-access-to-jobs analyses for Atlanta: regional studies (e.g., Brookings-style transit-access metrics) have reported that roughly 18% of jobs in the Atlanta metro area are reachable by public transit, while about one‑third (≈33%) are reachable for residents of the City of Atlanta. These figures depend on the accessibility definition used (typical studies measure jobs reachable within a given transit travel-time threshold).

claim: With voting by mail, "you get thousands and thousands of people sitting in somebody's living room, signing ballots all over the place."
rationale: The claim portrays mail voting as routinely producing 'thousands' of people gathered in private homes signing ballots, which is not supported by evidence. In practice voters complete ballots individually at their own residences and return them by mail or secure dropboxes, with signature checks and chain-of-custody procedures; large-scale organized signing in living rooms has not been documented. While isolated illegal ballot-harvesting incidents exist, they are exceptions, not the norm described by the claim.

claim: "Heitkamp has voted against Trump 68 percent of time."
rationale: I could not verify a reliable source that Heidi Heitkamp 'voted against Trump 68 percent of the time.' Vote-alignment statistics vary by source and timeframe (some track votes with the president rather than 'against'), and no widely cited tracker lists exactly a 68% opposition rate for Heitkamp. The claim lacks a clear timeframe and definition of which votes are being counted, so it cannot be confirmed as stated.

claim: Says he and Mitt Romney "always said that we agree with the 2014 deadline" for leaving Afghanistan.
rationale: The statement presents a direct quote but gives no identifiable speaker or source, and I could not confirm a verifiable record of anyone saying the exact line that they "always said that we agree with the 2014 deadline." Public discussion of Afghanistan withdrawal timelines (including Romney's comments during 2012) does not substantiate this precise, attributed claim. Without a clear attribution and supporting primary source, the claim is not supported.

claim: "Corporate entities are paying a lot less taxes this year than they have in the past. Part of that is from a loophole in a bill that was passed in 2015."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and appears incorrect as stated: the major U.S. corporate tax law change that substantially lowered corporate taxes was the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (rate cut from 35% to 21%), not a 2015 bill. Corporate tax payments and effective rates do vary year-to-year due to profits, timing, and policy details, but there is no well‑known 2015 federal statute that created a broad loophole causing corporations to pay “a lot less” this year. Without a specified country, year, or identified statutory provision, the assertion is unsubstantiated.

claim: "Child support card" in Delaware "controls what mothers can and cannot buy with child support money."
rationale: This is false as stated. Child support is private financial support and, in the U.S., state disbursement methods (including debit cards) are generally a payment mechanism and do not impose categorical controls over what custodial parents may purchase. Restrictions on purchases apply to means-tested public benefits (SNAP/TANF) administered via EBT, not routine child-support payments.

claim: This is the first time since World War II that five nuclear-powered aircraft carriers were docked together.
rationale: The claim is misleading and likely incorrect. Nuclear-powered carriers did not exist in World War II (the first nuclear carriers entered service decades later), so the phrasing “since World War II” is odd; moreover there is no well-documented precedent-free record showing that five nuclear-powered carriers have never been in the same port before, but major carrier concentrations (though rare) have occurred and contemporary reporting of any such unprecedented gathering would note the novelty. Given the lack of clear evidence this is an unprecedented first and the ambiguous wording, the claim is judged false.

claim: Says Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger "faces espionage charges."
rationale: There are no known federal or state indictments charging Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger with espionage. Espionage charges are high-profile felony allegations that would be publicly filed and widely reported; public records and mainstream reporting do not show such charges against him. The statement appears to be a mischaracterization or rhetorical exaggeration rather than a factual legal claim.

claim: The U.S. "only ranks 25th worldwide on defense spending as a percentage of GDP."
rationale: This specific numeric ranking is misleading: U.S. military spending as a share of GDP is typically in the roughly 3–4% range, which puts it well below many small states and Gulf countries, but its exact global rank varies by year and data source. Some datasets place the U.S. around the mid‑20s in certain years, while others place it higher or lower, so the categorical claim that it “only ranks 25th worldwide” as a single definitive fact is inaccurate without a cited year and source.

claim: Under Mayor Angel Taveras "Providence’s bond rating was downgraded from A to BBB, two steps above junk-bond status."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and likely incorrect as stated. Credit ratings differ by agency (S&P, Moody’s, Fitch) and use different notches (A, A-, A+ etc.); saying Providence was downgraded “from A to BBB” without naming the agency and timeframe is misleading, and the characterization “two steps above junk” misstates how many notches separate BBB from speculative-grade. Available public accounts show varying downgrades and agency actions during Taveras’s term, but not a clear, single A→BBB two-step downgrade as asserted.

claim: "Biden’s plan will immediately let in 25,000 asylum-seekers who’d been waiting in Mexico as their cases were judged."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate: Biden-era announcements described processing up to 25,000 migrants per month at ports of entry or setting monthly intake caps for parole/asylum processing, not an immediate blanket admission of 25,000 people who had been waiting in Mexico. Remaining legal, vetting, and court constraints (and phased implementation) meant MPP/“Remain in Mexico” cases could not simply be instantaneously admitted en masse.

claim: Photo shows Joe Biden "doesn’t wear a mask on a plane."
rationale: The claim makes a specific factual assertion about a particular photo but no image or provenance was provided to verify identity, location, or timing. Without the original photo, metadata, or trustworthy reporting confirming it depicts Joe Biden aboard a plane and unmasked, the claim cannot be substantiated and may be a miscaption or taken out of context.

claim: Under his leadership, more people in Wisconsin "have access to health care."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as presented because it does not identify who "his" refers to, what time period is meant, or what metric defines "access to health care." Without a named leader, dates, and data (e.g., insurance coverage rates, Medicaid enrollment, clinic availability), the assertion cannot be confirmed. Some Wisconsin leaders have enacted policies that increased coverage for certain groups, but that does not validate the broad, context-free statement.

claim: A list shows over 14,000 dead people voted in Wayne County, Michigan.
rationale: Investigations by Michigan election officials and multiple independent fact-checkers found the circulated list was misinterpreted and inaccurate. Many entries were duplicates, matches to different people with the same names, records of people who died after casting lawful ballots, or clerical/data errors — not thousands of confirmed cases of deceased people voting in Wayne County.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez took a "$10 million payout from Netflix."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or financial disclosure showing Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez received a $10 million payment from Netflix. Public financial disclosures for members of Congress and contemporary news reporting do not record any such payout, and the claim has circulated as misinformation on social media.

claim: "27 U.S. Air Force pilots resign over COVID-19 vaccination mandate."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or official Department of Defense/Air Force report confirming that exactly 27 U.S. Air Force pilots resigned specifically over the COVID-19 vaccine mandate. Public reporting and fact-checkers found only isolated cases and broader numbers of separations for vaccine refusal, but not a verified count of 27 pilots resigning for that reason. The claim appears to be an unverified, rounded figure circulated on social media rather than a documented fact.

claim: Says Texas voters are being asked to act this November on a proposed constitutional amendment affecting property taxes.
rationale: The claim is ambiguous about which November and gives no specific amendment to verify, so I cannot confirm that Texas voters are being asked 'this November' to act on a property-tax constitutional amendment. While Texas does place proposed constitutional amendments (including some affecting property taxes) on November general-election ballots, confirming this specific statement requires the election year and amendment details. Without that context the assertion is unverifiable.

claim: Says President Barack Obama failed "to stand up for the bipartisan debt solutions of the Simpson-Bowles Commission."
rationale: The Simpson-Bowles commission released a bipartisan deficit-reduction plan in 2010 that neither Congress nor the Obama administration moved to enact as a package. President Obama praised the commission's work and adopted some similar ideas in later proposals, but he did not formally endorse or vigorously lead an effort to pass the commission's specific bipartisan package, so the characterization that he failed to stand up for those solutions is supported by the record.
cited_knowledge: Knowledge that the Simpson-Bowles commission issued recommendations in 2010, that Obama publicly praised but did not formally adopt the commission's full plan, and that Congress did not enact the commission's recommendations as presented.
safety_notes: Phrase 'stand up for' is subjective—could mean formal endorsement, active leadership to pass the plan, or support for individual ideas. Different interpretations affect the judgment.

claim: "I am the only (state attorney general) in America fighting to hold the big tech companies accountable for their behavior."
rationale: Multiple state attorneys general have opened investigations and filed lawsuits against major technology companies over antitrust, privacy, content moderation, and consumer-protection issues. Several multistate coalitions and individual AGs have publicly pursued Big Tech firms, so the claim of being the only state AG in America doing so is demonstrably incorrect absent a very narrow qualifier.

claim: "If you put the $47 billion in revenue (raised over 10 years by the Buffett rule) into infrastructure you could create 611,000 infrastructure jobs."
rationale: The statement is misleading because it mixes a ten-year revenue total with a jobs number without specifying whether those are job‑years or permanent positions. $47 billion divided by 611,000 jobs is about $77,000 per job, which plausibly represents one job‑year of spending, but spread over 10 years the $47 billion equals $4.7 billion per year and would sustain only about 61,000 jobs annually at that cost. Thus the claim overstates employment impact absent clarification of the time frame and job‑year assumption.

claim: Says "in this next biennium, the cost of primary and secondary education is going to increase by more that $1000 per student. Half of that $1000 – $500 per student – is accounted for by the increased cost of PERS alone."
rationale: The claim is specific but provides no jurisdiction or source and cannot be verified from general knowledge. State-by-state biennial budget documents are required to compute per‑student changes, and while PERS (public pension) costs have risen in some places, it's not possible to confirm that PERS alone will account for $500 of a >$1,000 per‑student increase without the cited budget arithmetic. Because the statement is precise yet unsupported, it should be treated as false until documentation is provided.

claim: "No one knows who bought the [38 Studios] bonds. And there was some language put in the bond offer that they must remain anonymous."
rationale: The claim is too absolute. While the ultimate beneficial owners of the 38 Studios bonds were not fully publicly disclosed, bond purchasers are recorded by the trustee/issuer and reporters and investigators have identified purchasers or intermediaries; there was no binding provision that forever forbade anyone from knowing who bought the bonds. Offering documents and book‑entry arrangements can limit public disclosure of beneficial owners, but that is not the same as a clause that legally forces permanent anonymity for all parties.

claim: Says under his leadership "Wisconsin median household income" is up 2.7%, while it is down 1.3% nationally under President Obama.
rationale: The claim is inaccurate or misleading. Census and BLS series show U.S. median household income rose during Barack Obama’s presidency overall, not down 1.3%, and the 2.7% Wisconsin increase is a narrow or cherry‑picked interval that does not support the broad comparative framing. Comparing different baselines/time windows or not adjusting consistently for inflation produces these conflicting percentages.

claim: "When Nancy Nusbaum was Brown County executive, spending went up nearly 50 percent."
rationale: I cannot confirm the specific claim that spending rose "nearly 50%" while Nancy Nusbaum was Brown County executive because I have no cited budget figures for the exact years of her tenure. Such a precise percentage requires examination of the county's annual budgets and the definition of 'spending' (total, operating, capital, or per‑capita), and without those records the claim is unsupported.

claim: "We admit more than 100,000 lifetime migrants from the Middle East each year."
rationale: The claim is implausible as stated because it provides no definition of “we” or of “lifetime migrants,” and available national immigration and refugee statistics do not show annual admissions from Middle Eastern countries exceeding 100,000 into major destination countries like the United States. Typical yearly counts of new permanent residents and resettled refugees from Middle Eastern countries have been substantially lower than 100,000 in recent years. Because the phrase is ambiguous, the specific numeric claim cannot be supported.

claim: Kathryn Starkey "aided and abetted the continued taxation on residents’ properties over 70 percent of the time by seconding motions and voting to keep the millage rate the same."
rationale: I cannot confirm the specific numeric claim. It asserts a precise frequency of voting/seconding ("over 70% of the time") and a culpable characterization ("aided and abetted") that would require consulting the official roll‑call records and meeting minutes for the relevant governing body and timeframe; those records are not available in my knowledge base. Because the statement is specific and unverified, I treat it as false pending review of primary voting records.

claim: Says Donald Trump has outlined "policies that read like a Kremlin wish list."
rationale: The statement is a value judgment rather than a verifiable fact — saying Trump’s policies “read like a Kremlin wish list” is an interpretive claim. While some of his stances (praising Putin, criticizing NATO, questioning Ukraine aid, and suggesting softer approaches to sanctions) align with Russian preferences, labeling them as a Kremlin wish list is subjective and not objectively provable. Given the ambiguity and reliance on opinion, the claim cannot be treated as a factual assertion.

claim: "It takes almost a year for a refugee to be processed in the United States."
rationale: The statement is overly broad and misleading: U.S. refugee processing times vary widely by program, nationality, and case complexity. While some refugees are processed in under a year, many undergo multi-year vetting (security checks, interviews, medical screening and clearance) and backlogs have often extended processing well beyond a year. Therefore saying it takes "almost a year" as a general rule is inaccurate.

claim: Kelly Loeffler has a "long history of donating to abortion-on-demand Democrats."
rationale: The claim overstates and mischaracterizes her record. Public contribution records show Loeffler made some donations to both Democrats and Republicans earlier in her business career, but there is no clear pattern constituting a “long history” of funding Democrats specifically for their support of unrestricted abortion; she is a Republican who ran as a conservative and has publicly supported anti‑abortion positions. The phrasing “abortion‑on‑demand Democrats” is partisan and not supported by a consistent donation history to such candidates.

claim: Says "$57,000 is the mean [income] in our state" for a family.
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it omits which state, which year, and which data source. State-level family mean (or household) incomes vary substantially and official figures from sources like the U.S. Census are needed to confirm whether $57,000 is accurate for any particular state and time period.

claim: Under New York's new abortion law, "If the baby was born alive, they would just let the baby expire."
rationale: This claim is false. New York’s Reproductive Health Act did not authorize allowing a liveborn infant to be left to die; federal and state law and standard medical practice require that infants born alive receive appropriate medical care. The RHA changed how abortion is regulated but did not remove legal or professional obligations to treat a baby born alive.

claim: The WIC program "is an incredibly cost effective program, serving nearly 10 million Americans each year and costing less than $100 per person. In my district, more than 18 percent of residents suffer from food insecurity and depend on WIC to make ends meet."
rationale: The claim mixes accurate praise with misleading numbers. Federal data show WIC has average monthly participation in the mid-to-high single millions (roughly 6–7 million) and while annual unique participants may be higher, characterizing it as "nearly 10 million" and costing "less than $100 per person" is inconsistent with typical per-participant spending figures and how costs are calculated. The local assertion that "more than 18 percent of residents ... depend on WIC" is implausible because WIC serves specific groups (women, infants, children) rather than the general population and food insecurity rates and program dependence vary widely by district.

claim: "According to the most recent report, Wisconsin’s high school graduation rates are also up again -- to third best in the country."
rationale: This claim overstates what available national data support. While Wisconsin has had a relatively high high-school graduation rate in recent years, national rankings vary by year and by data source (NCES/ACGR, state reports), and Wisconsin is not consistently listed as third-best in the most recent national datasets. Without a specific report and year, the assertion that it is "third best in the country" is not supported.

claim: "U.S. police killed more people in just one month than the U.K.’s did in over a century."
rationale: The claim is misleading and cannot be taken as a factual blanket statement. U.S. police kill on the order of hundreds to around a thousand people per year (roughly several dozen to ~100 per month), whereas deaths directly attributable to UK police (especially fatal shootings) are very rare over many decades; however the two systems count and classify deaths differently and including deaths in custody or restraint changes the comparison. Because the claim omits definitions and timeframes, it overstates a simple one-month vs. century comparison.

claim: Says Donald Trump "spent the least amount of money of any of the competitive primary contenders that he beat so badly."
rationale: This claim is false as stated. In the relevant GOP primary (commonly 2016), Trump was not the absolute lowest spender — major rivals such as Jeb Bush, Marco Rubio and Ted Cruz spent as much or substantially more than Trump, while some lower-tier candidates spent less, so he was not uniquely the least‑spending competitive contender he defeated.

claim: "The Red Cross sells your donated blood to hospitals for $150 and then that hospital charges you thousands for a blood transfusion."
rationale: This claim is misleading. Blood centers (including the Red Cross) do charge hospitals fees for processed blood products to recover collection, testing and storage costs, but per‑unit prices vary by product and region and are not a universal fixed $150. Hospitals may then bill patients for transfusion services (administration, facility and provider fees), which can produce high bills, but the simple ‘‘$150 sale then thousands charged’’ framing is inaccurate and oversimplified.

claim: The recently passed transportation funding bill is a billion-dollar tax increase for Georgians.
rationale: The statement is misleading because it asserts a specific, one-time "billion-dollar tax increase" without identifying the bill or timeframe. Recent Georgia transportation packages typically combine smaller tax/fee increases, bond measures, and reallocated funds, and official fiscal notes report revenues over multi-year periods rather than a single lump-sum billion-dollar tax on residents. Confirming the true fiscal impact requires the exact bill text and the legislature's revenue estimates.

claim: "In two terms in the Missouri General Assembly, Jason Kander passed ZERO bills that were signed into law."
rationale: This claim is incorrect. Public legislative records and contemporary fact-checking show that during his two terms in the Missouri House Jason Kander sponsored or co-sponsored legislation that was enacted; therefore it is not true that zero of his bills were signed into law. The blanket assertion omits distinctions like co-sponsorship and small/local measures that are part of the official record.

claim: Says Ted Cruz "has pledged to eliminate" the U.S. Department of Education, which would end federal aid to college students.
rationale: The claim mixes a true element and a false implication. Ted Cruz has publicly pledged in the past to eliminate the U.S. Department of Education, but abolishing the Department would not automatically end federal student aid because Pell Grants and federal student loan programs are created and funded by federal law and could be transferred or continued by other agencies unless Congress repealed those laws. Saying elimination would end federal aid overstates the causal effect of abolishing an agency.

claim: Claims the U.S. military is using "polymer drone flies" that look and act like a large fly.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the U.S. military is deploying ‘polymer drone flies’ that look and act like large flies. While researchers (including DARPA-funded projects and academic teams) have built insect-scale flying prototypes in labs, these are experimental prototypes, not operational, widely used military systems; many viral images are toys or models misrepresented. The claim overstates and misattributes research prototypes as active U.S. military deployment.

claim: Marijuana today is "genetically modified," with THC levels that "far surpass the marijuana" of the 1970s.
rationale: The claim mixes a true fact (average THC concentrations in many commercial cannabis products are substantially higher than the low single-digit percentages typical of much 1970s street cannabis) with a false implication: modern cannabis has generally been selectively bred/hybridized, not broadly produced by genetic engineering. While breeding and cultivation techniques have increased potency, commercial cannabis is not generally a transgenic "genetically modified organism."

claim: Malia Obama was "among 10 arrested in racist Antifa attack," and the cop who arrested her was "found dead under suspicious circumstances."
rationale: This claim is false. There are no credible news reports, police records, or reliable fact-checks showing Malia Obama was arrested in a racist Antifa attack, nor any evidence that an officer who arrested her was later found dead under suspicious circumstances. The story appears to originate from viral social-media rumors and has been debunked by reputable sources.

claim: Says the Vatican confirmed that Pope Francis and two aides tested positive for coronavirus.
rationale: This claim is false: while the Vatican did confirm that some Vatican employees/aides tested positive for COVID-19 during the early pandemic, it never confirmed that Pope Francis himself tested positive. Vatican statements and subsequent reporting indicated aides tested positive and the Pope was not reported or confirmed to have COVID-19.

claim: "Last year, ExxonMobil made $19 billion in profit. Guess what. They paid zero in taxes. They got a $156 million refund from the IRS."
rationale: The claim mixes a plausible profit number with incorrect tax assertions. Although ExxonMobil reported roughly that scale of net income in the referenced year, its public filings and contemporaneous reporting show it recorded and paid substantial income taxes (and any refunds or credits are subject to accounting and timing rules), so the blanket statement that it paid zero in taxes and got a $156 million IRS refund is inaccurate.

claim: New York is "leading the nation with the lowest imprisonment rate of any large state"
rationale: The claim is not reliably true as stated. While New York’s imprisonment rate has fallen and is lower than many states, rankings depend on the year and how “large state” is defined, and several states (e.g., Massachusetts, New Jersey, Minnesota) have had equal or lower imprisonment rates in recent years, so New York is not unambiguously the lowest.

claim: Says to Hillary Clinton, "You heard what I said about (the Trans-Pacific Partnership trade deal), and all of a sudden you were against it."
rationale: There is no verifiable record of the exact quoted line being said to Hillary Clinton. While Clinton did shift to opposing the Trans‑Pacific Partnership publicly in 2015 after pressure from primary opponents and activists, the specific quoted phrasing appears to be an unsourced paraphrase rather than a documented statement.

claim: The seven nations identified in Donald Trump's travel ban were "identified by the Obama administration as the seven most dangerous countries in the world in regard to harboring terrorists."
rationale: The Trump executive order listed seven countries (Iran, Iraq, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria, Yemen), but the Obama administration did not formally label those seven as the "most dangerous countries" for harboring terrorists. The Obama State Department issued travel warnings and maintained a separate "state sponsors of terrorism" list and other country-specific advisories, but it did not produce an official seven-country ranking described in the claim. Some of the named countries appeared in various advisories or designations, but not as a single ordered list of the seven most dangerous.

claim: President Barack Obama supports immigration amnesty.
rationale: As president Obama repeatedly supported legalization measures for undocumented immigrants, including advocating comprehensive immigration reform with a pathway to citizenship and taking executive actions (DACA in 2012 and proposing DAPA in 2014) that deferred deportations. Opponents labeled those policies 'amnesty,' and his public positions consistently favored relief and legalization rather than strict mass deportation.

claim: Kyle Rittenhouse was an "armed person" crossing state lines when he came to Kenosha protests in 2020.
rationale: Contemporary reporting and court records show Kyle Rittenhouse traveled from Antioch, Illinois to Kenosha, Wisconsin on August 25, 2020 and was carrying an AR-15–style rifle during the incidents there. That description — an armed person crossing state lines to attend the Kenosha protests — is factually accurate.

claim: Says Connie Mack "failed to pay his child support."
rationale: I am not aware of reliable, verifiable reporting or court records establishing that the politician Connie Mack (commonly referring to Connie Mack IV) was legally found to have “failed to pay his child support.” There have been occasional accusations or campaign-era attacks, but I could not confirm an adjudicated failure to pay child support from widely reported sources.

claim: "Just passed into law today: You cannot go 5 miles over speed limit" in North Carolina.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that North Carolina just enacted a statewide law prohibiting driving 5 mph over the posted speed limit. Changes to state traffic law require passage by the General Assembly and a governor’s signature and would be widely reported; no such statewide statute or emergency enactment has been documented. Enforcement practices or local ordinances vary, but that is different from a new statewide ban announced 'today.'

claim: Says four Republican representatives "voted to impeach President Donald Trump."
rationale: This is inaccurate as stated. In the House's second impeachment (Jan 13, 2021) ten Republican members voted to impeach President Trump; the first House impeachment (Dec 2019) had no sitting House Republicans voting to impeach (Rep. Justin Amash had already left the GOP and voted as an independent). So saying "four Republican representatives voted to impeach" misstates the known vote counts without additional context.

claim: "95 percent of the income gains in the last few years have gone to the top 1 percent."
rationale: The statement is misleading because it gives no timeframe or income definition. Some researchers (e.g., Saez/Piketty using tax data) reported that roughly 95% of income gains went to the top 1% over a specific short recovery window after 2009, but that finding does not generalize to 'the last few years' and shares vary widely by time period, dataset, and whether capital gains or pre/post-tax income are counted.

claim: Robert Mueller’s investigative team has "13 hardened Democrats, some big Crooked Hillary supporters, and Zero Republicans."
rationale: The claim is false. Public reporting and campaign-donation records show Mueller’s team was composed of career DOJ prosecutors with mixed political donations and affiliations, not exclusively Democrats, and some staff had donated to Republicans or had no partisan donations. The specific phrase '13 hardened Democrats, some big Crooked Hillary supporters, and Zero Republicans' is misleading: the roster size and partisan makeup varied and cannot be accurately summarized that way.

claim: Says Donald Trump "cashed in" on Sept. 11,  "collecting $150,000 in federal funds intended to help small businesses recover — even though days after the attack Trump said his properties were not affected."
rationale: I could not find clear, reliable evidence that Donald Trump personally "cashed in" $150,000 of federal 9/11 recovery funds while publicly saying his properties were unaffected. While federal small-business disaster programs did send assistance in the aftermath and some firms in Manhattan received loans or grants, contemporary documentation tying a $150,000 federal payment directly to Trump personally (and contradicting his public comments) is not established. The claim appears to conflate different programs, recipients, or statements without clear sourcing.

claim: Says with the ongoing economic downturn, child abuse is on the rise.
rationale: The claim is too general and not reliably supported as a universal fact. While economic downturns increase stress and risk factors linked to child maltreatment and some studies have found rises in abuse during recessions, empirical data vary by place and by how abuse is measured (reports, hospitalizations, self-reports). Reporting can fall when schools or services are disrupted, so an asserted contemporaneous rise everywhere with the ‘ongoing economic downturn’ is not firmly established.

claim: Says the Trump administration’s new policy for legal immigrants on welfare "has been around for a while. This is not a new thing that the president is trying to implement here, that the United States has been this way."
rationale: While the public‑charge concept (denying admission or green cards to those likely to become primarily dependent on the government) is longstanding, the Trump administration's 2019 policy significantly expanded which benefits (including non‑cash programs like SNAP, most Medicaid, and housing aid) could count against immigrants — a change that was new, legally contested, and later rescinded. Therefore saying the specific policy “has been around for a while” and is not new is misleading.

claim: A record number of immigrants not from Mexico are "being apprehended at the border."
rationale: U.S. Customs and Border Protection data and reporting through 2023–early 2024 showed historically high numbers of "other-than-Mexico" (OTM) encounters at the southern border, and multiple news outlets and officials described those non-Mexican apprehensions as record monthly/annual totals. However, counts differ by reporting period and whether agencies label events as "encounters," "apprehensions," or "inadmissibles," so exact records depend on the metric and timeframe used.

claim: Says Jimmy Carter was the last "U.S. president to say flat out those (Israeli) settlements are illegal."
rationale: The claim is misleading. While Jimmy Carter has explicitly called Israeli settlements illegal, he was not the definitive “last” U.S. president to address their legality: U.S. administrations after Carter have repeatedly criticized settlements and the U.S. position has shifted over time, and international bodies (and many U.S. officials) have characterized settlements as lacking legal validity. Whether a later sitting U.S. president used the exact phrase “illegal” varies by administration and context, so saying Carter was the last to “flat out” call them illegal is inaccurate.

claim: "The latest unemployment numbers have shown that nearly 315,000 Americans have simply given up hope when it comes to finding a job."
rationale: The statement gives a precise, recent figure but provides no date or source; BLS reports a distinct category called “discouraged workers” and totals fluctuate monthly, and the most recent releases around my knowledge cutoff do not consistently show exactly 315,000. Without a specific report or date the claim is unsupported and likely inaccurate as stated.

claim: "Obamacare isn't helping anyone."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement that no one benefits from the Affordable Care Act (Obamacare), which is incorrect. The law expanded coverage to millions through Medicaid expansion and marketplace subsidies, allowed young adults to remain on parental plans, and instituted protections for people with preexisting conditions, though some individuals have faced higher premiums or limited plan choices in certain markets.

claim: "President Obama pledged to go through the budget 'line by line,' but on his watch, non-defense spending has spiraled out of control, increasing by 67 percent in the last year alone."
rationale: While President Obama did publicly say he would go through the budget "line by line," the statement that non-defense spending "increased by 67 percent in the last year alone" is not supported by federal budget data. No major federal budget category labeled "non-defense spending" rose by 67% in a single year during his presidency; year-to-year increases were much smaller even when stimulus and crisis-era outlays are included. The claim conflates rhetoric with an exaggerated and unsupported numeric assertion.

claim: "When they say Mexico can't pay for the wall, I say of course they can. We have a trade deficit with Mexico that's unbelievably big. ... It's billions and billions of dollars -- far more than what we're talking about for the wall."
rationale: The United States has historically run a multi‑billion‑dollar goods trade deficit with Mexico (typically tens of billions per year in recent years), which is larger than many independent estimates of the one‑time cost of a border wall (commonly cited in the low tens of billions). Saying the trade gap is "billions and billions" and larger than the wall cost is a fair characterization of available data. This statement, however, conflates the existence of a trade deficit with the political and legal feasibility of forcing Mexico to pay.

claim: "Florida is one of only three states that require licenses for commercial interior designers."
rationale: This is false. While Florida has a certification/registration regime for interior designers, many other states also regulate interior designers through licensure, registration, certification or title-protection, so Florida is not literally one of only three states with any requirement for commercial interior design. State rules differ by scope (title protection vs. practice restrictions), so counting depends on definitions and recent law changes.

claim: Says CNN deleted an online poll showing Bernie Sanders won the first Democratic presidential debate to help out Hillary Clinton.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that CNN deleted a post-debate online poll to favor Hillary Clinton. Independent fact-checkers investigated similar claims after the early Democratic debates and found no proof CNN removed a poll showing Sanders as the winner; online, transient polls are often edited or taken down for routine or technical reasons and are not conclusive evidence of manipulation.

claim: Palin "inherited a city with zero debt, but left it with indebtedness of over $22-million."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate. Wasilla carried municipal obligations before Palin took office and the $22 million figure conflates different kinds of long‑term bonded obligations and later financing across multiple administrations; fact-checkers have determined Palin did not literally inherit zero debt nor personally cause a jump to $22 million. The statement misstates the city’s financial history and timing.

claim: "Autopsy results from Vince Foster’s exhumed body — Cause of death to be changed!"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Vince Foster’s remains were exhumed or that an official cause-of-death determination has been changed. Multiple official investigations and medical examiners concluded Foster died by suicide in 1993, and no reputable news outlets or government officials have reported an exhumation or revised autopsy. The claim matches recurring conspiracy-language rather than documented facts.

claim: Republicans included "the Akin amendment in the Republican Party platform, which bans abortion, even for rape victims."
rationale: The 2012 Republican platform committee adopted language proposed by Rep. Todd Akin that opposed abortion and did not include exceptions for rape and incest, which many reported as Akin's amendment. However, a party platform is a policy statement and does not itself "ban" abortion — only laws or court rulings can ban abortions. The claim conflates adoption of platform language with an actual legal ban.

claim: "There are hit squads being trained all over this country" to violently oppose a second term for President Donald Trump.
rationale: There is no credible, corroborated evidence or public reporting that organized "hit squads" are being trained nationwide to violently oppose a second Trump term. Law enforcement statements and major news investigations have documented isolated plots, threats, and arrests, but those incidents do not substantiate the sweeping claim of training "all over this country."

claim: "Not even Tim Kaine is willing" to say he trusts Hillary Clinton.
rationale: False. Tim Kaine, Hillary Clinton's 2016 running mate, publicly campaigned for her and repeatedly defended and endorsed her judgment; there is no reliable record that he categorically refused to say he trusted her. While specific interview excerpts might show him answering carefully, the overall public record shows he expressed support and trust.

claim: "The Books Sarah Palin tried to have banned."
rationale: The claim as written is vague and presents no specific titles or documented incidents; there is no well-documented, verifiable list of “books Sarah Palin tried to have banned.” While Palin has been involved in disputes over curriculum and criticized certain materials, authoritative reporting does not support a generalized assertion that she attempted to ban a set of books. Without concrete examples or reliable sourcing, the blanket claim is not supported.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Trey Gowdy’s 8-year-old son found dead "in a dumpster in D.C."
rationale: This claim is false. There are no credible news reports, official statements, or public records confirming that Rep. Trey Gowdy’s 8-year-old son was found dead in a dumpster in Washington, D.C.; the story has circulated as a fabricated social media hoax and has been debunked by reliable outlets and lack of official corroboration.

claim: Says William Taylor and George Kent, the public witnesses in the House impeachment inquiry, are "Never Trumpers."
rationale: Labeling William Taylor and George Kent as 'Never Trumpers' is misleading. Both are career State Department diplomats who served under multiple administrations and testified as professional witnesses in the impeachment inquiry; there is no public record that they were part of the political 'Never Trumper' movement or repeatedly campaigned against Trump. The term has been applied by partisan commentators, but it does not accurately describe their professional backgrounds or documented political activism.

claim: "Barack Obama will somehow manage to add more than $8 trillion to the national debt, which is more debt than the 43 presidents who held office before him compiled together."
rationale: The claim mixes a true and a false element. It is true that during Barack Obama’s two terms the federal debt rose by more than $8 trillion (roughly $9–10 trillion from early 2009 to early 2017). However, it is false that this increase exceeded the cumulative debt accumulated under the 43 presidents before him, since the debt entering his presidency was already over $10 trillion, larger than his incremental increase.

claim: When it comes to urgency on passing a budget repair bill, "there’s no rush on this thing" because the fiscal year doesn’t end until June 30, 2011.
rationale: Even if a fiscal year technically ends June 30, that does not mean there is no urgency to pass a budget repair bill. State budgets commonly require timely enactment to authorize spending, address current-year shortfalls, and manage cash flow; a delay can force stopgap measures or legal problems. Thus the claim that the fiscal-year end date alone negates any rush is misleading and incorrect.

claim: In Virginia, "people are going and getting marriage licenses who are 12 and 13, and 14 and 15 years old."
rationale: Presented as a current fact, the claim is false. Virginia law now requires parties to be 18 to marry (the state has moved to ban child marriage), so 12–15 year‑olds are not currently eligible to get marriage licenses; though historical marriage records in Virginia do show rare cases of minors as young as 12 being issued licenses in past years. The claim conflates past occurrences with current law.

claim: "We are within the margin of error."
rationale: The claim is context-free and cannot be verified as stated. Whether a result is "within the margin of error" requires the specific reported estimate, the stated margin of error, and the direction/threshold being tested; without those details the statement cannot be confirmed. Given the lack of supporting numbers or context, I must treat the claim as unsupported.

claim: Says Miami Congressman Carlos "Curbelo supports drilling offshore" and "repeatedly voted against President Obama's ability to fight pollution and combat climate change."
rationale: The claim is misleading. While Curbelo did vote with Republicans on some energy and regulatory measures, he also was a bipartisan advocate for addressing climate change (he co‑founded the Climate Solutions Caucus and sponsored carbon‑pricing proposals) and publicly opposed drilling near South Florida beaches. Saying he “supports drilling offshore” and “repeatedly voted against Obama’s ability to fight pollution and combat climate change” overstates and simplifies a mixed record of votes and public positions.

claim: "Michelle Nunn’s own plan says she funded organizations linked to terrorists."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Michelle Nunn's campaign plan or public materials admit she funded organizations linked to terrorists. Her record is in nonprofit and volunteer work and references to supporting local NGOs or partners do not equate to funding terrorist-linked groups; the claim appears to be a distortion without supporting documentation.

claim: Says the USMCA is the "biggest trade deal ever made."
rationale: The USMCA is a trilateral modernization of NAFTA covering the United States, Mexico, and Canada, but it is not the largest trade deal ever. Larger arrangements—most notably the European Union single market and the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP)—cover bigger combined economies and populations and are commonly described as larger trade pacts. Thus calling USMCA the "biggest trade deal ever made" is inaccurate.

claim: "President Obama himself attempted to filibuster Justice Alito, who now sits on the Supreme Court."
rationale: False.
