claim: "When the law stopped Tony Evers from revoking a teacher's license for viewing pornography, Tony worked with lawmakers from both parties to change the law so offenders could be kicked out of the classroom."
rationale: As Wisconsin state superintendent Tony Evers publicly complained that changes in state law had limited the Department of Public Instruction’s ability to revoke licenses in cases such as teachers viewing pornography, and he publicly worked with legislators from both parties to pursue statutory changes to strengthen disciplinary tools so offending teachers could be removed from classrooms. The basic sequence — a legal limit on revocation followed by bipartisan legislative efforts advocated by Evers to restore or expand removal authority — is accurate, though exact bill numbers and timing vary by incident.

claim: "People are less likely to just vote for party now. … They’re looking at the personalities."
rationale: The claim is an oversimplification. While candidate personality can influence some swing voters and modern campaigns often highlight traits, political science research shows party identification remains the single strongest predictor of vote choice in many democracies and partisan polarization and sorting have kept party-based voting high. Thus it is misleading to state broadly that people are now less likely to 'just vote for party.'

claim: Says George Soros and Bill Gates are funding a bioweapons lab in Sierra Leone that caused the Ebola outbreak.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that George Soros or Bill Gates funded a bioweapons laboratory in Sierra Leone or that such a lab caused any Ebola outbreak. WHO and independent epidemiological investigations attribute Ebola outbreaks to zoonotic spillover and subsequent human-to-human transmission, and public records of the Gates Foundation and Open Society Foundations show philanthropic health and civil-society funding, not offensive bioweapons programs. Assertions tying these donors to causing Ebola are conspiratorial and contradicted by available scientific and funding records.

claim: "Actually, I won Wisconsin."
rationale: The statement is ambiguous because it does not identify who “I” refers to or which election or year is meant, so it cannot be verified as presented. Election outcomes for Wisconsin are specific to particular races and years and are publicly documented; lacking that context there is no evidence to treat this as true. By default I label it false pending specification and corroborating facts.

claim: Since he took office as Milwaukee County executive, "we have never raised" bus fares and "this year there’ll be a million route-miles more than there were five years ago."
rationale: The claim is unlikely to be true. Milwaukee County Transit operations underwent pandemic-related service cuts and later restorations, and agencies nationwide adjusted fares, promotions, and fare-collection practices since 2020; annual route- or revenue-miles also fell sharply in 2020 and only gradually recovered, so an unqualified statement that fares were "never raised" and that there are a million more route-miles than five years ago is not supported without precise definitions and dates.

claim: "Kim Martin Morrow the CEO of Netflix has just been charged with 15 charges for child pornography"
rationale: This claim is false. Netflix's chief executives are Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters (co-CEOs) and there are no credible reports that any Netflix CEO named 'Kim Martin Morrow' has been charged with 15 counts of child pornography. The name does not match Netflix leadership and major news outlets and official statements have not reported such a charge, suggesting this is misinformation or a mistaken identity.

claim: Says he "was the only Republican" to vote against creating a House panel to investigate Planned Parenthood.
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it gives no name, date, or specific roll-call to check; without that context I cannot confirm the claim. Congressional roll-call records are public and multiple votes to create investigative panels involving Planned Parenthood have had more than one Republican dissent in different Congresses, so the unsupported blanket claim is unreliable.

claim: "Portland Schools spend $500K to deem PB&J sandwiches racist."
rationale: This claim is false. Reliable fact-checks and statements from Portland-area school officials found no evidence the district spent $500,000 to declare peanut butter and jelly sandwiches 'racist'—the story arose from mischaracterized guidance and conflated spending on unrelated equity training and food-program expenses. No official policy bans or labels PB&J as racist.

claim: Says Gov. Tony Evers’ 2021-22 state budget "increases taxes $1 billion +"
rationale: The claim is not supported by the record. While Gov. Tony Evers proposed various revenue changes, the enacted 2021-22 state budget did not implement a net tax increase of more than $1 billion; the Republican-controlled Legislature removed or altered major tax hikes and the final actions did not match a $1B+ tax increase. Independent reporting and budget summaries of the enacted measures do not show a $1B-plus statewide tax increase attributable to Evers’ 2021-22 budget.

claim: Ron Klein "sponsored an amendment that specifically allows price gouging."
rationale: There is no credible legislative record showing Rep. Ron Klein sponsored an amendment that expressly 'allows price gouging.' Price-gouging laws are primarily state statutes and Congressional amendments rarely state they permit gouging; allegations claiming he sponsored such an amendment appear to be mischaracterizations or lack supporting evidence. Without a clear citation to a specific bill or amendment text, the claim is not supported.

claim: "If they made no changes whatsoever, the [state employees pension] plan still had enough money to go forward for approximately the next 16 years."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it does not identify which state's plan, the date, or the actuarial assumptions used. Pension solvency horizons depend critically on assumptions about investment returns, employer/employee contributions, and benefit payouts, so a blanket claim of 'approximately the next 16 years' cannot be confirmed without the specific plan's actuarial report. Given the missing context, the claim is judged false as stated.

claim: Says "city leadership is threatening to lay off police and emergency services personnel to balance the budget."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it names no specific city, officials, statement, or source; I could not confirm any explicit threat to lay off police and emergency services without those details. While municipalities sometimes consider personnel reductions to close budget gaps, asserting a general threat across unspecified 'city leadership' is unsupported. Because no concrete evidence was provided, the claim cannot be treated as fact.

claim: "Nearly 200,000 Florida voters may not be citizens."
rationale: The headline number came from a database match that flagged up to roughly 180,000 DMV records as noncitizen at one point, but that did not mean nearly 200,000 registered voters actually were noncitizens. State reviews and independent fact-checks found many false positives (people who later naturalized, duplicate or mismatched records, or registrations not tied to those flags) and only a very small number of confirmed noncitizen registrants or voters. The raw flag count is misleading and does not support the claim as stated.

claim: Says Conor Lamb "ran on a campaign that said very nice things about me."
rationale: There is no independently verifiable evidence in the prompt identifying who said this or citing a source showing Conor Lamb's campaign explicitly ran ads or messaging that praised that person. Without a named speaker, date, or supporting documentation, the claim cannot be confirmed. Given the lack of context and verifiable sourcing, the appropriate determination is that the assertion is unproven and treated as false for fact-checking purposes.

claim: "I never was in favor of shutting down the government. … (I) voted to fund the government fully."
rationale: The statement cannot be verified as presented because no speaker, dates, or specific votes are identified. Without that context, one cannot confirm that the person 'never' favored a shutdown or that every relevant funding vote they cast was to fully fund the government; it is possible they voted to fund in at least one instance while supporting or voting for measures that could lead to a shutdown in others. Given the lack of specific, corroborating roll-call and public-record evidence, the claim is treated as unproven and therefore labeled false.

claim: Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp "mandates restaurants reopen"
rationale: Governor Kemp issued an executive order during the COVID-19 pandemic that allowed restaurants to resume in-person dining under safety restrictions and preempted local governments from imposing stricter closures, but he did not issue a directive that forced individual restaurants to reopen. Businesses retained the choice to remain closed, so characterizing the action as a mandate to reopen is inaccurate.

claim: I spent only $36.29 on my campaign for governor.
rationale: The claim is implausible without corroborating, state-level campaign finance records. Gubernatorial campaigns ordinarily incur expenses far beyond $36.29, and candidates must file detailed expenditure reports with state election authorities that would confirm such an unusually low total. In absence of specific evidence or filings proving this exact amount, the statement should be considered false.

claim: Says U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement "will be at every polling station" on Nov. 3, 2020.
rationale: There is no evidence that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement planned to be "at every polling station" on November 3, 2020. ICE publicly denied any intent to conduct enforcement operations at polling places and multiple fact-checkers and news organizations found the claim unsubstantiated. Logistics, legal protections around polling places, and lack of any announced nationwide deployment make the statement implausible.

claim: "We have more people working in the state of New Jersey today than we've ever had in our history."
rationale: The claim is unverified and ambiguous: whether it means 'jobs located in New Jersey' (BLS payroll jobs) or 'residents employed' (household survey) and the exact date matters. My training through mid‑2024 indicates New Jersey employment recovered after the pandemic and approached or exceeded prior peaks on some measures, but I do not have definitive, up‑to‑date BLS/NJ Dept. of Labor data to confirm an all‑time high 'today.' Given the ambiguity and lack of current confirmation, I judge the categorical claim false pending specific, current statistics.

claim: The COVID-19 vaccines "were released to the public after only two months of testing in healthy humans."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate. COVID-19 vaccines underwent preclinical work and multi‑phase clinical trials (phase 1/2 and large phase 3 trials) that began months before emergency authorizations; the EUAs in late 2020 were supported by large trials with many months of data. A related factual point often misrepresented is that regulators required a median of about two months of safety follow‑up after vaccination for EUA consideration — that is not the same as ‘only two months of testing.’

claim: Says his barehanded catch posted on YouTube is real.
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and provides no verifiable details (who, which video, or independent corroboration). Many online "bare‑handed catch" clips are staged, edited, or misleading, and without provenance or third‑party verification the assertion that the posted clip is real cannot be substantiated. Given the lack of evidence, the responsible conclusion is that the claim is unverified and should be treated as false until authenticated.

claim: "If we went back to the obesity rates that existed back in the 1980s, the Medicare system over several years could save as much as a trillion dollars."
rationale: There is no well-established, peer-reviewed estimate showing that returning to 1980s obesity rates would yield up to $1 trillion in savings to Medicare alone over a defined multi-year period. Published figures for obesity-attributable medical costs are substantial on a national level (hundreds of billions per year across all payers in some estimates), but Medicare-specific savings are a fraction of those totals and depend heavily on timeframe and modeling assumptions, so the blanket trillion-dollar claim is unsupported as stated.

claim: "I'm the only candidate in the Democratic primary, or actually on either side, who Wall Street financiers and hedge fund managers are actually running ads against."
rationale: The absolute claim that one person is the only candidate in either party being targeted by Wall Street financiers or hedge-fund managers is not supported. Public ad-tracking and reporting show finance-industry–backed groups and wealthy financiers have paid for ads opposing multiple candidates (especially progressive Democrats) and have also been active in Republican contests, so this is not uniquely true.

claim: Says the Obama Administration has fulfilled all of Texas’ requests for fire management assisting grants.
rationale: This is inaccurate. Fire Management Assistance Grants (FMAGs) are awarded by FEMA on a case-by-case basis, and during the Obama administration some Texas requests were approved while others were not or were only partially funded. The absolute claim that "all" requests were fulfilled is not supported by available records and is implausible given how FMAG determinations are made.

claim: The stimulus bill "promised to keep unemployment under 8%."
rationale: No major US stimulus law contains a binding promise to keep unemployment under 8%. Supporters sometimes claimed a stimulus would substantially reduce job losses or prevent unemployment from rising as high, but the legislation itself does not guarantee a specific unemployment-rate cap and actual rates depend on many economic factors beyond any single bill.

claim: "Even today part of Romney’s fortune is invested in China."
rationale: Public reporting shows Romney historically had ties to investments (via Bain Capital) in companies that did business in China, but there is no clear, current public evidence that a portion of his personal fortune is directly invested in China today. As a public official he has used blind trusts and diversified U.S.-based funds in more recent disclosures, which reduces the likelihood of identifiable direct Chinese holdings. The claim is ambiguous about timing and what counts as "invested in China," so it cannot be treated as a verified present fact.

claim: Says Don Lemon’s show has been canceled and he is leaving CNN.
rationale: This is accurate: CNN announced Don Lemon was terminated and his primetime show ended in April 2023 following an internal investigation, and he subsequently left the network. Major news outlets at the time reported his departure and the cancellation of his show.

claim: Says Mitt Romney belittled middle-class tax cuts "as nothing more than 'little Band-Aids.' "
rationale: I am not aware of a verified record of Mitt Romney literally calling middle‑class tax cuts “nothing more than ‘little Band‑Aids.’” Romney did criticize short‑term or targeted tax measures during his 2012 campaign as insufficient long‑term solutions, but the specific quoted phrase appears to be a paraphrase or misattribution rather than a documented direct quote. Given the lack of a clear, sourced instance of him using those exact words, the claim as stated is not supported.

claim: "This week the House of Representatives voted to remove the word ‘lunatic’ from federal law."
rationale: I have no reliable record up to my June 2024 knowledge cutoff that the House of Representatives held a vote that week specifically to remove the word “lunatic” from federal law. Congress has periodically considered updating archaic language, but the claim as stated gives no date and appears to conflate occasional code-revision efforts or proposals with a distinct, recent House vote. Without a specific date or bill number this claim is not supported by verifiable information I have.

claim: "All non-US citizens, illegal or not, will be provided with free health care services."
rationale: This claim is false. U.S. federal law does not guarantee universal free health care to all non‑U.S. citizens regardless of immigration status; most public insurance programs (Medicaid, ACA marketplace) generally require lawful presence, though emergency care is required by EMTALA and some states/localities provide limited or subsidized services to certain immigrants. There is no current nationwide policy that provides free health care to every non‑citizen, documented or undocumented.

claim: Photo shows "the aftermath of the ‘CHOP’ Zone’ in Seattle, WA. July 2020."
rationale: I cannot verify that an unspecified photo depicts the aftermath of Seattle’s CHOP in July 2020 without seeing the image, its metadata, or independent sourcing. Many images circulating online have been misattributed to CHOP, so a claim about a photo’s subject/time requires reverse-image searches and provenance checks; absent that evidence the claim should be treated as false.

claim: "Congressman Kasich wants to use our tax dollars to give secret bonuses to his corporate friends."
rationale: The statement asserts a specific intent and a secret program but there is no public record showing a Congressman Kasich proposing to use taxpayer money to pay undisclosed bonuses to corporate allies. Publicly known Kasich (John Kasich) voting and policy history centers on tax cuts and business incentives, not secret bonus schemes; without a cited bill or statement this accusation is unsubstantiated.

claim: Says a "Local Hero" was "arrested after killing 30 pedophiles in murder spree"
rationale: There are no credible news reports or reliable sources documenting a person described as a “Local Hero” being arrested after killing 30 pedophiles; a killing spree of that scale would have generated widespread national and international coverage. The phrasing matches common sensationalized or fabricated social-media posts rather than verified journalism, so the claim is not supported by available evidence.

claim: Health reform will "give every American the same opportunity" to buy health insurance the way members of Congress do.
rationale: Health reform (e.g., the Affordable Care Act) expanded access through exchanges, subsidies, and Medicaid expansion but did not give every American the exact same access or employer-style benefits that members of Congress receive. Members of Congress participate in the Federal Employees Health Benefits program with employer contributions and broad plan choices; most Americans remain in employer plans, on the exchanges with income-based subsidies, or subject to state Medicaid rules, so the opportunities and subsidies are not identical. Therefore the claim that reform gives every American the same opportunity as members of Congress is inaccurate.

claim: MSNBC’s Mika Brzezinski said, "Elon Musk is trying to control how people think. That’s our job."
rationale: This appears to be a misquote. Coverage and transcripts of Mika Brzezinski’s remarks show she criticized Elon Musk for trying to influence public discourse and did not state “That’s our job”; if anything she framed such control as inappropriate for a private company or media figure. The claim flips her intended meaning.

claim: "Many of the people in DACA, no longer very young, are far from ‘angels.’ Some are very tough, hardened criminals."
rationale: The claim overstates the criminality of DACA recipients. DACA eligibility requires background checks and bars people with serious felonies or significant misdemeanors, and multiple studies and government data indicate DACA recipients and immigrants have lower rates of serious crime than native-born populations; isolated cases exist but do not support the claim that many are "hardened criminals." While many recipients have aged since 2012, that does not imply widespread violent criminality.

claim: "A lot of the move to free the slaves ... did not come from the federal government. It came from a growing movement among the people, particularly people of faith."
rationale: The statement is broadly accurate: the abolition of slavery in the U.S. was driven for decades by a popular abolitionist movement in which religious groups (e.g., Quakers, evangelical Christians), activists, the Underground Railroad, petitions, and abolitionist presses played major roles in shifting public opinion and pressuring politicians. That grassroots momentum helped make federal measures—Lincoln’s Emancipation Proclamation and ultimately the 13th Amendment—politically possible, but the legal end of slavery required federal action.

claim: "Florida Governor Rick Scott now listed as ‘critical’ after bizarre hurricane cleanup accident."
rationale: The claim is false. Rick Scott is a U.S. senator (not the current Florida governor), and there are no credible news reports or official statements indicating he was critically injured in a hurricane-cleanup accident. The story appears to be a viral/misleading social-media claim rather than a verified incident.

claim: "On my last trip to New Hampshire, I think I met the guy who founded the first and only bank since Dodd-Frank passed, since the financial crisis. One bank in the country."
rationale: This is incorrect: numerous new banks (de novo charters) have been created in the United States since the financial crisis and since Dodd‑Frank (2010). Regulatory records and industry reporting document multiple bank charters and recent fintech bank charters, so it is not true that only one bank was founded in the country since Dodd‑Frank.

claim: Starbucks executive "believes white men are the root of all evil."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that any current or former Starbucks executive publicly stated that "white men are the root of all evil." The claim appears to originate from social media misattribution, satire, or a fabricated quote rather than any verified statement by a named Starbucks official.

claim: "When Fidel Castro came into office, you know what he did? He had a massive literacy program."
rationale: This is accurate. After Fidel Castro's 1959 revolution the Cuban government launched a nationwide literacy campaign in 1961 that mobilized thousands of volunteer teachers and dramatically reduced illiteracy across the island. The program is widely cited as a major early policy achievement of the revolutionary government.

claim: "People were hopeless. Sixty percent of the population, 70 percent of the population wanted to live somewhere else. . . . By the time I left, 70 percent wanted to stay."
rationale: The claim presents specific polling-style percentages (60–70% wanting to leave, later 70% wanting to stay) without any identified time, place, or source. I could not verify these exact shifts in widely available public-opinion data, and such large, precise reversals would require documented polls or surveys. Without sourcing, the assertion is unsubstantiated and therefore judged false.

claim:
Says 
"With nearly 75 percent of Americans supportive of the construction of the pipeline, Schrader needs to explain to Oregon families why he voted against this needed project."
rationale: The statement is unsupported and ambiguous: it cites “nearly 75 percent of Americans supportive” without naming a specific pipeline, poll, or date, and public opinion on pipeline projects varies widely by the project and timing. Because the claim lacks that necessary context and no consistent national poll shows ~75% support for a generic “construction of the pipeline,” the broad assertion and implied criticism of Schrader’s vote cannot be verified as stated.

claim: Says Vicks VapoRub caused a child’s death.
rationale: There is no reliable, widely corroborated evidence that Vicks VapoRub directly caused a child’s death when used as directed. Health authorities and the manufacturer warn against use on infants under two and against ingestion or intranasal application, and misuse or preexisting conditions could plausibly lead to harm, but the blanket claim is unsubstantiated without specific case details or coroner findings.

claim: "More people die from hands, fists, feet, than rifles."
rationale: The claim is unsupported as stated. Global and national homicide statistics show that firearms and sharp instruments account for a large share of lethal violence, while deaths solely from bare hands/fists/feet (blunt-force-only homicides) are a smaller proportion. Also, the term “rifles” is a subset of firearms and many jurisdictions record higher firearm deaths overall, so the blanket comparison is misleading without specifying geography and timeframe.

claim: Says Thom Tillis "refuses to say what we should do to combat ISIS."
rationale: The claim is vague and unsupported as a blanket statement — there is no clear, documented instance showing Thom Tillis categorically 'refused to say what we should do to combat ISIS.' Public records show he has made statements endorsing use of military force, coalition-building, and other measures against ISIS, so portraying him as universally refusing to state a plan is misleading. Without a specific time or quote, the claim overgeneralizes and lacks evidence.

claim: Says the U.S. Department of Justice has "seen in the past" that police department "consent decrees don’t work, that there’s very little change, that oftentimes immediately after a consent decree goes into effect, crime actually goes up."
rationale: The U.S. Department of Justice has not issued a general finding that consent decrees “don’t work” or that they typically cause immediate increases in crime. DOJ routinely uses consent decrees and pattern-or-practice settlements to require police reforms and has documented improvements in many cases; empirical studies of crime after decrees are mixed and do not show a consistent, ubiquitous spike caused by decrees. The quoted blanket claim misrepresents DOJ practice and the available evidence.

claim: "Some neighborhood schools are closing."
rationale: As a general, context-free statement this matches widespread, ongoing patterns: many school districts periodically close or consolidate neighborhood schools because of declining enrollment, budget shortfalls, or facility issues. Without a specified time or place the claim is nonspecific but accurately reflects reality in numerous jurisdictions.

claim: Says a change in law he carried stopped a $100 million tax increase in the Dallas school district.
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because it gives no named individual, no specific statute, nor a timeframe or documentation tying a legislative change to preventing a $100 million tax increase for the Dallas school district. Stopping a district tax increase would be documented in legislative records, school budget calculations, and media reporting; absent those specifics the assertion is unverified and likely misleading.

claim: "McCain lobbied for (a) $10-million pork project honoring conservative justice."
rationale: There are no well-documented reports showing Senator John McCain (or another prominent McCain) lobbied for a specific $10 million earmark to honor a conservative Supreme Court justice. McCain was widely known as an opponent of earmarks and pushed earmark reform, and mainstream reporting does not corroborate this specific claim. Given the lack of specific details (which McCain, which justice, what project), the claim is unverified and likely false.

claim: "Here are the facts: there is no massive wave of migrants pouring into California. Overall immigrant apprehensions on the border last year were as low as they’ve been in nearly 50 years (and 85 percent of the apprehensions occurred outside of California)."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate overall. Recent official CBP encounter/apprehension data show overall border encounters in the past few years were very high compared with historical levels, not “as low as they’ve been in nearly 50 years.” It is true that California accounts for a relatively small share of Southwest border apprehensions (most occur in Texas and other sectors), but that partial fact doesn’t make the overall statement correct.

claim: Says the private sector in Texas created 1 million jobs over the past decade.
rationale: This is likely false because official payroll data indicate Texas added well more than one million private‑sector jobs over the last ten years, so saying only “1 million” understates the growth and lacks precision. Exact counts depend on the chosen start/end months and whether the speaker means private‑sector payrolls vs. household employment, but BLS nonfarm payroll series for Texas show net private‑sector job gains exceeding a million in the relevant decade. The claim as stated is imprecise and misleading.

claim: "We've seen local union after local union rush to their school boards, their city councils, their technical school boards and rush through contracts in the past two weeks that had no contributions to the pension and no contribution to health care."
rationale: The claim is a broad, time‑bounded assertion about many unions and multiple types of local boards, but it provides no jurisdiction or examples and I find no corroborating evidence that a widespread wave of contracts in the past two weeks universally eliminated pension and health contributions. While isolated agreements could omit employer or employee contributions in some places, the sweeping phrase “local union after local union” is unsupported without specific contract documents or local reporting. Therefore the generalized claim is not supported as stated.

claim: "If your employer is mandating any pokes, do not quit. Make them fire you. That way you get unemployment benefits."
rationale: This statement is an oversimplification that is not universally true. Eligibility for unemployment benefits depends on the jurisdiction and the reason for separation: voluntary quits are often disqualifying, but being fired can also be disqualifying if the employer shows the firing was for misconduct (and outcomes in cases of refusing medical/vaccine mandates have varied).

claim: When Joe Biden’s son Hunter was serving as "a director to Ukraine’s largest private gas producer," the elder Biden "threatened to withhold $1 BILLION in U.S. aid to Ukraine if they didn’t fire a prosecutor looking into" the gas company.
rationale: The claim mixes a true element and a false implication. It is true Joe Biden, as VP, publicly pressured Ukraine in 2015–16 and said he threatened to withhold about $1 billion in U.S. loan guarantees to push for the removal of prosecutor Viktor Shokin, and Hunter Biden did serve on the board of Burisma (a large private gas company). However, credible reporting and investigations found there was no evidence Shokin was actively pursuing a Burisma probe at the time, and the international community sought Shokin’s removal over corruption and ineffectiveness rather than to stop an active investigation into Burisma.

claim: "Yale study: Vaccinated people more likely to be infected than those without the jab."
rationale: This blanket claim is false. There is no credible Yale study that shows vaccination increases the risk of infection; randomized trials and real-world studies generally show vaccines reduce risk of infection (though protection can wane and be lower against some variants). Reports claiming the opposite typically misinterpret short time windows, subgroup analyses, or are confounded by differences in testing, behavior, or prior immunity.

claim: "No candidate has run more negative ads in American history than Barack Obama did in 2008, especially in the general.’’
rationale: The claim is false. While the 2008 campaigns (including outside groups) featured many negative advertisements, independent ad-tracking and historical analyses do not support that Barack Obama personally ran more negative ads than any candidate in U.S. history; earlier races (e.g., Lyndon Johnson vs. Goldwater in 1964, Nixon-era campaigns, and George H.W. Bush vs. Dukakis in 1988) produced widely documented, highly negative advertising efforts. Moreover, much of the 2008 negativity came from McCain, third-party groups, and contrast ads rather than solely from Obama’s campaign.

claim: When the United States "first created the federal income tax, frankly, nobody below a million dollars a year paid anything."
rationale: This is incorrect. The modern federal income tax (after the 16th Amendment) was established by the 1913 Revenue Act, which imposed a 1% tax on net incomes above roughly $3,000 (with exemptions) plus surtaxes on higher amounts — so many people with far less than $1 million were subject to tax. Earlier Civil War–era income taxes also had much lower thresholds. Therefore it is false that “nobody below a million dollars a year paid anything.”

claim: During the past four years, "average wages have barely budged."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and misleading. Nominal average wages in the U.S. have risen noticeably over the past four years, while inflation caused real (inflation‑adjusted) wages to fall in 2022 and then recover partially, so it is not accurate to categorically say average wages have 'barely budged' without specifying which wage measure and whether it’s adjusted for inflation.

claim: Says George Soros’s son is married to Adam Schiff’s sister.
rationale: There is no evidence that any of George Soros’s children are married to a sister of Rep. Adam Schiff. Public biographies and reputable fact-checks show no marital or familial link between the Soros family and Schiff’s immediate family, indicating this is a baseless rumor.

claim: Says Ted Cruz "never denied" his father was photographed with Lee Harvey Oswald.
rationale: Ted Cruz and his campaign publicly denied that his father, Rafael Cruz, was the man in the widely circulated photo with Lee Harvey Oswald. Both Ted Cruz and Rafael Cruz gave on-the-record statements rejecting the identification, and multiple contemporary fact-checks concluded the claim was unproven or false.

claim: "Doctors who discovered cancer enzymes in vaccines all found murdered."
rationale: This claim is false. There is no credible evidence that vaccines contain so-called 'cancer enzymes,' nor is there any verified record or pattern of doctors who made such a discovery being 'all found murdered.' The allegation appears to be an unsubstantiated conspiracy theory with no support from peer-reviewed science, regulatory agencies, or reputable reporting.

claim: Says Gov. Andrew Cuomo and Democratic lawmakers are "granting free tuition to illegal immigrants while closing Excelsior Scholarship applications to citizen students."
rationale: This claim misstates policy. New York did expand eligibility for some state financial aid to undocumented immigrants under recent legislation, but there is no evidence the state "closed" Excelsior Scholarship applications to citizen students as part of that change. Excelsior remains an application-based program with eligibility rules and deadlines; undocumented eligibility and temporary administrative changes are distinct issues rather than a deliberate cut-off of citizens' access.

claim: Says a "5G LAW PASSED while everyone was distracted" with the coronavirus pandemic and lists 20 symptoms associated with 5G exposure.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a secret or widely unnoticed “5G law” was passed during the COVID‑19 pandemic, and major health and regulatory bodies have found no causal link between 5G exposure at regulated levels and the broad set of non‑specific symptoms often listed in such claims. The purported list of 20 symptoms aligns with long‑standing misinformation linking radiofrequency radiation to diverse health complaints without supporting epidemiological or mechanistic proof.

claim: Says Marco Rubio "knows full well I voted for his amendment to increase military spending to $697 billion."
rationale: The claim presents an unattributed quotation asserting a vote for a Marco Rubio amendment to raise military spending to $697 billion, but there is no verifiable record or widely reported statement matching that exact quote or a clear Rubio amendment setting a $697 billion figure. Public roll calls and media coverage of defense appropriations and amendments show different amounts and do not corroborate this specific claim. Because the speaker, date, and legislative context are missing, the assertion cannot be verified as factual.

claim: Under the 2017 tax law, "people who make under $75,000 will have their taxes raised in 2021 and every 2 years after that until 2027."
rationale: The 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act did not create a scheduled biennial tax increase for people earning under $75,000 beginning in 2021. Most individual tax cuts in that law are set to expire after 2025 (not produce automatic hikes every two years), and the law does not single out a $75,000 threshold for recurring scheduled increases; any tax changes for specific households depend on expiring provisions, indexing and individual circumstances.

claim: "In America, there is a father who is holding down two jobs and paying more taxes than the richest 400 families in America."
rationale: The claim is implausible and unsupported by available data: the 400 wealthiest American families together pay very large amounts in federal and other taxes that far exceed what a single person (even someone holding two jobs) would pay. IRS tax distribution data and wealth estimates for the Forbes 400 show aggregate tax liabilities for that cohort are orders of magnitude larger than typical individual tax bills. No credible evidence was found showing a lone father’s tax payments exceed the taxes paid by the richest 400 families.

claim: Says the D.C. city council passed a law banning lethal rat trapping.
rationale: There is no clear evidence that the D.C. Council enacted a blanket law banning all lethal rat trapping. Recent D.C. actions have targeted specific products and methods (for example restrictions on glue traps or certain rodenticides and moves toward integrated pest management), but they have not enacted an across-the-board prohibition on lethal rodent control by residents and pest professionals. The claim appears to conflate proposals or targeted bans with a universal ban on lethal trapping.

claim: Since 2009, the Ohio Republican Party has made more contacts with voters — nearly 6.6 million — than any other GOP state organization in the nation.
rationale: I could not find independent, verifiable national data showing the Ohio Republican Party has made nearly 6.6 million voter contacts since 2009 and more than any other GOP state party. The figure appears to originate from party self-reporting, and there is no standardized, publicly available dataset comparing contact totals across all state GOP organizations. Because reporting methods and definitions of "contacts" vary, the specific comparative claim is unverified.

claim: "90,000 Californians are unsheltered and homeless."
rationale: This statement is consistent with recent HUD Point-in-Time counts showing roughly 89,000 unsheltered people in California, so rounding to 90,000 is reasonable. The unsheltered share of California’s homeless population has been large in recent PIT counts, making the claim a fair approximation for those data years.

claim: Says Marilinda Garcia supports "$150 billion in new taxes."
rationale: There is no clear public record or statement showing Marilinda Garcia endorsed a policy described as "$150 billion in new taxes." As a Republican congressional candidate she generally opposed broad tax increases, and claims of a $150 billion figure appear to be an attack-ad-style distortion or taken out of context rather than a documented pledge she made. Without a specific bill, time frame, or quote tying her to that exact number, the assertion is not supported.

claim: Says Iranian Gen. Qassem Soleimani "was a designated terrorist by President Obama, who didn't do anything about it."
rationale: The claim conflates different actions and timelines. The U.S. did impose sanctions on Iranian entities and individuals over many years, but Soleimani was not publicly labeled an FTO by President Obama, and while Obama did not order Soleimani killed, he did authorize actions against Iranian-backed proxies; the blanket phrasing 'designated terrorist by President Obama, who didn't do anything about it' is therefore misleading and inaccurate.

claim: "There's no negative advertising in my campaign at all."
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim that cannot be verified without identifying which campaign, timeframe, and how “negative advertising” is defined. In modern elections, campaigns often run or are associated with direct, contrast, or third‑party negative ads, so absent exhaustive evidence it is not reasonable to accept “no negative advertising at all.”

claim: "Shakespeare said: ‘I always feel happy. You know why? Because I don’t expect anything from anyone. Expectations always hurt. Life is short. So love your life. Be Happy. & Keep smiling."
rationale: The quoted lines do not appear in Shakespeare's plays or sonnets and use modern colloquial phrasing (e.g., 'You know why?', 'Keep smiling', ampersand) inconsistent with Early Modern English. This is a common modern aphorism frequently misattributed to historical figures rather than found in Shakespeare's verified corpus.

claim: Says his plan would cut taxes without increasing the deficit.
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as written because it omits who “he” is and which specific plan is meant; without a named actor and a scored legislative text it cannot be confirmed. In general, many politicians claim tax-cut plans won’t raise deficits, but independent budget scores (CBO/JCT/analysts) typically show tax cuts increase deficits unless matched by explicit offsets or rely on optimistic growth assumptions.

claim: "After a decade of progress, the rate of uninsured children is now rising."
rationale: The statement is too general and not currently supported. In the U.S. there was about a decade-long decline in uninsured children after expansion of CHIP/ACA, and a small uptick in the late 2010s, but more recent data show stabilization or improvements rather than a clear continuous rise "now." Without a specified country and timeframe the blanket claim that rates are "now rising" is not accurate.

claim: Obama's budget plan would "take national debt up to about 80 percent of gross national product. ... Historically, it's been about 40 percent."
rationale: Contemporary CBO projections around the time of President Obama’s budgets showed federal debt held by the public rising toward roughly 70–85% of GDP over the following decades under then‑current policies, so the “about 80 percent” figure is a reasonable summary of those projections. Likewise, long‑run historical averages of U.S. federal debt (excluding wartime spikes) have been near the 35–45% of GDP range, so saying “historically, it’s been about 40 percent” is broadly accurate. The claim compresses projection timing and terminology, but the magnitudes are supported by official budget projections and historical debt ratios.

claim: "TSA WILL ACCEPT DRIVERS PRIV CARDS FOR ID AT THE AIRPORT"
rationale: The claim is overbroad. Whether TSA will accept a "driver's privilege" card depends on the issuing state and whether the card is REAL ID–compliant; many driver privilege cards are not REAL ID acceptable and therefore cannot be used for federal air travel ID after REAL ID enforcement. TSA accepts only forms of ID it recognizes under federal rules, so some privilege cards will be refused.

claim: Says John F. Kennedy "smoked cannabis in the White House, while president, because he suffered from severe back pain and Addison's disease."
rationale: There is no credible historical evidence that President John F. Kennedy smoked cannabis in the White House. Contemporary medical records and detailed biographies document extensive treatment for chronic back pain (including injections, opioids and other drugs) but do not substantiate marijuana use, and Addison's disease is not a well-supported diagnosis in his medical records as a reason for cannabis use.

claim: Regarding her State Department email practices, "my predecessors did the same thing."
rationale: The blanket claim is false. While some prior Secretaries of State occasionally used non-official or personal email accounts for limited communications, none are documented to have maintained a private, non-governmental email server or conducted State Department business on the scale and manner that Hillary Clinton did. Independent reporting and official records found predecessors used personal addresses only sporadically and did not replicate the centralized private-server setup Clinton employed.

claim: Says that as president, Barack Obama has not gone to the Texas-Mexico border
rationale: The claim that President Barack Obama never went to the Texas–Mexico border is false. Public presidential travel records and contemporary news reports show he visited border areas and federal border facilities in Texas during his presidency, including trips tied to immigration and border-security issues. Therefore the categorical assertion that he never went is incorrect.

claim: "Since 1990, in inflation-adjusted dollars, per-student funding of the (Florida) state university system from general revenue has dropped by about $4,000."
rationale: The general claim that per-student state general-revenue support in Florida fell since 1990 is directionally correct, but the precise drop of “about $4,000” cannot be confirmed without specifying the measure, inflation index, and student-count method. Different analyses (FTE vs. headcount, general revenue only vs. total state funding, and choice of inflation adjustment) produce varying magnitudes, often in the several-thousand-dollar range but not uniformly ~$4,000. Because the statement gives a specific dollar change without those details, I judge it not reliably supported as stated.

claim: Says Texas schools have had "massive increases" in class sizes with Rick Perry as governor.
rationale: Statewide data from Rick Perry's tenure (2000–2015) do not support a uniform, "massive" increase in class sizes; average class sizes and pupil–teacher ratios shifted only modestly and trends differed by grade and district. Some local districts experienced notable increases due to enrollment growth or budget constraints, but that is not the same as a statewide massive rise under Perry.

claim: "The administration raises revenue for nationalized health care through a series of new taxes, including a light switch tax that would cost every American household $3,128 a year."
rationale: The claim is false. No credible federal policy or administration has proposed a literal 'light switch tax' that would cost every American household $3,128 per year; that specific levy and dollar figure have been debunked. Major health‑care revenue proposals (e.g., the ACA or Medicare‑for‑All proposals) include various taxes or offsets but not a universal per‑household light‑switch charge of that magnitude.

claim: Says Joe Biden has a medical device implanted in his skull so he can hear someone give him answers to questions.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that President Joe Biden has a secret medical implant in his skull to feed him answers. Public medical disclosures, news reporting, and observation of many public appearances provide no support for such a claim, and it would require a large, verifiable conspiracy to be true. The assertion appears to be a conspiracy theory without factual basis.

claim: U.S. Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz "has blamed the Republicans for the creation of Hamas."
rationale: There is no credible record in major reporting or primary-source quotes showing Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz saying Republicans "created" Hamas. While she has criticized Republican foreign-policy stances or rhetoric at times, that is different from a literal claim that the GOP founded or created the militant group Hamas. The broad assertion appears to be a mischaracterization or exaggeration of her remarks.

claim: "Satan flashed in the halftime Super Bowl satanic ritual."
rationale: The claim asserts a supernatural event (Satan physically appearing or "flashing") during a Super Bowl halftime show; there are no credible reports or evidence that any supernatural being appeared. Halftime shows are staged entertainment with performers, costumes, and visual effects, and sensational interpretations often stem from conspiracy theories or misread symbolism rather than documented fact.

claim: Says Congressmen Paul Ryan and Todd Akin co-sponsored legislation "to limit federal funding for abortion to victims of ‘forcible rape.’"
rationale: Contemporaneous reporting and fact‑checks after Todd Akin’s 2012 remarks noted that both Akin and Rep. Paul Ryan had sponsored or co‑sponsored House anti‑abortion legislation (around 2011–2012) that restricted federal funding exceptions and used language distinguishing ‘forcible rape’ or similarly narrow rape exceptions. Those measures aimed to limit taxpayer‑funded abortions to very narrow categories, effectively excluding many rape claims.

claim: "8% of the votes cast" in Michigan’s Aug. 4 primary, 864 mailed ballots, came from dead voters. "NOTHING TO SEE HERE!!!"
rationale: The claim misstates and misinterprets the facts. The 864 figure that circulated referred to mailings or records linked to deceased registrants in state data or to ballots mailed to addresses later identified as deceased — not to 864 confirmed votes counted from dead people, and 864 would be a tiny fraction of total ballots cast, not 8%. Michigan officials and contemporary fact-checks explained many of those mailings were data errors or occurred before a voter’s death and were not counted as votes.

claim: A recall election for Wisconsin governor would cost "$7.7 million -- $7.7 million that may already be allocated to merit raises for teachers or health care for the poor or school books for your kids."
rationale: The $7.7 million figure has been cited in some news reports and agency briefings as an estimate for a single statewide recall step, but official estimates for a full gubernatorial recall (primary plus general) varied and were not universally $7.7M. The second part — that this exact sum "may already be allocated to merit raises for teachers or health care..." — is speculative and misleading because election costs are budgeted differently and would not directly represent a specific pre-committed line-item for raises or health care. Overall the claim mixes a selective cost estimate with an unsupported claim about pre-allocated spending, making it misleading/false.

claim: "California won’t let law enforcement officers like you and your people transfer prisoners to ICE custody or even to communicate with ICE that you’re about to release them from your custody — people that ICE is looking for."
rationale: The claim is an overbroad characterization of California law. California's Values Act (SB 54) and related statutes restrict routine cooperation with ICE—for example, jurisdictions generally may not hold people solely on ICE civil detainers or turn over people without a judicial warrant—but they include exceptions (judicial warrants, written consent, certain serious criminal cases, or other limited circumstances). Thus it is false to say California categorically bars all transfers or any communication with ICE.

claim: Since 2009, "after-tax incomes are up nearly 14 percent."
rationale: The statement is unverified as presented because it omits the population, data source, and end date needed to check it. Different official series (median household income, after-tax disposable income from BEA or CBO, or Census after-tax estimates) show different percentage changes since 2009—some measures rise into the low double digits while others rise less or fluctuate—so the blanket claim “after-tax incomes are up nearly 14 percent” cannot be confirmed without more context. Given the ambiguity and variability across reputable data sources, the claim as stated is misleading.

claim: "In six years, (U.S. Rep. Gary) Peters introduced zero bills that became law."
rationale: False. Gary Peters served in the U.S. House from 2009–2015 and congressional legislative records indicate he was primary sponsor of at least one measure that was enacted; the statement that he introduced zero bills that became law misstates the legislative record. The claim also appears to conflate introduction, sponsorship, and cosponsorship definitions.

claim: Most of Kathy Manning’s donors are from out-of-state.
rationale: There is no clear, corroborated evidence that a majority of Kathy Manning’s donors are from out-of-state. Campaign contribution patterns for House members typically include substantial in-state support, and claims about a majority require checking FEC or OpenSecrets data for a specific time period and metric (number of donors vs dollars). Without that specific filing data, the assertion is unproven and likely inaccurate.

claim: "More people now die in Wisconsin from drug overdoses than car crashes."
rationale: Recent years' data from the CDC and Wisconsin health authorities show that drug overdose deaths in Wisconsin have increased and exceeded deaths from motor vehicle crashes. Multiple state and national reports since about 2017 indicate overdose fatalities surpassed traffic fatalities in Wisconsin and have remained higher in subsequent years.

claim: Gina Raimondo "paid 70 million in taxpayer dollars to millionaire hedge fund managers."
rationale: The claim is misleading. While Rhode Island’s public retirement system paid tens of millions in fees to private equity and hedge fund managers during periods when Gina Raimondo served as state treasurer and governor, those were investment fees paid from pension assets over time rather than a single $70 million direct payout by Raimondo from general taxpayer funds, and the specific figure and description of recipients as 'millionaire hedge fund managers' is not supported as stated.

claim: Says North Carolina Republican Senate candidate Thom Tillis "called Obamacare ‘a great idea.’ "
rationale: The claim presents a direct quote that Tillis called Obamacare “a great idea.” Contemporary reporting and fact-checks from his 2013–2014 campaign show he made limited positive remarks about the concept of expanding coverage (e.g., saying it was “not a bad idea” or that some elements were a “good idea”) but did not literally say it was a “great idea,” and he subsequently opposed the Affordable Care Act. Thus the specific quoted wording is inaccurate.

claim: Says Rep. Martha McSally "has repeatedly tried to limit women’s access to birth control, and she even cosponsored a bill to make contraception more expensive for women."
rationale: McSally has a voting and sponsorship record of supporting measures that reduce mandated contraceptive coverage (for example backing broader religious/conscience exemptions and votes to restrict Planned Parenthood funding). Those actions have been described by advocates and fact-checkers as attempts to limit access to birth control and would likely make contraceptives more costly for some women by removing insurance coverage. The claim summarizes this pattern accurately, though the exact bills and effects vary by text and context.

claim: "But for immigrants, we would have a contracting population..."
rationale: The claim is too general and therefore misleading: whether a population would contract without immigrants depends on the specific country and time period. Many high‑income countries with below‑replacement fertility would indeed see population decline without immigration, but many countries (and the U.S. in parts of its recent history) still have enough births to avoid immediate contraction. Without specifying which country and timeframe the statement cannot be accepted as universally true.

claim: "China has made enormous progress in its human rights. That is a fact recognized by all the people in the world."
rationale: The claim mixes a subjective praise with a universal assertion. While China has made measurable social and economic advances (notably large-scale poverty reduction and infrastructure/health improvements), its human-rights record remains widely disputed and criticized—credible reports cite mass detention in Xinjiang, restrictions in Tibet and Hong Kong, and limits on free expression—so it is false that such progress is a fact 'recognized by all the people in the world.'

claim: "The president is advocating a drone strike program in America."
rationale: There is no credible public evidence that the U.S. president has advocated creating a program to carry out drone strikes on American soil. Presidents have authorized overseas drone strikes for counterterrorism, but U.S. domestic law and constitutional protections make a formal program of lethal drone strikes inside the country legally and politically extraordinary and unreported. Thus the claim is not supported by known facts.

claim: "Democrat Senators high-five after voting in favor of late-term abortion."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a group of Democratic senators collectively high-fived specifically 'after voting in favor of late-term abortion.' Footage that circulates on social media is often miscaptioned — when senators are seen celebrating, it typically follows a procedural or unrelated vote (or the defeat of an amendment), not a singular, explicit vote to authorize 'late-term abortion.' Senate votes are on specific bills or amendments and are part of the public record; the claim conflates or misrepresents that context.

claim: "There is a 34 percent increase in violent crime in the state of California. … And that’s just within the last year."
rationale: Statewide official data from California DOJ and FBI reporting does not show a roughly 34% single‑year jump in total violent crime for the state in recent annual reports; year‑to‑year changes in statewide violent crime have been much smaller and any very large percentage increases were limited to specific cities, categories (e.g., homicides) or short anomalous periods. The claim appears to conflate or misstate the geographic scope, timeframe, or specific crime category.

claim: "Hedge fund managers and others in private equity pay much lower (tax) rates on their income than do truck drivers and teachers and nurses."
rationale: Many hedge fund and private equity managers receive large portions of pay as carried interest or long-term gains taxed at the preferential capital gains rate (plus NIIT and state tax), while truck drivers, teachers, and nurses are paid wages taxed as ordinary income and subject to payroll taxes. As a result, analyses and reporting have found that some investment managers can have substantially lower effective federal tax rates than typical wage earners. That said, outcomes vary by individual compensation structure and taxes paid at state/local level.

claim: Says Mitt Romney and Paul Ryan would "eliminate the guarantee of Medicare."
rationale: Romney and Ryan endorsed transforming Medicare from a guaranteed, defined-benefit program into a premium-support/voucher-style system under plans promoted in 2012. Paul Ryan authored the proposal and Romney backed replacing the traditional Medicare guarantee for future beneficiaries, which critics described as eliminating the guaranteed benefit.

claim: "Actress Emma Stone: ‘For the first time in history we have a president that…"
rationale: The claim is an incomplete, truncated quote attributed to Emma Stone with no verifiable source. Reliable news outlets and fact‑checks do not document a verified public statement by Emma Stone beginning 'For the first time in history we have a president that...' and such snippets are commonly misattributed on social media.

claim: Says Sens. Lisa Murkowski, Susan Collins and Mitt Romney "are pro-pedophile."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Sens. Lisa Murkowski, Susan Collins, or Mitt Romney have expressed support for or advocated legalization or endorsement of sexual activity with minors. Public records, speeches, and voting histories show no statements endorsing pedophilia; claims calling them "pro-pedophile" appear to be rhetorical smears rather than factual descriptions of their positions. Given the seriousness of the accusation, the lack of verifiable supporting evidence makes the claim false.

claim: Says "John James supported Betsy DeVos’ agenda to cut public school funding and put it into wealthy private schools instead."
rationale: This claim overstates the record. John James has publicly supported Betsy DeVos and school‑choice policies such as vouchers and education savings accounts that critics say can divert money from public schools, but there is no clear public statement from James explicitly saying he wanted to cut public school funding or to direct it specifically to “wealthy” private schools. Characterizing his support as an intent to fund wealthy private schools is an interpretive leap beyond the available evidence.

claim: "It costs more to live in many Florida cities than New York City."
rationale: This is inaccurate as stated. New York City is consistently among the most expensive U.S. cities on broad cost-of-living and housing measures, while the majority of Florida cities (Miami, Tampa, Orlando, Jacksonville, Fort Lauderdale, etc.) have lower overall living costs than NYC; only a small number of exclusive Florida enclaves can exceed NYC prices for certain luxury properties. Because the claim asserts that 'many' Florida cities cost more than New York City, it overstates the reality.

claim: The novel coronavirus was "man-made."
rationale: Multiple independent genomic analyses and assessments by virologists find no signatures of genetic engineering in SARS-CoV-2 and show it is closely related to known bat coronaviruses with patterns consistent with natural evolution. Major public-health agencies and peer-reviewed studies conclude the virus is not man-made, though the precise zoonotic pathway remains under investigation.

claim: Says Democratic Senate candidate "Bruce Braley voted to cut $700 billion from Medicare to support Obamacare."
rationale: This claim is misleading. Bruce Braley did vote for the Affordable Care Act as a House member, and that law included reductions in projected Medicare spending often cited around $700 billion over a decade, but those were cuts to future payment rates (largely to Medicare Advantage plans and providers) and reductions in projected spending — not direct cuts to benefits for current Medicare beneficiaries. Framing it as Braley having voted to "cut $700 billion from Medicare to support Obamacare" implies benefit cuts and a direct, one-time rollback of Medicare benefits, which is inaccurate.

claim: "There are precious few religions that actually say you cannot" get vaccinated.
rationale: Most major world religions (Christianity, Islam, Judaism, Hinduism, Buddhism) do not have doctrines that categorically ban vaccination; objections typically come from specific denominations, sects, or individuals rather than whole religions. Only a small number of religious groups or movements have explicit teachings discouraging medical interventions, so the claim that few religions actually say you cannot get vaccinated is accurate.

claim: Under my platform, "I will make no changes to the current (Medicare) system for current retirees and anyone approaching retirement."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it lacks a named speaker, specific platform document, and timeframe; blanket promises like “no changes” are rarely strictly true once detailed policy proposals are examined. Many campaigns that promise to leave Medicare for current retirees intact have nonetheless proposed funding, benefit-implementation, or drug-pricing changes that can indirectly alter the program’s operation or future costs. Without the exact platform text and context this assertion cannot be validated as a factual, unconditional guarantee.

claim: "In 1968, a full-time worker earning minimum wage, could actually support a family of three above the poverty line. Today, that same worker would earn less than the poverty line for a family of two."
rationale: This claim accurately reflects widely reported comparisons: the 1968 federal minimum wage was at its peak in real terms and, when inflation-adjusted, yielded annual full-time earnings that exceeded the official poverty threshold for a three-person family. The current federal minimum ($7.25/hr) yields about $15,080 annually for full-time work, which is below recent official poverty thresholds for a two-person household (~$17K–$19K depending on year).

claim: Six states "decided to stop counting" votes as Donald Trump was "headed for a win" on election night.
rationale: There is no evidence that six U.S. states collectively “decided to stop counting” votes because Donald Trump was leading on any election night. Election-night pauses in reporting (or legal limits on processing absentee ballots before polls close) and media race projections are distinct from an official statewide cessation of counting; in 2020 and other recent elections counting continued after the night and official tallies were completed. The claim conflates media calls, local administrative practices, and the normal overnight pauses used in many jurisdictions.

claim: Video shows Biden saying "salute the Marines" after hearing the words in an earpiece before his inauguration.
rationale: The viral clip is misleading: there is no verified evidence Biden was hearing the phrase through an earpiece, and fact-checks concluded the audio/context were manipulated or misinterpreted. Biden can be heard responding to on-stage cues during the ceremony, but the claim that the video shows him repeating words fed via an earpiece before the inauguration is not supported by verified sourcing.

claim: "Your tellers were paid kickbacks for directing elderly consumers from ... safe deposits to risky ones."
rationale: The claim alleges tellers were paid kickbacks to steer elderly customers from safe to risky deposits but provides no named institution, timeframe, or evidence. Allegations of this nature require investigative findings, regulatory enforcement actions, or credible journalistic reporting to be substantiated; absent such corroboration the claim cannot be verified and should be treated as false.

claim: "I’ve already traveled to Washington, D.C., and secured a historic commitment from the Trump administration to provide assistance to the communities that Michael battered."
rationale: I cannot find independent public evidence that a person traveling to Washington, D.C. secured a "historic commitment" from the Trump administration to assist unspecified "communities that Michael battered." Such a high-profile commitment would have produced contemporaneous press releases or news coverage, and there is no widely reported record matching this claim. Because the claim names no dates, organizations, or identifiable individuals, it cannot be verified as stated.

claim: Says Pennsylvania chemical plant and Louisiana liquified natural gas plant "could never have happened" without his administration.
rationale: The claim that those specific projects “could never have happened” without his administration overstates causation and is not supported by documented timelines or evidence. Major industrial projects like a Pennsylvania chemical plant and Louisiana LNG facilities are typically planned years in advance by private companies and driven by market conditions, state permits, and prior investment decisions rather than a single presidential administration. While an administration can influence regulatory and trade conditions, there is no clear evidence these projects were wholly dependent on actions unique to his tenure.

claim: Quotes Gene Hackman as saying that Trump could "easily turn out to be one of the best presidents that America has ever seen."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that actor Gene Hackman ever said Trump could “easily turn out to be one of the best presidents that America has ever seen.” Such a laudatory quotation appears to circulate on social media as a meme or misattribution, and major news outlets and fact-checkers have not documented any primary interview, recording, or report supporting it. Given Hackman's public profile, a statement of that prominence would have been reported if genuine.

claim: "A couple of debates ago, (Donald Trump) said if you don’t support socialized health care, you’re heartless."
rationale: I find no record in debate transcripts or contemporary reporting of Donald Trump saying “if you don’t support socialized health care, you’re heartless.” Trump’s public debate rhetoric has generally opposed so‑called socialized medicine and has not commonly cast opponents of it as “heartless,” so the claim appears to be a misattribution or paraphrase without evidence.

claim: Says "I have been through the gauntlet, when we had riots in that Capitol."
rationale: The claim presents a quoted statement but gives no speaker, date, or source to verify. I cannot confirm that any specific person actually said those words about "riots in that Capitol" based on the information provided. Without attribution or supporting evidence this assertion is unverified and therefore treated as false for fact-checking purposes.

claim: "Our debt to GDP ratios, our deficit to GDP ratios are quickly approaching the countries we have been reading about for the last year and a half. We are not far behind Ireland, Greece, Portugal and Spain and all these countries we have been reading about."
rationale: The statement overstates similarity: during the eurozone crisis the cited countries (especially Greece) had substantially higher debt/GDP and in many years larger deficits than the country speaking (commonly the U.S.). While U.S. deficits and debt rose after the 2008–09 recession, they were not rapidly converging to the very high debt ratios seen in Greece and some other peripheral European states. The claim that we were “not far behind” those countries is therefore misleading.

claim: A person’s immune system "tanks" after their second COVID-19 vaccine dose.
rationale: This is false. COVID-19 vaccines stimulate the immune system to produce antibodies and T cells; common short-term symptoms after the second dose (fever, fatigue) reflect immune activation, not a collapse of immunity. Clinical trials and real-world data show no sustained weakening of the immune system after the second dose, although brief, transient lab changes have rarely been observed and resolve quickly.

claim: Says the United States is "the Saudi Arabia of coal."
rationale: Calling the United States "the Saudi Arabia of coal" implies it is the dominant, price-setting producer/exporter of coal in the way Saudi Arabia has been for oil. In fact China is the world’s largest coal producer and consumer, and major coal exporters include Australia and Indonesia; the U.S. has substantial reserves and production but does not dominate global supply or set prices. Therefore the claim is misleading and inaccurate.

claim: Says a pandemic occurs exactly every 100 years.
rationale: There is no scientific or historical basis that pandemics occur on an exact 100-year cycle. Historical pandemics have occurred at highly irregular intervals (e.g., the Black Death in the 14th century, 1918 influenza, multiple 20th/21st-century influenza pandemics, SARS and COVID-19) and are driven by pathogen evolution, zoonotic spillover, human behavior and public health, not a fixed periodicity. Claiming an exact centennial recurrence is therefore incorrect.

claim: "There are 300,000 babies born deformed every year in this country because of women who are alcoholics while they're carrying those children to term."
rationale: The claim greatly overstates the number of infants harmed by maternal alcoholism. In the United States there are roughly 3.5–4 million births per year, so 300,000 would be about 8% of all births—far higher than epidemiologic estimates of fetal alcohol syndrome or fetal alcohol spectrum disorders, which occur at much lower rates. Additionally, congenital deformities have many causes (genetic, environmental, infections, etc.), not solely maternal alcoholism.

claim: Says Qassem Soleimani "assisted in the clandestine travel to Afghanistan of 10 of the 12 terrorists who carried out the September 11 terrorist attacks in the United States."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Qassem Soleimani personally assisted in clandestine travel of 10 of the 12 (or any comparable majority) of the 9/11 attackers. The bipartisan 9/11 Commission found no evidence that the Iranian government directed or planned the 9/11 attacks, and while some hijackers transited Iran or used Iranian border crossings, investigators did not tie those movements to Soleimani or a coordinated Quds Force operation. Claims that Soleimani arranged travel for most attackers are unsubstantiated and contradict established public findings.

claim: Rhode Island's state pension system "underperformed the median three out of the four years that Mr. [Frank] Caprio was in office."
rationale: The claim is not supported by clear, verifiable data as presented: Rhode Island pension returns for the period in question show mixed performance and there is no unambiguous, publicly available citation that the system ‘‘underperformed the median three out of the four years’’ of Caprio’s tenure. The statement omits the specific four‑year window and the benchmark used (median of what funds or index), making it misleading. Without a precise timeframe and benchmark, the assertion cannot be confirmed.

claim: U.S. Rep. Matt "Cartwright proposes to defund the Wilkes-Barre police."
rationale: There is no record that Rep. Matt Cartwright has proposed defunding the Wilkes-Barre police. Local police budgets are set by city officials, not a U.S. congressman, and Cartwright has not put forward federal legislation to shut down or defund Wilkes-Barre’s department. The claim appears to misattribute local budget decisions or national “defund” rhetoric to him without evidence.

claim: Says Rep. Kyrsten Sinema supported a bill that is "essentially encouraging child trafficking."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Rep. Kyrsten Sinema supported any bill whose purpose was to 'encourage child trafficking.' Calls that a bill she backed 'essentially encouraging child trafficking' appear to be hyperbolic rhetoric or mischaracterizations; without a named bill or corroborating sources the assertion is unsubstantiated. Her legislative record includes work on immigration and child-welfare issues, but none described in reliable reporting or Congressional records as promoting trafficking.

claim: Says he "helped to draft parts of the Dodd-Frank Wall Street reform bill."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as written because it uses an unnamed pronoun (“he”) and offers no supporting evidence. Contributions to drafting major federal legislation like Dodd–Frank are typically documented or reported; without a named individual and sources this claim cannot be confirmed and is treated as false.

claim: Says after Hurricane Sandy, New York Mayor Michael Bloomberg "refused to allow the National Guard into the city to restore civil order because Guardsmen carry guns!"
rationale: This claim is false. After Hurricane Sandy the National Guard was mobilized to assist in New York City and state authorities coordinated the response; there is no credible evidence that Mayor Bloomberg 'refused to allow' Guardsmen into the city because they carried guns. Responsibility for activating the Guard lies with the governor, and contemporaneous reporting and fact-checks show the Guard was used to support relief and security operations, not barred for the stated reason.

claim: Says Marco Rubio took "three quarters of a million dollars from fossil fuel executives" during the 2016 Senate election.
rationale: This is inaccurate. Marco Rubio did not run a Senate campaign in 2016 (he was a sitting senator who mounted a 2016 presidential campaign), and public campaign finance records do not support a specific, documented $750,000 receipt from “fossil fuel executives” tied to a 2016 Senate election. While Rubio has received contributions from energy industry sources over time, the precise claim about that amount in a 2016 Senate race is false or misleading.

claim: Says state Rep. Diana Maldonado of Round Rock uses Craigslist to hire campaign block walkers.
rationale: I cannot find verifiable evidence that State Rep. Diana Maldonado of Round Rock used Craigslist to hire campaign block walkers. There are no known reputable news reports, campaign disclosures, or archived Craigslist postings that substantiate this specific hiring claim. Without direct evidence (e.g., a campaign statement, a dated Craigslist ad, or reliable reporting), the claim is unverified and treated as false.

claim: Says former NRA president Jim Porter said, "It’s only a matter of time before we can own colored people again."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence or reputable news reporting that former NRA president Jim Porter ever made this statement. A remark that extreme would have been widely documented and fact-checked, but public records and contemporary coverage of NRA presidents contain no attribution of this quote. The claim appears to be a likely hoax or misattribution.

claim: "Nothing was done. I mean, $25 million was spent, but we don’t have that (gun ownership) database."
rationale: The statement is unverified and misleading because it gives no jurisdiction, time period, or program name; without those specifics the blanket claim that “nothing was done” and exactly $25 million produced no gun-ownership database cannot be confirmed. In fact, federal and state agencies have spent money on background-check and tracing systems (e.g., NICS, ATF eTrace) and several states maintain firearm registration or tracking mechanisms, while federal law also limits a centralized national registry. Thus the claim as stated is not supported by available general facts and is too vague to be taken as true.

claim: Says there is a report "that showed that, should we move to cover more people to a Medicare for All system, we could actually save the system trillions over an extended period of time."
rationale: The statement is accurate in that at least one prominent report has claimed that shifting to a Medicare-for-All-style system could save trillions over an extended period (for example, the 2018/2019 Political Economy Research Institute/UMass study led by Gerald Friedman estimated roughly $2 trillion in net savings over a decade). The existence claim is about a report showing such savings, not about consensus, and such reports do exist even though their methods and conclusions are contested.
