claim: Today, the deficit is "below the average deficits over the past 40 years."
rationale: The statement is misleading or incorrect as presented. For the U.S., recent annual federal deficits (notably during and after the COVID years) have generally been large and are at or above long‑run averages when measured as a share of GDP; comparing raw nominal dollar deficits without inflation adjustment also produces a misleading result. Without clear specification of country, time, or whether the comparison is in nominal dollars or percent of GDP, the claim cannot be supported.

claim: The Banking Committee voted a 1,336-page bill "out of committee in 21 minutes with no amendments, with the understanding that before the bill came to the floor, we would reach this bipartisan agreement."
rationale: There is no public record or contemporaneous reporting indicating a Banking Committee formally moved a 1,336‑page bill out in a 21‑minute, no‑amendment vote with a prior pledge to reach a bipartisan floor agreement. Congressional committee markups and votes are documented and typically take longer and include amendments or recorded statements; the specific combination of page count, timing, and process described does not match known committee actions up to my knowledge cutoff.

claim: Says the Multnomah County Library system "is the second busiest in the nation."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Multnomah County Library is the "second busiest" public library system in the United States. National rankings by common metrics (annual circulation, visits, branches) consistently place much larger systems—e.g., New York, Los Angeles, Chicago, and Queens—above Multnomah; Multnomah is regionally significant but not #2 nationally. The claim also fails to specify a metric or timeframe, which makes it unsupported as stated.

claim: Says Ron Johnson voted to turn Medicare "into a voucher program."
rationale: There is no single Senate law that Ron Johnson voted into effect that literally converts traditional Medicare into a voucher program. Johnson has supported Republican budgets and proposals that endorse a future shift to a “premium‑support” or voucher‑style approach (and has praised Paul Ryan‑style Medicare reforms), but he did not cast a vote that directly and immediately turned Medicare into vouchers. The claim conflates support for proposals or budget language with a concrete enacted vote to convert Medicare.

claim: Says El Chapo testified in court that he paid off Nancy Pelosi to keep the U.S.-Mexico border open for drug cartels.
rationale: This claim is false. Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán did not testify that he paid Nancy Pelosi; in the 2019 U.S. trial prosecutors presented evidence and wiretaps about bribing Mexican officials and security forces, and El Chapo himself did not make any verified court statement accusing Pelosi. Major news outlets and court records contain no credible report of such an allegation.

claim: "The fact is" the Clinton Foundation has "got about 80 percent in overhead and 20 percent of the money is actually getting into the places it should."
rationale: This claim is incorrect. Public IRS Form 990 filings and charity watchdog analyses show the Clinton Foundation's program expenses have typically made up the majority of its spending (often well above 50–70%), not that 80% is overhead and only 20% reaches programs. Multiple fact-checks and financial statements contradict the 80% overhead figure and indicate the claim inverts the foundation's reported spending pattern.

claim: Says 2012 was the "first year in American history that more minorities are being born than people in the majority."
rationale: This claim is incorrect about the year. U.S. government birth statistics indicate that the tipping point occurred in 2011, when births to non-Hispanic white mothers fell below 50% and births to minorities collectively became the majority, not 2012. Thus 2012 was not the first year for that milestone.

claim: Says personal-injury trial lawyers "have provided over 80 percent of the funding for the Texas Democratic Party for over a decade."
rationale: Public campaign finance records and reporting show the Texas Democratic Party receives contributions from a wide range of sources (individuals, unions, PACs, national party committees and various industries); there is no evidence that personal-injury trial lawyers alone supplied over 80% of the party’s funding for more than a decade. While trial lawyers have been a notable donor bloc in some cycles, the claim greatly overstates their sustained share and conflates categories of giving. Such a large, long-term concentration would be visible in disclosure reports but is not supported by them.

claim: "We have one senator who’s a ‘yes’ vote ... but he’s in the hospital. And he’s a ‘yes’ vote. So we can’t do it by Friday. So we have the votes" to pass a health care bill.
rationale: The claim is unsupported by verifiable reporting or public roll-call records for any major recent health-care bill. Senate votes and news coverage make it straightforward to confirm if a single hospitalized senator was the decisive ‘yes’ and prevented a Friday vote, but no credible sources document that exact circumstance as stated. Without a clear date, senator name, or bill, the assertion appears to be unverified and likely inaccurate.

claim: Says Beto O’Rourke wants "open borders and wants to take our guns."
rationale: The claim is a misleading oversimplification. O’Rourke has explicitly supported an assault‑weapons ban and a mandatory buyback for those weapons (and once said “Hell yes, we’re going to take your AR‑15” in that context), but he has not advocated confiscation of all firearms. He has also called for comprehensive immigration reform and stronger humanitarian and legal channels at the border, not a policy of eliminating border controls or instituting truly “open borders.”

claim: "Nearly half of African-American children under the age of 6 are living in abject poverty."
rationale: This is false as stated. U.S. Census and ACS-based poverty statistics for Black children under age 6 have generally been well below 50% in recent years (more typically in the mid-20s to mid-30s percent range), and the claim that "nearly half" are in "abject poverty" overstates those figures. Moreover, "abject poverty" is not an official statistical category and likely conflates different measures such as deep poverty, which is lower than 50%.

claim: Republican gubernatorial candidate Eric Greitens "spent another $600,000 on image consultants" to rebrand his charity, The Mission Continues.
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Eric Greitens or The Mission Continues paid "another $600,000" specifically to image consultants to rebrand the charity. Public nonprofit filings and contemporary news coverage document some marketing and professional service expenses for the organization but do not corroborate a $600,000 payment for image consultants tied to Greitens' rebranding. The claim appears to conflate or exaggerate routine nonprofit expenses or separate campaign-related spending.

claim: "Republicans in the General Assembly cut teacher pay so much when they took over in 2011 that even with recent pay raises, we are still below pre-Recession pay levels."
rationale: Republicans won control of the North Carolina General Assembly in 2011 and enacted budget and retirement changes that reduced take-home pay and froze or slowed raises for teachers. State-level teacher salary data and reporting show average/real (inflation-adjusted) teacher pay fell after the recession and had not fully recovered to pre-recession levels even after later raises in the late 2010s. Therefore the broad claim is accurate in its core contention for the commonly referenced state and period.

claim: "About halfway through fiscal year 2009, Washington has run out of money."
rationale: This claim is false. There is no evidence that ‘Washington’ (federal government or Washington State) literally ran out of money about halfway through fiscal year 2009 (around spring 2009). Although the 2008–2009 recession produced large budget shortfalls, governments managed through reserves, borrowing, and federal stimulus rather than ceasing operations for lack of funds.

claim: "We paid down the debt for four years -- paid down $600 billion on the national debt."
rationale: The United States did not sustain a four‑year reduction in the national debt totaling $600 billion in recent history. The only multi‑year paydown occurred in the late 1990s and was much smaller (on the order of a few hundred billion in debt‑held‑by‑the‑public reductions), while gross federal debt did not fall by $600 billion over a four‑year span. More recent administrations saw net increases in the federal debt well above $600 billion over four‑year periods.

claim: "Last year," Obama "administration officials released into our neighborhoods more than 36,000 criminal immigrants who had nearly 88,000 convictions. The crimes included hundreds of convictions for murder, rape and kidnapping and thousands of drug-related crimes."
rationale: The claim mixes and misrepresents government data. The ~36,000 figure appears derived from ICE encounter/release tallies, but those counts refer to many different categories (including releases by local jails, non‑detainers and people not placed into ICE custody) and do not mean the Obama administration proactively ‘freed’ 36,000 violent criminals into neighborhoods. The nearly 88,000 convictions count double‑counts multiple convictions per person and includes many minor or old offenses; independent fact‑checks found the characterization of hundreds of murders/rapes/kidnappings and thousands of serious drug convictions as a direct result of administration releases is misleading and unsupported.

claim: "The Katy Freeway, or Interstate 10 west of Houston, is the widest freeway in the world, with up to 26 lanes, including frontage road lanes."
rationale: The Katy Freeway (I‑10 west of Houston) was widened and in places does reach about 26 travel lanes when you count main lanes, frontage/collector lanes and managed/reversible lanes. However, calling it the single "widest freeway in the world" is disputed and depends on how lanes are counted; other highways/road complexes internationally have configurations that equal or exceed that lane count. Thus the 26‑lane figure is essentially correct for some segments, but the absolute superlative is not reliably true.

claim: Superdelegates "have never been a determining factor in who our nominee is since they've been in place since 1984."
rationale: Superdelegates were created after the 1980 reforms and first used in 1984, but it is incorrect to say they have never been a determining factor: in tightly contested cycles (notably 2008) unpledged delegates had the potential to decide or to swing the outcome and their collective endorsements materially shaped the race. The party later changed rules (after 2016) to limit their role, which acknowledges they could be decisive in close contests.

claim: As Florida secretary of state, Kurt Browning "allowed 1,800 illegal voters to register in Florida."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Kurt Browning, as Florida Secretary of State, "allowed 1,800 illegal voters to register." Voter registration is performed by county supervisors, and past controversies involving Browning concerned preliminary matches of possible noncitizen registrations from DMV data that produced many false positives; follow-up reviews did not substantiate a confirmed block of 1,800 illegal registrations attributable to Browning’s approval. The claim therefore overstates and mischaracterizes the facts and the Secretary of State’s role.

claim: "Two-thirds of our kids can’t read at grade level."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and therefore misleading without context. If taken to mean U.S. 4th-graders scoring 'proficient' on the NAEP reading test, roughly one-third are proficient (so about two-thirds are not proficient) in some recent assessments, but 'can’t read at grade level' is a different, broader claim that varies by grade, state, assessment, and year. Because the statement lacks specification and is not universally true across ages, places, and measures, it is categorized as FALSE.

claim: "U.S. deaths since 1/22 (2020): COVID-19: 27, flu, 4,700; abortion: 118,000."
rationale: The numeric claims are inconsistent with official public-health data. U.S. COVID-19 deaths since January 2020 number well over one million, not 27; CDC estimates for influenza fatalities across recent seasons are in the thousands to tens of thousands, and reported deaths directly attributable to legal abortion are extremely rare (far far fewer than 118,000). The figure 118,000 more closely matches counts of abortions performed over a time span, not deaths from abortion.

claim: Says Allen West violated federal law by scuba diving with U.S. flag.
rationale: There is no federal criminal law that makes scuba diving with a U.S. flag illegal; the U.S. Flag Code contains advisory guidelines about proper treatment of the flag but does not create criminal penalties. Supreme Court rulings protecting symbolic acts involving the flag (e.g., burning or desecration) further limit federal prosecution for expressive uses of the flag. No credible record shows Allen West was found to have violated a federal law for scuba diving with a U.S. flag.

claim: Congressman Jeff Denham "has agreed all illegal immigrants should be detained, arrested and deported."
rationale: This is a mischaracterization. While Rep. Jeff Denham has supported tougher immigration enforcement and deportations for people with criminal records, there is no clear public record of him saying he agrees that every undocumented person should be detained, arrested and deported without exception; that absolute claim overstates his documented positions and ignores legal and practical limits.

claim: "NFL attendance and ratings are WAY DOWN. Boring games yes, but many stay away because they love our country."
rationale: The claim mixes two assertions that aren’t supported together. While NFL TV ratings have fluctuated and have declined in some seasons compared with peak years, overall league attendance has generally remained high (stadiums are often near capacity) and ratings drops are not uniformly or dramatically “WAY DOWN.” There is no clear evidence that a large share of people are staying away primarily out of patriotism; studies and polls attribute viewership changes to many factors (scheduling, streaming, competition, pandemic effects, team performance), not a dominant patriotic boycott.

claim: Says "Bush Jr. handed Obama a $1.4 trillion deficit" and Obama "reduced Bush Jr.’s deficit to just $492 billion."
rationale: The claim mixes a partly accurate figure with an inaccurate and misleading one. The federal deficit for FY2009 (the year Obama inherited) was about $1.41 trillion, but by later years of Obama’s term annual deficits fell to the $400–600 billion range (e.g., Treasury reports show about $438 billion in FY2015), not precisely $492 billion; moreover attributing the change solely to Obama ignores the timing of fiscal years and broader economic and policy factors. Because the end figure and the causal framing are incorrect/misleading, the overall claim is false.

claim: Says a crisis actor played the parts of a shooting victim and the mothers of shooting victims in Las Vegas, Orlando and Thousand Oaks.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a single "crisis actor" portrayed victims or the mothers of victims across the Las Vegas, Orlando (Pulse), and Thousand Oaks shootings. Victims and family members from those events have been identified and confirmed by law enforcement, hospital records, and reputable news organizations; independent fact-checkers have repeatedly debunked similar “crisis actor” claims. The allegation relies on superficial appearance comparisons and conspiracy reasoning rather than verifiable documentation.

claim: Say a "left wing extremist, chases down, rams car over Trump bumper sticker."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated as presented: it alleges a specific violent incident by a 'left wing extremist' but gives no time, location, names, or sources and I find no verifiable, widely reported account matching that description. Without corroborating evidence from credible news or official reports the claim cannot be treated as factual. Because the assertion is specific and extraordinary but unsupported, it should be considered false until reliable documentation is provided.

claim: "We haven't had any legislation which took away one gun in the past 20 years from anybody in this country--not one."
rationale: The claim is incorrect. Over the past 20 years many state and some federal statutes have required people subject to protective orders, criminal convictions, mental-health adjudications, or extreme-risk ("red flag"/ERPO) orders to surrender firearms, and those laws have resulted in firearms being removed from individuals. These are legislative actions that have legally compelled surrender or confiscation of guns.

claim: The Milwaukee County Board’s staff grew from four workers to 38 over four decades and now costs taxpayers "a lot more," while the total county workforce was more than cut in half in the same period.
rationale: The claim mixes true elements with unverified or misleading numbers. Milwaukee County Board professional staff has grown over past decades, and the overall county workforce has declined in some periods, but the specific assertion that staff grew from exactly four to 38 over four decades and that the total county workforce was "more than cut in half" in the same period is not clearly supported and depends on definitions and timeframes. Without a consistent baseline (which years, FTEs vs. positions, inclusion of contractors) the precise figures are unreliable.

claim: Statistically, law-enforcement officers die 10 years earlier than the general population.
rationale: The statement is too broad and not supported as a general, consistent statistic. Research on police mortality shows increased risks for certain causes (cardiovascular disease, suicide, some cancers) and results vary by country, cohort, and how age/sex are adjusted; there is no consensus that law-enforcement officers on average die exactly 10 years earlier than the general population. Some specific studies or subgroups have reported several years' lower life expectancy, but the claim as stated is an oversimplification.

claim: "Cancer and matters to do with kidney failure kill more people in Kenya today than malaria, tuberculosis and AIDS combined."
rationale: Available public health data and major international estimates show that HIV/AIDS, malaria and tuberculosis have historically been among Kenya's leading causes of death and their combined mortality still exceeds deaths from cancer plus kidney disease. Although noncommunicable diseases (including cancer and chronic kidney disease) are rising, I find no robust evidence that they now kill more people in Kenya than malaria, TB and AIDS combined.

claim: "The federal government spent over $500k trying to force fish to exercise on treadmills, an additional $150k to see if gingerbread houses are earthquake proof."
rationale: This is a misleading summary. There have been federally funded projects that involved zebrafish exercise and gingerbread-house demonstrations, but the descriptions and dollar figures are exaggerated or taken out of context: the fish treadmill work was legitimate biomedical research into muscle/heart physiology (part of larger grants) rather than ‘‘forcing fish to exercise’’ as a frivolous stunt, and the gingerbread-house activity was an educational/outreach demonstration tied to earthquake engineering, not a $150K study to see if edible houses are quake-proof. The claim conflates program goals and funding lines to portray routine research/outreach as wasteful.

claim: "(Texas Republicans) believe in abolishing Social Security, abolishing V.A. health care."
rationale: The claim overgeneralizes. While some Texas Republicans and conservative policy advocates have proposed privatizing or restructuring Social Security or changing how veterans' care is delivered, there is no broad, official or widely held position among Texas Republicans to abolish Social Security or VA health care outright. Positions vary by individual and platform language typically emphasizes reform rather than elimination.

claim: "My state of Florida is now the third-largest state. We have surpassed New York in population."
rationale: The 2020 U.S. Census and subsequent population estimates show Florida's population exceeded New York's, making Florida the third-most populous state behind California and Texas. Therefore the claim that Florida has surpassed New York in population and is now the third-largest state is correct.

claim: Says Rick Scott’s per-pupil education spending is "about $200 less" than what it was under Charlie Crist during the recession.
rationale: The statement is misleading because per‑pupil figures vary by which year of Crist’s term is used, whether amounts are inflation‑adjusted, and whether local and federal dollars are included. Independent fact‑checks and budget comparisons show no consistent, single “about $200 less” gap for Rick Scott’s tenure versus Crist’s recession years once these factors are accounted for; depending on the metric the difference can be smaller, larger, or reversed.

claim: Says Gerald Daugherty is endorsed by the Austin American-Statesman.
rationale: There is no evidence in the Austin American-Statesman's publicly known endorsement lists or widely reported endorsement announcements that the paper has endorsed a candidate named Gerald Daugherty. Without a verifiable endorsement statement from the newspaper, the claim that he is endorsed by the Austin American-Statesman appears false.

claim: Florida Democrats "put my Social Security number and my wife's Employment Identification Number in a mail piece."
rationale: I am not aware of any credible reporting or verifiable evidence that the Florida Democratic Party printed an individual’s full Social Security number and their wife’s Employer Identification Number on a campaign mailer. Publishing such sensitive identifiers would be a major, widely covered data‑privacy incident and is inconsistent with standard campaign practice and legal risks. Without a specific mailer image or date, the claim remains unsubstantiated.

claim: Members of Congress and their families and staff are exempt from repaying student loans.
rationale: There is no statute or policy that automatically exempts members of Congress, their families, or congressional staff from repaying student loans. They are generally subject to the same federal loan rules as other borrowers; some individuals may separately qualify for general programs (e.g., PSLF, income-driven repayment forgiveness) or temporary relief, but that is not a blanket exemption.

claim: The Republican tax bill is "not being scored by the Congressional Budget Office, as it is traditionally."
rationale: This claim is inaccurate as a general statement. Major tax legislation is typically analyzed by both the Joint Committee on Taxation (JCT) for revenue estimates and the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) for budgetary scoring and cost analyses; in recent Republican tax proposals CBO did produce analyses or was expected to produce official scores even if JCT provided detailed revenue numbers. Saying the bill is "not being scored by the CBO, as it is traditionally" misstates the usual bipartisan scoring process and ignores that CBO involvement either occurred or was forthcoming.

claim: "The Pentagon itself says that we could eliminate 20 percent of U.S. bases."
rationale: The Department of Defense has not made a clear, blanket statement that "we could eliminate 20 percent of U.S. bases." While DoD studies and outside analysts have at times identified excess infrastructure or proposed closures that, depending on definitions, have been framed as sizable percentages, there is no authoritative Pentagon declaration endorsing a simple 20% cut across U.S. bases. The claim removes important context about which bases, definitions, and source of the figure.

claim: In the recent House special election in Florida, Democrats "got outspent in a Republican district."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it does not identify which "recent" Florida special election is meant; campaign spending varies by race and must be checked against FEC/Florida filings. Without a specific district and date I cannot confirm Democrats were outspent; some Florida specials have seen Democrats outspent, others have not. Because the statement is ambiguous and lacks a verifiable reference, I judge it false as presented.

claim: A study found an "82% miscarriage rate" among women between 30 days and 20 weeks pregnant who got an mRNA COVID-19 vaccine.
rationale: This claim is false: no credible, peer-reviewed study has shown an 82% miscarriage rate after mRNA COVID-19 vaccination. The 82% number arises from misinterpreted, extremely small or nonrepresentative data sources (or raw adverse-event reports) and contradicts larger cohort and registry studies that found no increased miscarriage risk and rates similar to expected background levels.

claim: The Baucus health care bill would require taxes on medical devices such as X-ray machines, female condoms, HIV tests and surgical needles.
rationale: This overstates and mischaracterizes the proposal. The Baucus/Finance Committee discussions and drafts considered levies on medical-device industry sales (and the eventual ACA included a 2.3% manufacturer excise), but the proposal was an industry/manufacturer levy with definitional limits and exemptions — not a direct consumer tax that explicitly singled out items like X‑ray machines, female condoms, HIV tests and needles as being taxed at retail. Many small items and diagnostic tests are categorized differently or could be exempt under device definitions, so the claim is inaccurate as stated.

claim: Supported in-state tuition in Arkansas for illegal immigrants "if you'd sat in our schools from the time you're 5 or 6 years old and you had become an A-plus student," among other things.
rationale: The claim presents a quotation and an assertion of support but gives no speaker, date, or source, so it cannot be verified as true. Without attribution or corroborating evidence, I cannot confirm that this statement was made or that the person supported in‑state tuition in Arkansas as quoted, so I mark it false under uncertainty rules.

claim: Says Donald Trump "just promised that if he wins reelection, he’ll gut Social Security and Medicare."
rationale: There is no clear public statement in which Donald Trump explicitly and plainly promised to “gut Social Security and Medicare.” Trump has repeatedly said during campaigns and public remarks that he would protect those programs, and while critics point to broader Republican calls for entitlement reform or spending cuts as evidence of potential future reductions, that is not the same as a direct promise to gut them. Therefore the claim as phrased is not supported by available public statements.

claim: Says "J.B. Pritzker’s tax plan" includes a "new tax per mile you drive with government tracking device."
rationale: The claim is false as stated. Pritzker’s proposals and Illinois discussions have included exploring mileage-based user fees and limited pilot programs, but they did not create a new mandatory per-mile tax that requires a government tracking device. Public proposals emphasized pilots, technology-neutral approaches, or use of odometer readings and toll transponders rather than a statewide compulsory GPS surveillance tax.

claim: "In the last 29 months, our economy has produced about 4.5 million private-sector jobs."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because no concrete 29‑month window is given; totals of private‑sector job gains depend on the exact start and end months and BLS monthly payroll data. Without dates, the figure of “about 4.5 million” is unsubstantiated and likely incorrect for several plausible 29‑month periods (BLS private‑sector payroll series shows different cumulative gains depending on the interval).

claim: "#GradInsurance debacle is a DIRECT result of #ObamaCare. #MIZZOU has to break the law to do the right thing."
rationale: The claim asserts a direct causal link between the Affordable Care Act ("Obamacare") and a specific "GradInsurance debacle" at Mizzou, and further claims the university must break the law to fix it. That is not supported: disputes over graduate student insurance typically stem from institutional budget/contract decisions, interpretation of eligibility and coverage, and state/regulatory details rather than a single direct effect of the ACA. Saying the university "has to break the law" is a normative assertion with no evidence; institutions can seek legal remedies, policy changes, or compliance alternatives without illegal action.

claim: "...the earth moves closer to the sun every year – you know the rotation of the earth. We’re moving closer to the sun."
rationale: The claim is incorrect. Earth’s distance from the Sun oscillates seasonally because of orbital eccentricity (perihelion/aphelion), but there is no steady yearly approach caused by Earth’s rotation; daily spin does not change orbital radius. Long-term effects like solar mass loss and planetary perturbations produce a tiny net outward, not inward, drift of Earth's orbit over time.

claim: "COP26 luxury EVs to be recharged using diesel generators"
rationale: Contemporary news coverage and photographic evidence from COP26 showed onsite EV charging points being powered by diesel generators as a temporary/back-up measure because parts of the venue lacked sufficient grid capacity. While not every electric vehicle at the conference was charged this way, the core claim that diesel generators were used to recharge EVs at COP26 is accurate.

claim: "Seismic airgun blasting (used for energy exploration) is ... 16,000 times louder than" a conventional airhorn.
rationale: The statement is misleading because "times louder" is ambiguous and the claim gives no measurement context (air vs. water, decibel reference, distance). Sound levels are logarithmic: claims about being 16,000× louder would require a specific intensity or pressure ratio and measurement reference. While seismic airguns produce extremely high underwater source levels and can be many orders of magnitude greater than some airborne sounds when compared using certain metrics, there is no single, context-free, accurate fact that they are "16,000 times louder" than a conventional airhorn.

claim: "General Motors is sending Mexican made model of Chevy Cruze to U.S. car dealers-tax free across border."
rationale: The claim is misleading. General Motors has imported Mexican‑built Chevy Cruzes into the U.S., but such imports are not automatically "tax free" — duty exemption depends on meeting rules of origin and documentation under trade agreements (NAFTA/USMCA); otherwise normal U.S. import duties apply. The blanket statement that GM is sending Mexican Cruzes to U.S. dealers tax‑free across the border is therefore inaccurate without qualification.

claim: "Dolphins are rapists. Look it up."
rationale: The claim is an overbroad, anthropomorphic generalization. Scientific observations document that some male bottlenose dolphins engage in coercive mating and forced copulation in certain populations, but this does not justify labeling all dolphins as "rapists." Behavior varies by species, population, and individual, and the human legal term doesn’t map cleanly onto animal behavior.

claim: There are "360,000 (deaths) a year from swimming pools. But we don’t shut the country down for that."
rationale: The cited number (~360,000) roughly matches commonly quoted global annual drowning deaths in WHO reports, but that total covers all drowning locations (rivers, lakes, bathtubs, boats, etc.), not just swimming pools. Fatal drownings that occur specifically in swimming pools are a small fraction of total drownings, so the claim that there are 360,000 pool deaths per year is inaccurate.

claim: "Have the suburbs been inundated with former residents of Atlanta housing projects? Absolutely not."
rationale: The broad claim that suburbs were not “inundated” by former Atlanta public-housing residents is supported by available evidence: while some residents did relocate to suburban zip codes after the demolition of large projects and via housing vouchers, moves were dispersed across the metro area and represented a small fraction of overall suburban populations rather than a massive, concentrated influx. Studies of Atlanta’s HOPE VI-era demolitions and voucher dispersal document relocation to a variety of destinations, not a wholesale suburban takeover.

claim: Dave Aronberg's career legal experience is "less than two years as Asst. AG/private attorney."
rationale: This claim understates Aronberg’s résumé. Public biographical information shows Dave Aronberg held multiple legal positions (including years in state prosecution and in the attorney general’s office as well as time in private practice), amounting to well over two years of professional legal experience. The statement appears to compress or mislabel those roles to produce a misleading total.

claim: "When you look at the nearly 150 men and women who have served us on the Texas Supreme Court, more than half of them had zero prior judicial experience."
rationale: I could not find authoritative evidence that a majority of the roughly 150 people who have served on the Texas Supreme Court had no prior judicial experience. Historical rosters show many justices came from prior judgeships (trial or appellate), elected office, or other legal posts, so the claim that "more than half" had zero prior judicial experience is unverified and likely incorrect without a precise count and definition. Because the statement combines an approximate total with a broad claim about backgrounds, it overstates what can be confirmed.

claim: Georgia has led the nation in student fatalities caused by motorists illegally passing stopped school buses.
rationale: The claim omits any timeframe and there is no clear, authoritative evidence that Georgia has consistently led the nation in student fatalities from motorists illegally passing stopped school buses. Georgia has had notable incidents and some years with multiple such fatalities, but national year-by-year counts fluctuate and other states (e.g., Texas, Florida) have also reported high numbers; without a specified period the claim is not supported.

claim: According to the Congressional Budget Office, "as many as 20 million Americans could lose their employer-based insurance thanks to Obamacare."
rationale: The Congressional Budget Office projected that, on net, the number of people with employer-sponsored insurance would be roughly 20 million lower at the law's initial implementation period than it otherwise would have been. CBO framed this as a projected reduction in employer-based coverage rather than a claim that 20 million would be left uninsured, and noted many would obtain alternative coverage through exchanges or Medicaid.

claim: Says up to a quarter of African Americans don’t have government photo ID.
rationale: Multiple reputable surveys and analyses have found that Black Americans are disproportionately likely to lack a government-issued photo ID, and several studies have produced estimates in the roughly 20–25% range; saying “up to a quarter” aligns with those findings. Exact percentages vary by data source, year, and how “government photo ID” is defined, but the claim is a reasonable summary of published estimates.

claim: Says in Texas "it's legal to shoot someone who's committing a ‘public nuisance’ under the cover of dark."
rationale: Texas law limits use of deadly force to narrow situations (self-defense, defense of others, or to prevent specific serious felonies such as arson, burglary, robbery, or theft at night). 'Public nuisance' is generally a nonviolent offense and is not a statutory justification for shooting someone merely because they are committing a nuisance, even at night. Shooting a person for a non-deadly offense would likely be criminal.

claim: Says Tennessee’s higher education funding model "is 100 percent outcomes-based" and "we are already seeing this model changing the way our postsecondary institutions do business."
rationale: Tennessee ties a portion of state higher-education appropriations to performance metrics, but the state’s entire higher-education funding is not ‘‘100 percent outcomes-based.’' Common implementations put only incentive/new funds or a portion of appropriations on an outcomes formula while base funding still follows other formulas. It is plausible institutions have adjusted behavior in response to the incentives, but the blanket claim that the model is entirely outcomes-based is inaccurate without the qualifier about which funds are affected.

claim: Says Google Earth blocked people from seeing the Suez Canal.
rationale: The claim is false: the Suez Canal is visible in Google Maps and Google Earth and was widely shown during the Ever Given grounding. Google does occasionally obscure very sensitive military sites but there is no evidence Google blocked public viewing of the Suez Canal.

claim: Joe Biden "wants to get rid of something called ‘stepped up basis’" that reduces inheritance taxes.
rationale: This is accurate in broad terms: President Biden has proposed changes that would curb or eliminate the “stepped-up basis” treatment that currently prevents capital-gains tax on appreciation accrued before an heir inherits assets. His proposals have focused on taxing unrealized gains at death or limiting step-up benefits above specified thresholds, aiming to reduce a common way wealthy estates avoid capital gains tax. The claim omits that proposals typically target gains above certain exemptions rather than an absolute, unconditional repeal for all estates.

claim: Photo shows a trashed venue in Glastonbury after climate activist Greta Thunberg spoke there.
rationale: The image has been widely misattributed online; there is no credible evidence that it shows a Glastonbury venue trashed immediately after a Greta Thunberg talk. Reports and image provenance in similar viral cases typically show the photo comes from a different event or time, not the specific occasion claimed. Without verifiable metadata or reputable news corroboration the attribution to Greta’s Glastonbury appearance is unsupported.

claim: "White supremacist who killed protester is a Democrat and visited (President Barack) Obama in Oval Office."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a known white supremacist who killed a protester was a Democrat and visited President Obama in the Oval Office. High-profile perpetrators (e.g., Dylann Roof, James Alex Fields Jr.) were identified as far‑right extremists and there are no records or reliable reports of Oval Office visits by them or similar killers. The claim appears to conflate or fabricate affiliations and an Oval Office visit.

claim: House Republican plan would increase costs for Oregon seniors by $6,000 with health care vouchers instead of Medicare
rationale: The claim gives a precise $6,000 increase for Oregon seniors from a generic “House Republican plan” replacing Medicare with vouchers, but there is no single, universally accepted estimate that matches that exact figure. Analyses of Republican premium-support/voucher proposals have found seniors could face higher out‑of‑pocket costs in many scenarios, but projected amounts vary widely by specific bill, year, and state; without an identified plan, timeframe, or source the $6,000 number is unverified and likely misleading.

claim: Says President Donald Trump "is still yet to say anything as the president of the United States about bounties on American troops."
rationale: The assertion that President Trump "is still yet to say anything as the president" about reported bounties is incorrect; when the allegations emerged he and his administration publicly addressed them and officials said he had been briefed. Trump made public comments and interviews about the matter and directed inquiries, so it is not accurate to say he said nothing in his capacity as president.

claim: Says Scott Walker's jobs agency gives financial incentives that lead "Wisconsin companies to look at shipping jobs elsewhere. ... A company got $4.6 million in taxpayer money and actually reduced its jobs by 300 people."
rationale: The broad claim is unverified as stated: while Wisconsin's jobs agency (WEDC) under Scott Walker was criticized and audited for some deals that did not produce promised jobs, I could not find credible, specific evidence that a single company received exactly $4.6 million and then cut 300 jobs as claimed. Audits and reporting documented some firms that failed to meet job targets or received incentives before reducing employment, but the precise dollar amount and 300-job reduction in one clear, attributable case are not supported by reliable public records.

claim: Says David Dewhurst "went out for drinks" during Senate debate on abortion bill.
rationale: There are no credible contemporaneous news reports or official records showing Lt. Gov. David Dewhurst left the chamber to “go out for drinks” during the high-profile Texas Senate abortion debate (notably the 2013 filibuster). Coverage from major outlets documents him presiding or otherwise remaining involved; the specific claim is uncorroborated and appears incorrect.

claim: Says Kelly Loeffler supports "raising taxes on Georgia's middle class."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Kelly Loeffler publicly advocated for raising taxes on Georgia’s middle class; as a Republican senator she consistently supported tax cuts and opposed tax increases. Ads or opponents may have claimed she favored measures that indirectly affected some taxpayers, but her voting record and public statements show opposition to raising middle‑class taxes. The specific quoted phrase appears to be a political attack rather than a documented Loeffler position.

claim: "A third of the budget for the city of Ferguson (Missouri) was being reaped by civil fines."
rationale: Multiple investigative reports, and the U.S. Department of Justice’s 2015 investigation of Ferguson, found that court fines and fees made up roughly one-third of the city’s general operating revenue in the years before the 2014 unrest. Reporting at the time characterized the city as heavily dependent on civil fines and municipal court revenue to fund its budget.

claim: "Actually, on some procedures, you're more likely to die if you're on Medicaid than if you're uninsured."
rationale: Multiple peer‑reviewed health services studies have found that for some specific surgical and emergency procedures, adjusted in‑hospital or 30‑day mortality is higher for patients insured by Medicaid than for uninsured patients. These findings are not universal and depend on the procedure, case mix, and how studies adjust for comorbidities and hospital factors, but the existence claim (that this occurs for some procedures) is supported by the literature.

claim: "101 utilities cut rates, credit GOP tax cuts."
rationale: Contemporary reporting and regulatory filings from 2018–2019 documented that roughly 101 U.S. utilities implemented rate reductions and explicitly cited the Republican tax overhaul (the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act) as the reason. The corporate tax rate cut from 35% to 21% led many utilities and regulators to approve passing savings through to customers, matching the claim's substance.

claim: "Ron Johnson pushed through a special tax loophole that benefited his own family's business … Then he cashed out of the company for $5 million … (he has) doubled his wealth since taking office."
rationale: This statement mixes accurate and unproven elements. Public disclosures and news reports indicate Ron Johnson sold his ownership stake in a business and his reported net worth has increased since taking office, but major fact-checkers and reporting do not support the specific claim that he 'pushed through a special tax loophole' designed to benefit his family’s business. The causal linkage and the precise characterization of a targeted loophole are unproven and appear to be misleading.

claim: "Hidden in the CARES Act was an obscure $135 billion tax break for 43,000 millionaires."
rationale: The CARES Act did include tax provisions (notably liberalized net operating loss carrybacks and other business tax changes) that produced substantial tax relief, but independent analyses and official estimates do not support a discrete, ‘hidden’ $135 billion tax break specifically for 43,000 millionaires. The $135 billion figure and the 43,000-person count appear to conflate or misattribute modeled corporate/passthrough tax relief and refund timing effects; fact-checkers have found the claim to be misleading.

claim: Obama "suggested bombing Pakistan."
rationale: There is no reliable record that President Obama proposed or publicly called for bombing Pakistan as a sovereign country. His administration did authorize targeted strikes (drone strikes) against militant targets inside Pakistan and carried out the 2011 raid on Osama bin Laden, and he warned the U.S. might act if Pakistan did not disrupt militant safe havens—statements and actions often mischaracterized as advocating bombing the country itself.

claim: California’s shipping backlog is, in part, caused by a "California Truck Ban which says all trucks must be 2011 or newer and a law called AB 5 which prohibits Owner Operators."
rationale: The claim misstates two laws. California’s heavy‑duty truck/emissions rules (CARB Truck and Bus Regulation) are phased compliance requirements with retrofit and compliance options rather than a blanket “2011 or newer” ban on all trucks, and AB 5 is a worker‑classification law that did not categorically outlaw owner‑operators (and was later modified/clarified and subject to exemptions). While regulatory costs and driver availability may have contributed modestly to logistics strain, the major causes of California port/backlog problems were pandemic demand surges, labor and chassis shortages, and congestion, not a simple truck ban or an outright prohibition of owner‑operators.

claim: President Barack Obama "had the legal authority" to strike Syria without a vote from Congress.
rationale: This is disputed and not a settled legal fact. The Obama administration and some legal scholars argued limited strikes could be justified under the President’s Article II powers or existing authorizations, but many other constitutional scholars, members of Congress, and the War Powers Resolution’s text indicated that use of significant military force without Congressional authorization would lack clear legal backing; Obama himself sought Congressional approval in 2013 rather than asserting unequivocal unilateral authority. There is no definitive judicial ruling affirming a categorical legal authority for the President to strike Syria without Congress, so the claim as stated is misleading.

claim: "Republicans control the U.S. Senate with 54 seats, but those 54 senators were elected by only two-thirds the number of voters who elected the Democrats. In the Senate, the majority party represents a minority of the people."
rationale: The numeric claim is inaccurate: at no recent Senate configuration did Republicans hold exactly 54 seats while receiving only two-thirds the total votes of Democratic Senate candidates. While it is true that Senate seat totals can diverge from the national sum of votes (because races are state-by-state and many are uncontested), the gap described (Republicans receiving only ~66% of the votes that Democrats received) is far larger than real aggregate vote differentials. The broader point — that a Senate majority can represent fewer total voters than the minority party — can occur in some election years, but the specific numbers in the claim are incorrect or unsupported without additional context.

claim: Says U.S. Sen. Ron Johnson wants to put 100,000 troops, including 25,000 Americans, "into the area where ISIS is."
rationale: I could find no reliable record of Sen. Ron Johnson explicitly calling for deployment of 100,000 troops with 25,000 Americans “into the area where ISIS is.” Public statements by Johnson have typically advocated arming, training, or supporting local forces and limited US advisory roles, not a mass US ground deployment of that scale. Major fact‑checks and reporting do not corroborate the quoted phrasing or specific numbers as his direct proposal.

claim: In Texas, "sexting is a felony sex offense for teenagers — that can mean up to 10 years in prison."
rationale: The claim is misleading. While historically minors who exchanged explicit images in Texas could be prosecuted under child‑pornography or related felony statutes, Texas law has provisions and reforms that often treat consensual teen sexting differently (including specific misdemeanor/juvenile diversion options) and felony prosecution with a 10‑year prison term is not the automatic or general outcome for teen sexting. Whether a felony charge and lengthy prison exposure apply depends on ages involved, distribution, and other factors (and adult involvement), so the blanket statement is false.

claim: Graduation rates of players at major football colleges "are still twenty points below their male campus peers and worsened in the past three years."
rationale: The claim states a uniform 20‑point gap and a three‑year worsening across “major football colleges,” but public NCAA graduation metrics and independent analyses show wide variation by school and sport, not a consistent 20‑point deficit for all major programs. In many Power Five programs the gap is smaller or has narrowed, and national athlete graduation metrics have not shown a uniform decline over the past three years.

claim: "I haven't switched my position" on the Trans-Pacific Partnership trade deal.
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as presented because it omits who “I” is and when the statement refers to; many public figures have altered their TPP positions over time. Without a named speaker and timeframe, the assertion that they haven’t switched position cannot be substantiated and therefore cannot be treated as a verified fact.

claim: "At the moment, energy companies spend 0.25 percent on R&D."
rationale: The statement is overly specific and unsupported: R&D intensity in the energy sector varies widely by subsector, company and year and is not a single current value of 0.25%. Many major energy firms and utilities report R&D or technology-related spending that is higher than 0.25% of revenue while some fossil-focused companies report lower shares, so the data show a range rather than a universal quarter-percent.

claim: "I'm not taking any corporate PAC money."
rationale: There is insufficient information to verify the speaker or timeframe, so the assertion cannot be confirmed. Whether a candidate accepts 'corporate PAC' money is a factual claim verifiable from campaign finance reports; without checking those filings for the named person and period the claim is unproven. Because many candidates receive PAC money (including from corporate-affiliated PACs) or funds routed through committees, the default position is that the claim is not reliably established here.

claim: "At John Lewis funeral Obama told a room full of people that rooms full of people is too dangerous so we must mail in vote."
rationale: There is no credible record or news coverage that Barack Obama told attendees at a John Lewis funeral that "rooms full of people is too dangerous so we must mail in vote." Transcripts and reporting from the multiple memorial events for John Lewis do not include such a statement; the claim appears to be a misattribution or fabrication. While Obama and other public figures did encourage mail-in voting during the 2020 pandemic in other contexts, he did not make that specific comment at Lewis’s funeral.

claim: Says Adam Hasner "gives the wealthy tax breaks worth $250,000 a year but hikes middle class taxes $2,000."
rationale: There is no clear, verifiable evidence that Adam Hasner authored or enacted a policy that simultaneously gave the wealthy tax breaks worth $250,000 per year while raising middle‑class taxes by $2,000. The claim uses precise magnitudes that are not supported without specifying which bill, jurisdiction, or time period is meant, and such ad‑style figures are commonly exaggerated or taken out of context. Without a specific, attributable legislative text showing those exact impacts, the statement is not substantiated.

claim: "On issue after issue that really were hard to explain or understand, you voted present . . . And anytime anyone raises that, there's always some kind of explanation."
rationale: The statement is a vague, unverified allegation about a person's pattern of voting "present" and about explanations given when challenged. Without a named person, specific votes, or time period, the pattern "on issue after issue" cannot be corroborated from public voting records or documented statements. Because it is not a concrete, verifiable factual claim as presented, I judge it false in this context.

claim: "Between late December of 2020 and last month, a total of 3,362 people apparently died after getting the COVID vaccine in the United States … The actual number is almost certainly higher."
rationale: The quoted number resembles a raw count of death reports submitted to VAERS, but VAERS reports are unverified and do not demonstrate that the vaccine caused those deaths. U.S. public-health agencies note VAERS is a passive system that can include coincidental, incomplete, or duplicate reports, and follow-up investigations have not shown evidence of thousands of vaccine-caused deaths. The claim's added assertion that the actual number is “almost certainly higher” is speculative and unsupported by available evidence.

claim: In President Barack Obama’s 2015 State of the Union address, "the words ‘al-Qaida’ were never used, the first time those words have not been used in a State of the Union address since February 2001."
rationale: The official transcript of President Obama’s 2015 State of the Union does not contain the words “al-Qaida” (or the common variant spelling “al-Qaeda”), and contemporary fact-checks noted this omission. Reviews of State of the Union transcripts show that the term had been used routinely in addresses after February 2001, making 2015 the first SOTU since that 2001 speech not to include the phrase.

claim: A proposed San Antonio ordinance will allow men into women’s restrooms in the city.
rationale: This wording is misleading. The proposal discussed in San Antonio concerns nondiscrimination rules that let people use restrooms consistent with their gender identity, not a blanket rule that 'allows men into women’s restrooms.' Critics often summarize it that way, but the ordinance’s text addresses gender identity and access rather than permitting any person regardless of identity to enter private spaces.

claim: Under the North American Free Trade Agreement, "we lost millions of jobs."
rationale: Most reputable economic analyses conclude NAFTA contributed to manufacturing job displacement in the U.S. but did not result in the loss of “millions” of net jobs. Estimates in academic and government summaries tend to put NAFTA-attributable job losses in the hundreds of thousands and find overall net employment effects were small or ambiguous, with job creation in other sectors offsetting some losses.

claim: "We’re 49th in the United States in new businesses created."
rationale: The claim as presented is ambiguous (it does not name which state, what year, or which metric of 'new businesses created' is used) and therefore cannot be verified as a blanket statement. Rankings of states on new business creation vary substantially depending on the data source (e.g., Census business formations, Kauffman Index), the year, and whether the measure is absolute counts or per‑capita rates. Without those specifics the assertion that 'we're 49th' is unsubstantiated and likely inaccurate when interpreted as a general fact.

claim: "As governor, Kasich delivered the largest tax cut in the nation."
rationale: Kasich did sign notable tax reductions in Ohio (including a 2013 tax overhaul and cuts to business taxes), but there is no defensible basis to claim they were the largest tax cut in the entire nation. Independent fact-checkers and state budget comparisons indicate other states enacted larger cuts by dollars, percentage or per‑capita measures depending on the metric and year. The claim overstates the relative size without specifying a clear metric or timeframe.

claim: One-third of the economic stimulus package was tax cuts.
rationale: The claim is ambiguous about which "economic stimulus package" it refers to and does not match the composition of major U.S. packages: in both the 2009 ARRA and the 2020 CARES Act, tax cuts made up a minority, not one-third, of total outlays. As a general statement without specifying the law or country, it is misleading and likely false.

claim: "The soda tax can make a difference by reducing consumption of unhealthy soda pop and sugary beverages."
rationale: Multiple peer-reviewed evaluations and real-world implementations show that taxes on sugar-sweetened beverages lead to measurable reductions in purchases and consumption (effects vary by tax size and context). Examples include Mexico and several U.S. cities where declines of several percent to double digits were observed; public-health bodies also conclude taxation is an effective tool to lower intake. While not eliminating consumption, the evidence supports the claim that such taxes can make a difference.

claim: "When the president's spokesman was asked about (Anwar) al-Awlaki's son, … he said he should have chosen a more responsible father."
rationale: Contemporaneous news accounts of the 2011 killing of Anwar al‑Awlaki’s teenage son quote a White House/National Security Council spokesman making a remark to the effect that the boy “should have had/should have chosen a more responsible father” when asked about the death. The comment was widely reported and drew criticism; however reports differ slightly on the exact wording and which spokesperson was quoted.

claim: "The United States was paying for anywhere from 70 to 90 percent of (NATO), depending on the way you calculate."
rationale: The claim is misleading. The United States does not pay 70–90% of NATO's budgets: its share of NATO’s small common budgets is roughly around 20–25%, while its share of total NATO members’ combined national defence spending is large but typically nearer two-thirds (around 60–75% in some years), not as high as 90%. Different ways of counting (common NATO budgets vs. aggregate national defence spending vs. specific mission costs) can change the percentage, but none legitimately support a stable 70–90% figure across standard measures.

claim: "Fifteen years ago, the assets of the six largest banks in this country totaled 17 percent of GDP ... The assets of the six largest banks in the United States today total 63 percent of GDP."
rationale: The statement gives precise percentages without specifying the exact baseline year or which six institutions are counted. Publicly reported aggregates do show the largest U.S. banks’ share of assets rose substantially after consolidation, but independent datasets put the top-six banks’ assets in the mid-2010s closer to roughly 50–60% of GDP (not exactly 63%), and the earlier-era share depends on the chosen year and bank list and is not reliably 17% in standard series. Because the claim is precise but under-specified and doesn’t match commonly cited aggregates, it is assessed as false.

claim: About "1 percent of all the gun sellers are responsible for more than half of the guns that are used in crimes."
rationale: This claim is misleading rather than strictly true. ATF trace analyses and academic summaries have found that a very small share of licensed dealers (around 1% in some analyses) account for a large share of firearms that are recovered by police and successfully traced to a dealer in certain years, but that statistic applies only to traced crime guns and licensed dealers and varies by year and methodology. It does not mean 1% of all 'gun sellers' are responsible for more than half of all guns used in crimes overall.

claim: Wisconsin’s economy has "tanked" under Gov. Scott Walker and "so far in 2015 over 6,685 people have been laid off, already more than in all of 2014."
rationale: The claim mixes a subjective judgment and an unsupported numeric assertion. Broad economic indicators (unemployment rate and payroll employment) generally improved during much of Scott Walker’s tenure, so saying the economy ‘tanked’ is not supported by objective trend data; the specific figure that 'over 6,685 people have been laid off so far in 2015, already more than in all of 2014' is not corroborated by official WARN/DWD tallies and appears to miscount or cherry-pick periods.

claim: Says "85 percent (of immigrants) don’t show up for a scheduled court hearing or call to schedule a court hearing."
rationale: The claim that 85% of immigrants fail to show up or call to schedule hearings is not supported by official immigration court data or independent fact-checks. EOIR/DHS statistics and multiple fact-checking organizations report substantially lower and variable nonappearance rates depending on program and year; no credible source shows a consistent 85% no‑show rate. The statement also mixes different actions (not appearing vs not calling) without evidence.

claim: Video shows Joe Biden saying "we can only re-elect Donald Trump."
rationale: There is no credible, unedited footage showing Biden saying “we can only re-elect Donald Trump.” Viral clips making this claim have been debunked as edited, spliced, or miscaptioned and contradict Biden’s well-documented public position opposing Trump. Because the available video evidence appears manipulated, the claim that a genuine video shows him saying that is false.

claim: North Carolina Republican Senate candidate Thom Tillis would let insurance companies "deny coverage for pre-existing conditions."
rationale: Tillis supported Republican repeal-and-replace proposals (including versions of the AHCA/Graham-Cassidy-era efforts) that would have let states seek waivers from ACA protections such as community rating and essential health benefits. Those waiver provisions would have allowed insurers or state-regulated markets to limit coverage or charge much more for people with pre-existing conditions, so saying he would let insurers deny coverage is a fair characterization of the effect of the policies he backed.

claim: "The (ARC Tunnel) project was originally estimated to be $8.7 billion, and New Jersey alone was on the hook for all overruns."
rationale: The ARC project was widely reported with an initial cost estimate of about $8.7 billion, so the first part is essentially correct. However, the claim that New Jersey alone would be on the hook for all overruns is false: the funding and liability picture involved federal grants/loans and other contractual arrangements, and analyses at the time concluded the state would not automatically bear every dollar of any cost overrun by itself.

claim: "No Democratic campaign for (Fla.) governor has ever had these kinds of resources this early on in an election cycle."
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim and is vague about what counts as “these kinds of resources.” Past Florida Democratic gubernatorial campaigns — notably Andrew Gillum’s 2018 effort — attracted substantial early national fundraising, donors, and organizational support, so it is not accurate to say no campaign ever had such resources early. Without a precise definition or timeframe the blanket “never” is not supportable.

claim: 47 percent of Americans "can’t pay for an unexpected $400 expense through savings or credit cards, without selling something or borrowing money."
rationale: The widely cited Federal Reserve survey of household finances reports about 40% of adults could not cover an unexpected $400 expense without selling something or borrowing, not 47%. While some other polls or earlier years show different percentages, the claim as stated (47%) does not match the main recent Fed estimate commonly used to summarize this question.

claim: Hepatitis outbreak in kids may be related to Johnson & Johnson COVID-19 vaccine.
rationale: There is no credible evidence linking the pediatric acute hepatitis outbreak to the Johnson & Johnson COVID-19 vaccine. Investigations have detected adenovirus (particularly type 41) in many cases and most affected children were too young or unvaccinated for COVID‑19 vaccines, and regulatory safety monitoring has not identified a signal tying the J&J vaccine to this syndrome. The claim is speculative and not supported by current epidemiologic data.

claim: "Jamaica has not recorded any case of the coronavirus."
rationale: This is false: Jamaica reported its first confirmed SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) cases in March 2020 and subsequently recorded many cases and deaths tracked by the Ministry of Health and international health agencies. The country did not remain free of coronavirus infections after the global spread in 2020.

claim: The Keystone pipeline creates "35 permanent jobs" after construction, according to a government report.
rationale: Multiple U.S. government analyses, most notably the Department of State environmental impact statement for the Keystone XL project, reported that the pipeline would support only about 35 long‑term/permanent U.S. jobs during operation after construction. That figure has been widely cited and distinguished from the many temporary construction jobs the project would create. The claim accurately attributes the 35 permanent jobs to a government report.

claim: Maj. Nidal Hasan, the man accused of the Fort Hood shootings, "was an ADVISOR to the Obama Administration."
rationale: Nidal Hasan was an Army psychiatrist stationed at Fort Hood and is the accused/convicted perpetrator of the 2009 Fort Hood shootings, but there is no record he served as an advisor to President Obama or the Obama administration. Major news organizations and official records do not list any White House or administration advisory role for Hasan; assertions that he was an "advisor" are mischaracterizations or political exaggerations.

claim: "Barack Hussein Obama will ... force local authorities to allow Occupy protesters to live in parks."
rationale: The President cannot unilaterally compel local governments to allow encampments in parks, and there is no record that President Obama announced or implemented a policy to force local authorities to permit Occupy protesters to live in parks. Park policing and regulations are primarily local or state responsibilities, and overriding them would require legislation, federal jurisdiction, or court orders, none of which occurred.

claim: "Most of, if not all of, the [DeKalb school construction] projects always came in on or were under budget."
rationale: The claim is an overly broad, near-absolute statement about all or most DeKalb school construction projects always meeting or undershooting budget. Large public construction programs commonly experience cost increases, and reporting/audits of DeKalb school construction programs have identified examples of delays and cost overruns, so the blanket assertion is not supported. Without precise program, timeframe, and baseline budget definitions the claim cannot be verified as true.

claim: I am the only U.S. Senate candidate who spoke out against bombing Syria, and who challenged Georgia’s governor and insurance commissioner over obstruction to the Affordable Care Act.
rationale: The claim asserts unique status (the only Senate candidate) on two separate public-policy actions. Public record and news coverage show multiple U.S. Senate candidates have publicly opposed U.S. bombing of Syria and others have publicly challenged Georgia officials over ACA obstruction, so the exclusivity claim is implausible and not substantiated. Without narrow temporal or definitional limits the statement cannot be verified and is likely false.

claim: Says Barack Obama didn't keep his promise to have an immigration bill in his first year.
rationale: Barack Obama campaigned and pledged to make comprehensive immigration reform a priority early in his presidency, but no major comprehensive immigration bill was enacted during his first year in office (2009). Legislative focus that year was on the economic crisis and health care, and the most significant congressional immigration action (a Senate comprehensive bill) did not occur until 2013 and did not become law.

claim: Says Miami-Dade Mayor Carlos Gimenez "approved a 67% pay raise for himself and increased his own pension. He makes $250,000 a year, more than almost every big-city Mayor in the country. He also kept his taxpayer-funded Mercedes-Benz after slashing $400 million in government jobs and spending."
rationale: The claim mixes accurate, exaggerated, and unsupported elements. While Gimenez's mayoral salary has been reported in the roughly $200k–$250k range, there is no clear evidence he personally “approved a 67% pay raise for himself” or unilaterally increased his pension — pay changes are typically set by commissions or council votes and reporting on any specific raise and pension change is inconsistent. The assertion he “kept his taxpayer-funded Mercedes-Benz after slashing $400 million in government jobs and spending” is also unsubstantiated and lacks necessary context (timing, what cuts specifically, and vehicle policy).

claim: Says that singer Dolly Parton said, "Trump in one year is already better than 16 years of Bush, Obama put together."
rationale: There is no record in reputable news sources or transcripts of Dolly Parton saying this quote; it appears to be a social-media misattribution or parody. Parton has generally avoided direct partisan endorsements and fact-checking organizations have debunked similar viral attributions of political praise to her. The specific phrasing comparing Trump to '16 years of Bush, Obama put together' is not supported by verifiable primary sources or interviews.

claim: It’s "typical" for a presidential candidate to release 10 or 11 years of tax returns.
rationale: This is false because there is no consistent norm requiring candidates to release 10–11 years of returns; practices have varied by campaign and era. Many candidates have released only a handful of years, while some have released more, so claiming 10–11 years is “typical” overstates the common practice.

claim: Emails show Democrats, Hillary Clinton and George Soros instigated and orchestrated racial protests in Charlottesville by trying to "control" and keep people "desperate."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or verified email trail showing Democrats, Hillary Clinton, or George Soros instigated or orchestrated the Charlottesville protests. Independent reporting and official accounts attribute the August 2017 violence to far‑right organizers and white supremacist groups, not to Democratic leaders or Soros. Claims tying leaked emails to a plot to “control” and keep people “desperate” rely on misinterpretation and conspiracy, not documented coordination.

claim: Says Florida Gov. Rick Scott "subtracted $1.3 billion from public schools."
rationale: The statement is misleading. The $1.3 billion number circulated during Rick Scott’s early years but referred to proposed reductions, accounting shifts (including one‑time funds and local property tax shifts) and year‑to‑year comparisons, not a single unilateral $1.3 billion subtraction from public schools enacted directly by the governor.

claim: "28.2 million Americans are still waiting under Obamacare and remain uninsured!"
rationale: The statement is misleading. While independent sources have reported the uninsured population in the high‑20s of millions in some years (figures vary by data source and year), claiming "28.2 million are still waiting under Obamacare" incorrectly implies they are enrolled and merely awaiting coverage under the ACA; in reality uninsured totals fluctuate by year and many uninsured people are ineligible, unaware, or have other reasons for lacking coverage. The precise 28.2 million figure without a date or source is therefore not a reliable factual claim.

claim: "The RI Board of Elections has heard official testimony from Providence residents who claim to have witnessed known illegal aliens voting in local elections."
rationale: There is no verifiable public record or credible news reporting through mid‑2024 that the Rhode Island Board of Elections accepted corroborated, official testimony from Providence residents proving they witnessed documented noncitizens (“illegal aliens”) voting in local elections. While election boards sometimes receive public comments or unverified allegations about voter eligibility, such claims in Rhode Island have not been substantiated or recorded as proven instances of illegal voting. The claim conflates unverified allegations with verified, official testimony of proven illegal voting incidents.

claim: "So that 2005 energy bill was a big step backwards on the path to clean, renewable energy. That's why I voted against it."
rationale: The statement mixes a subjective judgment (that the 2005 energy bill was “a big step backwards”) with a factual claim about the speaker’s motive for voting. Without knowing who “I” is and checking that person’s roll-call vote and stated rationale, the vote-and-motive portion is unverifiable here; the policy judgment about the bill is inherently subjective and contestable. Because key facts (speaker identity and voting record) are missing and the policy assessment is opinion, the claim cannot be confirmed as factual.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Michael McCaul is "the sixth-richest person in Congress."
rationale: Congressional wealth rankings shift yearly and depend on valuation and timing; public compilations (e.g., Roll Call, OpenSecrets, Forbes) have listed Rep. Michael McCaul among the wealthier members but not reliably as exactly the sixth-richest. Because the claim gives no date or source and current lists do not consistently place him at #6, the precise statement cannot be verified and is likely false. If a specific ranking date or source were provided, the claim could be confirmed or disproved more definitively.

claim: Cal Cunningham "voted for over $1 billion in new taxes."
rationale: There is no clear legislative record showing Cal Cunningham cast a single vote that explicitly enacted “over $1 billion in new taxes.” During his time in the North Carolina legislature he voted on budgets and revenue measures that included various fees and revenue adjustments, but the $1 billion figure appears to be an aggregation or a misleading characterization rather than a discrete vote for that amount of new taxes.

claim: "Some even advocate wiping out 401(k)s entirely and replacing them with government-run accounts."
rationale: This is accurate in a literal sense: in U.S. retirement-policy debates a number of academics, progressive think tanks, and some lawmakers have proposed eliminating or substantially replacing employer-based 401(k) plans with government-run or public retirement accounts. Those proposals (e.g., various public-account or MyRA-style ideas) are minority positions but have been publicly advocated.

claim: "We've had two members engage in a Democrat-led persecution of ordinary citizens who engaged in legitimate political discourse."
rationale: The claim is unverified and too vague to be treated as fact: it alleges that 'two members' carried out a 'Democrat-led persecution' of ordinary citizens but provides no names, dates, or concrete incidents. Without identifiable events or corroborating evidence showing Democratic leadership and that targets were merely engaging in "legitimate political discourse," the assertion amounts to a partisan allegation rather than a documented fact.

claim: Says that PolitiFact Ohio confirms that Betty Sutton "maxed out federal debt"
rationale: There is no record that PolitiFact Ohio issued a finding that Betty Sutton "maxed out federal debt." PolitiFact fact-checks specific claims and uses ratings, and it would not summarize a ruling with that vague phrase; without a cited article, the statement appears inaccurate or misleading.

claim: "I will need to show proof to do anything indoors in" New York City, "but not when I vote?"
rationale: This is false because New York City's vaccine mandate ('Key to NYC') required proof of vaccination for many indoor settings (restaurants, gyms, entertainment venues) but did not literally require proof to enter every indoor space. Separately, in-person voting has never required proof of COVID vaccination (elections generally do not require health-status documentation).

claim: "Only sign outside Bucks County voting place. Democrats shown, republicans blurred out. … More scamming in Pennsylvania!"
rationale: There is no verifiable evidence that Bucks County polling places systematically displayed only Democratic signs while Republican signs were blurred out; the claim appears to rely on an unverified or selectively edited image and leaps to an accusation of "scamming." Polling-place signage is regulated and isolated photos can be cropped or altered, so this broad allegation is unsupported by available information.

claim: "Principal bans candy canes."
rationale: The claim is too vague to verify — it names no school, principal, date, or jurisdiction. Without specific context there is no evidence that a principal generally or universally ‘bans candy canes’; such a statement is unsubstantiated and likely false as a general claim. It could be true in a particular school, but as presented it lacks verifiable detail.

claim: "(For) white working-class America, death rates among white men are up 20 percent."
rationale: The statement is misleading because it lacks a clear timeframe, age range, and definition of “white working‑class America.” Scholarly work (e.g., Case & Deaton) and CDC data show increased mortality for certain cohorts of white non‑Hispanic middle‑aged adults (driven by drug/alcohol/suicide) but the percent change varies widely by age, sex, cause and period — it is not a single, uniform “up 20 percent” for all white working‑class men. Without those specifics the claim overgeneralizes and can be incorrect for many definitions and time windows.

claim: "More suicide deaths than coronavirus death past two months."
rationale: The claim is unverified and likely false as written because it gives no location or exact two-month period; without that context you cannot compare counts. Global and national COVID-19 death totals have in many recent two-month periods exceeded suicide deaths, though the reverse could be true in some places and times. Because the statement is presented as a general fact without specifying time or place, it is not supported by evidence.
