claim: Says Rob Portman was a registered foreign agent whose "client was Haiti, at a time when the Baby Doc, Duvalier, who was a despot, was killing people."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Rob Portman ever registered under the U.S. Foreign Agents Registration Act to represent Haiti or that he acted as a foreign agent for the Duvalier regime. Portman’s public career and biographies list U.S. government and private-sector roles, and major reporting and FARA records do not show him representing Jean‑Claude “Baby Doc” Duvalier or the Haitian government. The claim appears to conflate or misattribute activities to Portman that are not supported by available records.

claim: Under changes being debated, state employees in Wisconsin "who earn $30,000, $40,000, $50,000 a year might have 20 percent of their income just disappear overnight."
rationale: This is an exaggeration. Wisconsin reforms being debated (notably Act 10 and related proposals) required employees to start contributing toward pensions (around 5.8% of pay) and to pay a larger share of health insurance and limited collective bargaining over raises — measures that reduce take-home pay by single-digit percentages for most workers. While lost raises and reduced benefits can lower overall compensation over time, there was no credible proposal that would make one-fifth of typical state employees' salary "disappear overnight."

claim: Terry McAuliffe favors "taking the Pledge of Allegiance and the 4th of July out of the (school) curriculum."
rationale: Reporting and contemporaneous fact-checks found no support that McAuliffe advocated removing the Pledge of Allegiance or the Fourth of July from school curricula. The statement appears to be a misleading paraphrase of comments taken out of context during a campaign debate and was used in attack ads, but there is no reliable evidence he called for eliminating those patriotic exercises from schools.

claim: Says 194 people were killed in mass shootings in 2018 while undocumented immigrants killed 83,211 people.
rationale: This is false. While some sources count roughly in the low hundreds of mass‑shooting fatalities in 2018 depending on the definition, there is no credible evidence that undocumented immigrants killed 83,211 people that year — total U.S. homicides in 2018 were on the order of ~16,000. The 83,211 number is implausible and appears to be a misinterpretation or fabrication.

claim: Forty percent of gross domestic product "is state, local, or federal money."
rationale: The statement is misleading. In normal years total government outlays (federal + state + local) are typically in the low-to-mid 30% range of U.S. GDP (federal ~20–25%, state/local ~10–12%), not a flat 40%; GDP is a measure of production, not 'money' owned. Exceptional years (e.g., large pandemic relief) temporarily pushed government spending nearer to 40%, so the claim is only true in specific contexts and definitions.

claim: U.S. Rep. John Barrow’s plan "puts the IRS in charge of your health care."
rationale: This claim is a hyperbolic mischaracterization. While tax authorities like the IRS/Treasury sometimes administer tax credits or enforce penalties tied to health-policy provisions, they do not run medical care, set treatment decisions, or operate insurance plans — those roles fall to HHS/CMS, states, insurers and providers. Even plans that use the tax code to deliver subsidies only make the IRS responsible for tax administration tasks, not for “your health care.”

claim: "We’re spending tremendous amounts of money to educate our kids. In the world, we're No. 1 per pupil by a factor of four."
rationale: The United States does spend among the highest amounts per student in OECD comparisons, but it is not "No. 1 by a factor of four." International data (OECD/World Bank) show U.S. per‑pupil K–12 spending is higher than the OECD average and similar in magnitude to other top spenders, not four times larger than other countries or the global average.

claim: Abraham Lincoln "visited and some say even danced in (the Ohio Senate) chamber."
rationale: There is no reliable historical evidence that Abraham Lincoln ever danced in the Ohio Senate chamber; the anecdote appears to be local lore or hearsay. While Lincoln traveled and spoke in Ohio on some occasions, reputable biographies and his travel records do not document him visiting the Ohio Senate chamber and dancing there.

claim: Says "76 percent of all voters in the United States say they want Johnson-Weld, by name, in the presidential debates."
rationale: No credible, representative national poll supports the claim that 76% of all U.S. voters by name said they wanted the Johnson–Weld ticket in the presidential debates. Most reputable polls from the 2016 cycle and later showed much lower levels of support for the Libertarian ticket and debate inclusion, and no widely reported survey produced a 76% figure for 'Johnson–Weld' specifically.

claim: "The Legislature spent the last decade passing laws deliberately making it even harder for people to access these critical supports when they need it most, exacerbating the problems with our already-outdated system."
rationale: The claim is a sweeping, causal assertion about a legislature’s intent over a ten-year period but gives no jurisdiction, specific laws, or programs. Legislative changes over a decade typically include both expansions and restrictions depending on the policy area and state, and proving deliberate intent requires documented legislative intent or consistent statutory patterns, which are not provided. Without specific evidence, the blanket allegation cannot be verified and is therefore judged false.

claim: Peter Kilmartin voted for the 38 Studios loan guarantee and his State House job was to "twist [legislator’s] arms to vote for deals like this."
rationale: There is no reliable record that Peter Kilmartin cast a roll‑call vote in favor of the 38 Studios loan guarantee, and the characterization that his State House job was to ‘twist [legislator’s] arms to vote for deals like this’ is an allegation reported by critics rather than an established fact about his official duties. The 38 Studios loan guarantee was approved in 2010 and criticism about lobbying/pressure around the deal has been documented, but the specific claim conflates an unverified quote with an asserted voting record.

claim: "Taking into account inflation, the federal minimum wage is actually worth less than what it was worth 50 years ago."
rationale: Adjusted for inflation, the federal minimum wage today (nominally $7.25 since 2009) has less purchasing power than the federal minimum in the mid-1970s (around $2.00–$2.10). Using CPI-based inflation, mid-1970s minimums convert to roughly $11–$12 in today’s dollars, which is higher than $7.25, so the real value has declined over the past ~50 years.

claim: "U.S. Department of Homeland Security has told banks -- in writing -- it may inspect safe deposit boxes without warrant and seize any gold, silver, guns or other valuables it finds inside those boxes!"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that DHS issued a blanket written directive allowing banks to open safe-deposit boxes without warrants and seize valuables. U.S. law generally requires warrants, court orders, or owner consent for searches and seizures, though law enforcement can obtain judicial orders or use statutory forfeiture processes in specific cases. Rumors conflate lawful bank cooperation, civil asset-forfeiture authority, or isolated agency communications with a universal no-warrant inspection power.

claim: "HR 1 is going to take your hard-earned tax dollars and millions more and send them to (a political candidate’s) campaign so (they) can put ads on TV."
rationale: The claim misstates what HR 1 (the For the People Act) proposed. HR 1 created a voluntary small-donor public matching program and other campaign-finance reforms for candidates who opt in and meet eligibility rules and limits; it did not authorize the government to seize individual taxpayers’ money and automatically send unlimited millions to a candidate’s campaign for TV ads. The proposal was regulatory and conditional rather than an unconditional transfer of taxpayers’ dollars to any campaign.

claim: Says fewer than 30 percent of Texas college students graduate in four years and only 58 percent graduate within six years.
rationale: The statement understates typical graduation rates and is ambiguous about which student cohort is meant. Official IPEDS and state higher-education data show four‑year graduation rates for first‑time, full‑time bachelor’s students at Texas four‑year institutions are generally well above 30%, and six‑year rates are near or above roughly 58–62% depending on cohort and institution. Because the claim mixes unspecified populations and gives lower figures than commonly reported for the defined cohort, it is misleading.

claim: Says Mike Pence was arrested.
rationale: There is no credible reporting or official record up to June 2024 that former Vice President Mike Pence was arrested. An arrest of a high-profile national figure would have been widely reported by major news organizations and official sources, which did not occur. The claim appears to be misinformation or confusion with another individual or rumor.

claim: Questions about whether she’s been vaccinated are "a violation of my HIPAA rights."
rationale: This claim is incorrect as stated. HIPAA restricts disclosure of protected health information by covered entities (health care providers, health plans, and their business associates), but it does not prohibit private individuals, employers, or businesses from asking someone whether they have been vaccinated. A HIPAA violation would only occur if a covered entity improperly disclosed a person’s health information without authorization.

claim: A photo taken on Jan. 6, 2021, at the United States Capitol riot was "doctored to look as if the Capitol was on fire."
rationale: Multiple independent fact-checkers analyzed a viral Jan. 6 image that purported to show the U.S. Capitol 'on fire' and concluded the picture was digitally altered — flames were overlaid onto an authentic Capitol photo. Authentic on-site photos and videos from Jan. 6 show smoke and limited small fires or flares in parts of the riot but do not show the Capitol building engulfed in flames as depicted in the doctored image.

claim: U.S. Sen. Kay Bailey Hutchison "voted to continue Roe v. Wade."
rationale: The claim is false as stated. The Senate does not 'vote to continue Roe v. Wade' because Roe is a Supreme Court decision, not legislation the Senate can directly continue; moreover Kay Bailey Hutchison was a Republican with a pro‑life record and there is no clear Senate roll call where she 'voted to continue Roe.' Without a specific bill or procedural vote cited, the assertion is misleading or incorrect.

claim: North Carolina’s health department is "telling hospitals that if they decide to do elective surgeries, they won’t be eligible to receive (protective equipment) from the state."
rationale: This statement mischaracterizes North Carolina Department of Health guidance. During COVID-19 the state urged postponement of elective procedures and established a needs-based PPE allocation/prioritization system, but there is no evidence the department issued a blanket rule that hospitals performing elective surgeries would be categorically ineligible to receive state-provided protective equipment. The policy framed distribution by urgency and need rather than an absolute ban tied solely to elective procedures.

claim: "Whales live as long at SeaWorld" as they do in the wild.
rationale: The claim is false. Multiple peer-reviewed studies and mortality records indicate that killer whales and other cetaceans in SeaWorld have higher early mortality and shorter average lifespans than wild populations—wild female orcas commonly live many decades (50–90 years) while captive orcas often die much younger. SeaWorld's own data and industry claims have been challenged by independent analyses showing a clear survival gap.

claim: The "Buffett rule" "raises virtually no money, maybe a day and a half of our borrowing per year."
rationale: Congressional tax estimates for the Obama-era “Buffett rule” put revenue at roughly $40–50 billion over 10 years (about $4–5 billion per year). With U.S. annual deficits in the $1+ trillion range at the time (roughly $3 billion+ borrowed per day), $4–5 billion is on the order of a day to two days of federal borrowing, so the claim’s characterization is accurate in scale.

claim: "449,000 Californians turned down jury duty because they were not citizens… but they were registered voters."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that 449,000 Californians who declined jury duty for being 'not citizens' were in fact registered voters. The 449,000 figure appears to conflate different administrative counts (people excused from jury service over time) with voter-registration status; California’s verified records and prior fact-checks find only a tiny fraction of registrants are noncitizens and far fewer confirmed cases of noncitizen registration. Therefore the specific claim that 449,000 were registered voters is unsupported and misleading.

claim: State budget cuts for local schools resulted in "nearly 4,000 educator layoffs"
rationale: The claim is presented without a named state, timeframe, or source, so it cannot be independently verified. Layoff tallies are specific to particular states and years and reporting varies; without those details the assertion that state budget cuts resulted in nearly 4,000 educator layoffs is unsupported.

claim: Under Republican-backed state budget, the state education agency estimates expansion of Wisconsin’s school voucher program "could cost nearly $2 billion annually"
rationale: Multiple analyses from Wisconsin’s Department of Public Instruction and contemporary news reports stated that the Republican-backed budget proposal to expand the school voucher program could increase state costs by nearly $2 billion annually. The figure was presented as an estimate or potential maximum impact depending on enrollment and implementation details, not an immediate guaranteed outlay.

claim: "Black Lives Matter, who are attacking law enforcement officers" -- Barack Obama "had them to the White House."
rationale: The claim bundles two assertions that together mislead: while President Obama and his administration did meet with Black Lives Matter activists and hosted discussions at the White House, there is no basis for the blanket statement that BLM as a movement is "attacking law enforcement officers." Black Lives Matter is a decentralized movement primarily organizing protests and advocacy against police brutality; isolated incidents at demonstrations do not support the generalized accusation of organized attacks on police.

claim: "Not a single Republican candidate, announced or potential, is clearly and consistently supporting a path to citizenship. Not one."
rationale: The claim is false because at least some Republicans (both current or potential candidates and prominent GOP figures) have publicly supported pathways to citizenship or earned legalization for certain undocumented immigrants, especially DREAMers. Examples include past and potential Republican figures who have advocated for some form of citizenship path or legal status rather than blanket opposition. The blanket statement that ‘not a single’ Republican supports any path is contradicted by those public positions.

claim: "American oil production is at its highest level since 2003."
rationale: This claim is inaccurate or misleading as stated. U.S. crude oil production rose well above 2003 levels during the shale boom years and reached multi‑decade record highs (notably around 2018–2019 and again in subsequent years), so current production has exceeded 2003 levels for many years rather than only now reaching a high not seen since 2003.

claim: "In Florida felonies can be things like buying weed, tampering with an odometer or disturbing a lobster trap. So basically spring break."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Simple purchase/possession of small amounts of marijuana in Florida is typically a misdemeanor (possession over certain thresholds can be a felony), tampering with an odometer can be a felony when done with intent to defraud, and interfering with lobster traps is regulated and can be criminal but is not automatically a felony in all circumstances. Whether any of these acts is a felony depends on quantities, intent, and specific facts.

claim: "A rural hospital in Missouri closes every 8 months. The legislature’s failure to expand Medicaid has brought crisis to many of Missouri’s rural health care providers."
rationale: The specific metric that 'a rural hospital in Missouri closes every 8 months' is not supported by available data and appears to conflate or misstate closure rates. Missouri voters approved Medicaid expansion by ballot (Issue 2) in August 2020 and the state implemented expansion thereafter, so it is incorrect to say the legislature simply 'failed to expand Medicaid' in a way that singularly explains ongoing rural hospital collapse. Rural hospital financial distress has multiple causes (low patient volumes, workforce shortages, payer mix) and while delayed expansion likely contributed in some places, the claim as stated is misleading and factually unsupported.

claim: "David Dewhurst currently owes more than $1 million to vendors for services provided to his 2012 U.S. Senate campaign."
rationale: The statement as written cannot be confirmed because it uses 'currently' without a date. While news reports after the 2012 Senate campaign indicated Dewhurst's campaign carried more than $1 million in vendor debts, those reports date to 2013 and campaign debts may have been repaid or changed since then, so the present-tense claim is unverified.

claim: "We’ve got an average of 5,600 soldiers committing suicide. That’s about 20 a day."
rationale: The arithmetic is incorrect and the terminology is misleading. 5,600 suicides per year corresponds to about 15 per day (5,600/365 ≈ 15.3), not 20; 20 per day would equate to roughly 7,300 per year. Also public data distinguishes active-duty service members (hundreds per year) from veterans (several thousand per year), so calling them all ‘soldiers’ is imprecise.

claim: "In New Jersey, Gov. Christie vetoed legislation to extend early voting."
rationale: True — during his time as New Jersey governor Chris Christie vetoed legislation that would have expanded early in-person (no‑excuse) voting. He cited cost, administrative and election‑integrity concerns when returning such measures unsigned. The statement is accurate though it omits which specific bill(s) and year(s).

claim: There were no American flags at the first Democratic presidential debate.
rationale: Contemporaneous reporting and photographs of the first Democratic presidential primary debate in June 2019 show the stage and backdrop without American flags, a fact noted widely in the press at the time. While other debates in other years or different formats have displayed flags, the widely-referenced 'first Democratic debate' of that cycle did not have U.S. flags on stage.

claim: Says the mayor’s job "is to make sure that if somebody is trying to build a set of water treatment plants to cure us from cryptosporidium we don’t have, we don't say yes even if CH2M Hill wants us to."
rationale: The statement attributes a specific quote to “the mayor” but gives no identifying context (which mayor, when, or where) and I could not verify a public record of that exact quote. While CH2M Hill is a known engineering firm and cryptosporidium is a real waterborne pathogen, the attribution as stated is unverified and therefore likely false without a sourced citation.

claim: Sen. Mark Kelly voted "for benefits to illegals."
rationale: The claim is vague and misleading: there is no single Senate roll-call labeled as a vote “for benefits to illegals.” Voting records are cast on specific bills or amendments, and without a bill name or date the statement cannot be verified. Public roll‑call histories for Sen. Mark Kelly do not show any indisputable single vote that can be accurately summarized by that phrase without additional context.

claim: As Massachusetts governor, Mitt Romney used a line-item veto to cut "millions of dollars for firefighting equipment," including firefighters' "coats, pants, helmets and boots."
rationale: True. As Massachusetts governor Romney used his line-item veto authority to eliminate several earmarked municipal grants totaling millions of dollars, and contemporary reporting noted that some of those cuts were for local firefighting equipment — commonly described as turnout gear (coats, pants, helmets and boots). The vetoes were public and widely reported at the time, though exact amounts and affected towns varied.

claim: Video shows Ukrainian soldiers saying goodbye to loved ones amid Russia’s 2022 invasion.
rationale: There is insufficient information to verify the specific video referenced. While videos of Ukrainian soldiers saying farewell circulated during the 2022 invasion, without the actual clip, source, timestamps, or corroborating metadata the claim cannot be confirmed and must be treated as unverified/false. Verification would require checking the video's provenance and geolocation.

claim: Federal border officials are allowing undocumented immigrants who are "known criminals who possess an arrest warrant to fly on U.S. aircraft (which) threatens our homeland security."
rationale: There is no substantiated evidence of a formal federal policy knowingly allowing people with identified U.S. arrest warrants to board domestic U.S. aircraft. While isolated incidents and reports exist of migrants released on alternatives-to-detention or traveling domestically after processing, federal law-enforcement agencies generally detain or arrest individuals when they are aware of valid U.S. warrants; airline/TSA screening systems also do not systematically convey all local warrants. The broad claim overstates and conflates sporadic operational gaps with a deliberate practice that threatens homeland security.

claim: Obama "voted for ... $3-million for an overhead projector at a planetarium in Chicago."
rationale: This claim is false. There is no record that Barack Obama specifically voted to spend $3 million for an “overhead projector” at a Chicago planetarium; the allegation is a mischaracterization of budget/appropriation language and conflates or exaggerates line items. Fact-checking of similar claims found no vote or earmark that matches that description, and the term “overhead projector” is inaccurate for professional planetarium equipment.

claim: Passage of Clinton budget bill in 1993 "led to an enormous flowering of the economy in America."
rationale: This is an overstatement. The 1993 Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act did raise taxes on higher incomes and helped reduce projected deficits, which likely contributed to a stronger fiscal backdrop, but the 1990s economic boom resulted from multiple forces (technology/productivity gains, monetary policy, globalization, and other factors). Claiming that the bill alone "led to an enormous flowering" misattributes primary causal credit and is therefore false.

claim: A majority of Americans have voted for a party that … wants a world in which you cannot call your parents mom and dad."
rationale: This claim is false because no major U.S. political party has an official policy or credible platform calling for banning the words “mom” and “dad,” and there is no evidence that a majority of Americans voted for a party with such a policy. The statement appears to be a rhetorical mischaracterization of debates over inclusive language and transgender rights rather than a factual description of party platforms or voter intent.

claim: Says Marco Rubio "voted to deport" young people known as Dreamers.
rationale: There is no clear record of Marco Rubio casting a roll‑call vote explicitly ‘to deport’ Dreamers as a single, discrete action. Rubio has a mixed record—supporting stricter immigration enforcement and opposing some protections while at times backing legislative proposals that would provide legal status rather than automatic deportation—so the blanket claim that he voted to deport Dreamers is misleading.

claim: "One out of every two kids who are graduating college right now can't find a job."
rationale: The claim that 1 in 2 college graduates can’t find a job is inconsistent with labor-market data: recent college-graduate unemployment rates are typically in the low single digits to low double digits at worst, and a majority of graduates obtain employment or enroll in further study. Even measures of underemployment (working below skill level or in part-time roles) do not support a 50% outright inability to find any job across all graduates.

claim: "We’re at the point of reaching 2 million deportations ... this is a historic level, more than any other president of the United States."
rationale: The statement is misleading. DHS data show roughly 2–2.5 million removals during the 2009–2016 period often cited, but ‘deportations’ can be counted several ways (formal removals, returns, expedited removals) and historical counts are not directly comparable across administrations. Because the claim lacks definition and context, it is incorrect to assert categorically that this is more than any other president without qualification.

claim: "Back in the Great Recession, when millions of  jobs across America hung in the balance, Donald Trump said rescuing the auto industry didn’t really matter very much. He said, and I quote again, ‘Let it go.’ "
rationale: Contemporary reporting from the 2008–2009 financial crisis shows Donald Trump publicly opposed government bailouts of the auto industry and said things to the effect of letting failing companies fail (e.g., suggesting Detroit should be allowed to go bankrupt). However, there is no reliable primary-source record of him saying the exact quoted phrase “Let it go.” The claim presents a specific direct quote that cannot be substantiated by available coverage.

claim: "Minnesota, Michigan, Iowa already have 70 mph" speed limits on rural interstates, and "we see that they’ve been able to do it safely."
rationale: The statement that Minnesota, Michigan and Iowa have 70 mph limits on many rural interstate segments is essentially correct, but the follow-on claim that “we see that they’ve been able to do it safely” is not well supported. Empirical traffic-safety research and state crash data generally show that higher posted speeds increase average speeds and are associated with higher crash severity and fatalities; whether a particular state saw no adverse change requires state-by-state analysis. Because the safety assertion is broad and not backed by conclusive evidence, the overall claim is judged false.

claim: The Senate seat won in a special election by a Democrat had been "held for more than thirty years by Republicans."
rationale: The claim is incorrect as stated because in the best-known recent example — Democrat Doug Jones winning the 2017 Alabama special election — the seat had been held by Republican Jeff Sessions for about 20 years, not more than 30. There are no prominent recent special-election flips where Republicans had held the specific seat continuously for over three decades prior to a Democrat win.

claim: "Kenosha car dealer kills himself after insurance won’t cover … damages caused by the riots."
rationale: The claim is not supported by credible reporting. Multiple reputable fact-checkers and searches of local news and police records found no evidence that a Kenosha car dealer killed himself over insurance refusing to cover riot damage, and viral posts appear to misattribute images or events.

claim: "This election marks the largest Senate gains for a president's party in a first midterm election since at least President Kennedy's in 1962."
rationale: The claim is incorrect because there have been larger first‑midterm Senate gains by a president's party since 1962. For example, in President George W. Bush's first midterm in 2002 Republicans netted two Senate seats, which exceeds the one‑seat net gain often cited for the most recent midterm. Therefore it is not the largest since 1962.

claim: "It costs a hell of a lot more money to put somebody in jail than send them to the University of Virginia."
rationale: The claim as an absolute statement is not reliably true. Annual incarceration costs vary widely by state and facility (commonly roughly $20k–$70k per inmate per year), while attending the University of Virginia typically costs on the order of tens of thousands per year as well (in-state tuition + room and board roughly $25k–$40k/year depending on year and category). Depending on which costs (tuition alone vs full cost of attendance, and which state prison figures) you compare, prison can be more expensive, similar, or in some cases less — so it isn’t universally “a hell of a lot more.”

claim: The Republican replacement for Obamacare does not give massive tax cuts to wealthy Americans.
rationale: Major Republican ‘‘replacements’’ for the Affordable Care Act (notably the 2017 AHCA and similar proposals) included provisions that independent analysts and the CBO said would disproportionately benefit high‑income households — for example by rolling back taxes enacted under the ACA and shifting federal spending cuts that lower benefits for lower‑income people. Multiple nonpartisan analyses found the net fiscal changes and tax-related elements favored wealthy Americans, so the blanket claim that the Republican replacement “does not give massive tax cuts to wealthy Americans” is incorrect.

claim: Says "for the first time ever," Texas lawmakers are not funding student population growth.
rationale: The absolute claim that this is the 'first time ever' Texas lawmakers are not funding student population growth is unsupported. Texas has long used attendance-based formulas and various adjustments (including hold-harmless and targeted growth funding) and past legislatures have at times changed or not fully fund growth in particular budget cycles, so asserting an unprecedented first occurrence is unlikely without precise session and program details.

claim: Virginia "spends less per student today than we did in 2008."
rationale: The claim lacks a time reference and does not specify whether spending is measured in nominal dollars or adjusted for inflation. In nominal terms, total and per‑pupil K–12 expenditures in most U.S. states, including Virginia, have increased since 2008; however, if one adjusts for inflation or isolates particular categories of spending, numbers can be lower than 2008. Because the statement as written is unqualified and likely false in nominal dollars today, I rate it FALSE but with moderate uncertainty.

claim: "This rule could prevent children under 18 from using such tools as a power screwdriver, a milking machine or something as simple as a wheelbarrow on the family farm . . . "
rationale: This claim is misleading. Existing U.S. child labor law and typical regulatory practice do not categorically ban children under 18 from using commonplace, non-powered tools like wheelbarrows on family farms, and many family-farm exemptions exist; regulations instead target clearly hazardous, power-driven agricultural machinery. While some proposals or agency interpretations have considered tighter limits on certain powered equipment (and specifics vary by jurisdiction), saying the rule would broadly prevent common tasks is an exaggeration without the exact rule text.

claim: "Medicare and Medicaid are the single biggest drivers of the federal deficit and the federal debt by a huge margin."
rationale: This is inaccurate. Medicare and Medicaid are major mandatory spending programs but they are not the single biggest drivers of the federal deficit or debt by a huge margin — Social Security is the largest single mandatory program and other factors (tax policy/revenue shortfalls, discretionary spending, and rising net interest on the debt) also materially drive deficits. Over different years and in long-term projections the relative contributions shift, so claiming Medicare/Medicaid alone are the dominant cause by a large margin is misleading.

claim: "Right now, in every major poll, national poll and statewide poll done in the last month, six weeks, we are defeating Trump, often by big numbers and always at a larger margin than Secretary Clinton is."
rationale: The claim that every major national and statewide poll in the last month–six weeks shows ‘‘we’’ defeating Trump, often by big numbers and always by a larger margin than Clinton, is implausible and inconsistent with available polling aggregates. Polls during relevant periods showed mixed results: some national and state polls favored Clinton, some favored Sanders, and margins varied; not every major poll showed a Sanders advantage or a larger margin than Clinton. The categorical language (“every,” “always”) is contradicted by multiple reputable polls showing different outcomes.

claim: Says a video captures sound from the surface of Mars
rationale: NASA's Perseverance rover carries onboard microphones and in 2021 publicly released audio recordings captured on the Martian surface, including ambient wind and sounds of the Ingenuity helicopter. Therefore a video that properly uses those recordings can legitimately be said to capture sound from the surface of Mars. However, not every online clip claiming to be 'sound from Mars' is authentic without source verification.

claim: "Republicans in Congress are plotting to take away Medicare, Medicaid and Social Security."
rationale: The claim overstates and generalizes. While many Republican lawmakers have repeatedly proposed cuts, block grants, privatization options, or eligibility changes for Medicare, Medicaid and Social Security in various budgets and policy plans, there is no clear, documented, unified conspiracy by all Republicans in Congress to abolish all three programs outright. Statements and legislative proposals vary across members and parties and generally seek reform or spending limits rather than unanimous, secret plans to "take away" the programs.

claim: "BREAKING: Queen Elizabeth II Dead At 94"
rationale: Queen Elizabeth II is deceased, but she died on 8 September 2022 at age 96, not at 94. The claim's core fact (death) is true in general terms but the stated age is incorrect, so the overall claim as phrased is false.

claim: New food safety legislation will regulate backyard gardening.
rationale: The statement is a sweeping, unsubstantiated claim. Most recent food safety laws target commercial producers, processors, distributors, and retailers rather than private backyard gardens; whether any specific new law would regulate home gardening depends entirely on the exact bill language and jurisdiction. Without a named law or jurisdiction, the general claim is false.

claim: Says Texas does not regulate the appearance of some kinds of imitation firearms sold in Texas.
rationale: State law in Texas does not broadly mandate how all imitation or replica firearms must look, and many realistic-looking airsoft, BB, and replica guns are legally sold without distinct non‑realistic coloring under Texas law. Federal toy‑gun marking rules apply in some cases, but there is no comprehensive Texas statute requiring bright markings or limiting realistic appearance for all categories of imitation firearms. Thus it is accurate to say Texas does not regulate the appearance of some kinds of imitation firearms sold in the state.

claim: "Within a few years, we will be spending more on interest payments than on national security."
rationale: The claim is a specific near-term prediction without specifying the country or definitions, and current public budget projections do not definitively show interest payments overtaking all national security spending universally 'within a few years.' While interest costs are rising and could become a much larger share of budgets over time, whether they surpass national security spending in the near term depends on interest rates, economic growth, and how 'national security' is counted. Given that outcome is uncertain and context-dependent, the precise blanket claim is not supported.

claim: Germany "is crime-riddled right now" because of migration to Europe.
rationale: The claim is an overstatement: official German crime statistics and most analyses do not show the country is "crime-riddled" at present. While some offender groups with migrant backgrounds are overrepresented in particular offense categories, overall crime rates in Germany have been stable or have declined in many categories, and causally attributing general crime levels to migration is unsupported without detailed, disaggregated evidence.

claim: Ninety pounds of cocaine was found on a boat owned by Mitch McConnell's family and that they are "financing his Senate campaigns with their cocaine drug profits."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that 90 pounds of cocaine was seized from a boat owned by Mitch McConnell's family, nor any evidence that his Senate campaigns have been financed with drug-trafficking profits. Law enforcement seizure records and mainstream news outlets do not corroborate this claim, and campaign financing is publicly reported and shows no such illicit funding.

claim: Says Rick Scott "cut Medicaid" so people can't "get Obamacare."
rationale: The claim is misleading. As Florida governor Rick Scott opposed and refused the ACA Medicaid expansion and supported cutting or privatizing parts of Medicaid funding, but there is no clear evidence he deliberately "cut Medicaid" specifically to stop people from "getting Obamacare." Medicaid and the ACA marketplace are different programs, and Scott’s actions consisted mainly of rejecting expansion and tightening Medicaid budgets rather than a documented scheme to block marketplace enrollment.

claim: In the plot to kidnap Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, "the perps were ANTIFA and BLM anarchists."
rationale: False. Federal investigations, criminal charges, and court records showed the plotters were members or associates of a far‑right militia (often described as the Wolverine Watchmen) and not affiliated with Antifa or Black Lives Matter. Prosecutors presented no evidence tying Antifa/BLM to the kidnapping plot, and several defendants pleaded guilty or were convicted consistent with a right‑wing extremist motive.

claim: The Keystone XL pipeline "would have produced 830,000 barrels of oil per day, more than enough to offset what we import from Russia."
rationale: The statement is misleading. Keystone XL was proposed with a capacity of about 830,000 barrels per day, but a pipeline transports rather than produces oil, and its flows would have been primarily Canadian crude not newly produced U.S. output. Even though 830,000 bpd exceeds recent U.S. imports from Russia in many years, claiming it would "offset" Russian imports ignores timing, contractual flows, refinery compatibility and market routing, so the assertion as phrased is false.

claim: "Anybody that wants a test (for the coronavirus) can get a test."
rationale: The claim is false in typical contexts. During large parts of the COVID-19 pandemic testing capacity, supplies, and lab throughput were limited and many jurisdictions imposed eligibility criteria or required referrals, so not everyone who wanted a test could obtain one. Reports from multiple countries documented people turned away, long waits, or inability to get tested due to shortages.

claim: "Make no mistake -- Sherrod Brown is one of the main D.C. politicians responsible for Ohio jobs moving to China."
rationale: Sherrod Brown has a long record as a pro-labor, anti‑outsourcing politician who has criticized trade deals and advocated for manufacturing jobs, rather than promoting policies to move Ohio jobs to China. Responsibility for jobs shifting to China is attributable to a complex mix of corporate offshoring decisions, broader trade policies across administrations and Congress, automation, and global competition, not a single senator.

claim: Says President Obama has cracked down "on employers who are attracting undocumented immigrants and hiring them more than any previous president."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement that Obama cracked down on employers more than any previous president; that cannot be substantiated. Employer sanctions and workplace enforcement date back to the 1986 Immigration Reform and Control Act, and while the Obama administration increased certain workplace audits and penalties, comparisons across administrations depend on different metrics (raids, audits, fines, prosecutions) and timeframes and do not uniformly show Obama exceeded every prior president.

claim: Says Tony Evers wants to give in-state tuition and drivers licenses to "illegal aliens."
rationale: Governor Tony Evers has publicly supported policies that would let certain undocumented residents qualify for in-state tuition and has backed proposals to allow undocumented immigrants to obtain driver’s licenses. These positions were part of his campaign and gubernatorial policy statements and were debated in the Wisconsin Legislature. The claim captures the general policy goals, though implementation details and eligibility limits vary.

claim: Wrote that in 2006, Nancy Pelosi said she didn’t think capturing Osama bin Laden "makes us any safer," but in 2011 called his killing "historic."
rationale: Contemporaneous reporting and congressional press statements show Pelosi made a remark in 2006 expressing skepticism that capturing Osama bin Laden would "make us any safer," and after the 2011 raid she publicly praised the outcome, calling it "historic." Both characterizations match widely reported quotes from those two periods. The wording may vary slightly across reports, but the gist of both statements is accurate.

claim: Says he could be "the first president in modern history to be outspent."
rationale: The claim that someone could be “the first president in modern history to be outspent” is false because incumbents have been outspent by challengers in multiple recent U.S. presidential elections. Notable recent examples include Hillary Clinton outspending Donald Trump in 2016, and other incumbents in late 20th century contests were also outspent by their challengers. Therefore this would not be a unique first.

claim: "Right now, one third of all illegal aliens are going to California."
rationale: This is not supported by available data. Estimates from sources such as the Pew Research Center, DHS and Migration Policy Institute put the unauthorized immigrant population in the U.S. at roughly 10–11 million, with California hosting on the order of 2.0–2.6 million — about 20–25%, well under one-third. The claim also uses vague wording ('going to') and no clear timeframe, which makes it misleading even if referring to new arrivals rather than residents.

claim: Says he was "not part of transferring" any priests accused of sexual abuse.
rationale: The claim as written is ambiguous because it omits who “he” refers to, and without a named person or a source for the quoted denial I cannot verify that the statement was actually made. I found no way to corroborate this specific quote or attribute it to a public figure from the provided text, so the claim cannot be treated as a verified fact. Given the missing context, asserting it as true is unsupported.

claim: Says President Donald Trump as a candidate mentioned WikiLeaks "over 160 times in speeches" in the last month of the campaign.
rationale: I found no independent, reliable tally showing Trump (as a candidate) said “WikiLeaks” more than 160 times in speeches during the final month of the 2016 campaign. Fact-checkers and news analyses that examined his public remarks and social media found many references but not a documented, verifiable count at that level, and such high figures usually traced to broadened or unclear counting methods. The precise claim is therefore unsupported.

claim: Fundamental changes made to the language describing the Wisconsin Idea in the University of Wisconsin System's mission statement were the result of a "drafting error."
rationale: Although UW System officials publicly characterized the removal/rewording of the Wisconsin Idea language as a “drafting error,” contemporaneous reporting and board materials show the changes appeared in earlier drafts and were the product of edits made during the drafting process rather than a simple typographical mistake. In short, the official explanation labeled it an error after backlash, but available public records and journalism indicate the language change was introduced deliberately in drafting/edits and then described as an error later. Thus the claim that the fundamental changes were the result of a mere “drafting error” is not supported.

claim: Says the majority of candidates in Texas’ 25th Congressional District live outside the district.
rationale: The statement lacks a timeframe or list of candidates and therefore cannot be verified as a general fact. Residency for U.S. House candidates is required only at the state level, so while some TX‑25 candidates in a particular cycle may live outside the district, claiming a majority does so is unsupported without specific, up‑to‑date candidate data.

claim: The home-mortgage deduction is widely thought to be "a middle-class benefit. It's not -- 73 percent of it goes to people making a quarter-million dollars or more a year."
rationale: The mortgage interest deduction does disproportionately benefit higher-income households, but authoritative distributional analyses do not support the precise claim that 73% of the benefit goes to taxpayers with incomes of $250,000 or more. Published IRS, CBO and tax-policy analyses show the bulk of the deduction accrues to the top quintile or higher-income filers, but the exact shares are substantially lower and vary by year and by whether one looks at tax units or homeowners and pre- vs post-2017 tax-law changes.

claim: "We now consume at the federal level 25 percent of the gross domestic product. Historically we were at 20 percent. So we've taken 5 percent away from the private sector."
rationale: The claim mixes a loosely defined statistic with a causal conclusion. While federal outlays as a share of GDP have been in the mid‑20s percent in recent years and historically have varied around ~20% in some earlier periods, the statement that a 5 percentage‑point rise was literally “taken away from the private sector” is incorrect: changes in government share of GDP depend on the time period chosen and on whether spending is financed by taxes, borrowing, or monetary policy, so it does not translate to a one‑for‑one subtraction from private activity.

claim: "Once again, a police officer has been killed with an illegal gun from Georgia – a state that last year did the NRA’s bidding and weakened its already lax gun laws."
rationale: The statement strings together two factual claims that are not reliably supported: there is no verifiable, generalizable proof that the referenced officer was killed by an illegally sourced Georgia gun, and the characterization that Georgia “last year did the NRA’s bidding and weakened its already lax gun laws” is a partisan summary that overstates and lacks specific legislative attribution. While Georgia has debated and passed some pro-gun measures in recent years, calling them definitively “NRA’s bidding” and saying they uniformly “weakened” laws is an opinionated interpretation rather than an established fact tied to the asserted shooting.

claim: U.S. military uniforms are manufactured in China.
rationale: The claim as stated is false because it asserts that U.S. military uniforms are manufactured in China without qualification. U.S. defense procurement is generally subject to domestic sourcing rules (e.g., the Berry Amendment) and the majority of core uniform items are produced under contracts requiring U.S. or approved domestic sources, although there have been isolated cases where components or subcontracted items were made overseas, including China.

claim: Says "Rep. Jim Weidner proposed a bill taking away health care for 80,000 of Oregon's children."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Rep. Jim Weidner introduced a bill that explicitly 'takes away health care for 80,000 of Oregon's children.' Public legislative records and contemporaneous news reporting do not corroborate that specific claim; it appears to be a misleading characterization or misattribution of some policy proposal.

claim: "While we were in harm’s way in uniform, Kyrsten Sinema was protesting us in a pink tutu and denigrating our service."
rationale: The claim mixes activist imagery and an accusation of denigrating service in a way that is not supported by reliable evidence. Kyrsten Sinema was involved in anti-war activism in the early 2000s and opponents have circulated images/stories about colorful protest clothing, but there is no substantiated record that she specifically protested in a pink tutu targeting deployed service members or explicitly denigrated their service while they were ‘in harm’s way.’ The statement therefore overstates and distorts available facts.

claim: "Since 1970, the Clean Air Act has reduced toxic and health-threatening air pollution by 60 percent while our economy has grown more than 200 percent."
rationale: This summary aligns with widely cited EPA findings that since 1970 emissions of major harmful air pollutants have fallen by roughly half to two‑thirds while U.S. economic output (real GDP) has more than doubled. The Clean Air Act and subsequent regulations are credited with driving large reductions in health‑threatening pollution even as the economy expanded. Exact percentages depend on which pollutants and end year are measured, but the claim reflects the mainstream government accounting.

claim: Says the Georgia Dome would need up to $350 million in work over the next five to seven years.
rationale: Contemporaneous reporting and statements from Georgia World Congress Center Authority and other officials in the mid-2010s stated that the Georgia Dome would require hundreds of millions in repairs, with assessments citing figures as high as $350 million to keep it functional over the coming several years. That estimate was repeatedly referenced in public discussions about replacing the Dome with the new Mercedes‑Benz Stadium.

claim: Says Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez tweeted, "Let’s begin ‘The Purge’ to roundup all Conservative traitors."
rationale: This attribution is false. There is no credible evidence that Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez tweeted a call to "begin 'The Purge'" or to round up conservatives; viral screenshots have been debunked and no such post exists on her verified timeline. The phrasing is extreme and would have been widely documented if authentic.

claim: "Back when they did NATO, there was no such thing as terrorism."
rationale: False. Terrorism as both a concept and a category of violent political action long predates NATO (founded in 1949). Examples include the French Revolution's "Reign of Terror," 19th‑century anarchist attacks and assassinations, and multiple early 20th‑century bombings and political murders. Thus the claim that there was "no such thing as terrorism" when NATO began is incorrect.

claim: Says Scott Walker supports "a health care plan that would gut protections for pre-existing conditions."
rationale: Scott Walker has backed repealing the Affordable Care Act and supported replacement approaches (state waivers and flexibility on essential health benefits) that independent analysts and Democrats warned would allow states or insurers to reduce protections for people with preexisting conditions. While Walker sometimes said he wanted protections preserved, the policy options he endorsed were widely judged to permit weakening or circumvention of those protections.

claim: "Flip Flop! After opposing term limits for decades, Adam Putnam adopts Donald Trump and Ron DeSantis’ position."
rationale: The claim is misleading and unsubstantiated as phrased. Public records do not show a clear decades-long opposition by Adam Putnam to term limits nor definitive evidence that he recently ‘‘adopted’’ a specific, publicly stated term‑limits platform identical to Donald Trump’s and Ron DeSantis’s; Putnam’s statements on term limits have been mixed and context-dependent. Because the claim compresses time, lacks detail about which term limits are meant, and asserts a sudden alignment without clear supporting evidence, it cannot be verified as true.

claim: Says an NBC producer at the Olympics was caught on a hot mic saying "60% of people in this stadium will be dead within 10 days."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that an NBC producer at the Olympics was caught on a hot mic saying that “60% of people in this stadium will be dead within 10 days.” Major news organizations and independent fact-checkers have not verified such a quote, and the claim appears to have originated and circulated on social media without substantiation. It matches patterns of fabricated hot-mic claims and misattributed audio.

claim: "The stock market does better when you have a Democratic president in the White House."
rationale: Multiple long‐run comparisons of major U.S. stock indices show that average returns have historically been higher during Democratic presidencies than Republican ones. This is a statistical pattern supported by several analyses, but it is a correlation and not definitive proof that party control causes the difference.

claim: Says Mitt Romney flip-flopped on gun control.
rationale: A broad claim that Romney “flip-flopped on gun control” is not clearly supported by the public record: his national campaigns have generally emphasized pro-Second Amendment positions while his record as Massachusetts governor included limited, state-level gun-safety measures rather than a clear reversal on core gun-policy stances. Major, well-documented reversals in his career are more prominent on issues like health care and abortion than on guns.

claim: "A Florida judge ruled parts of Obamacare unconstitutional."
rationale: This statement is accurate in a general sense: in January 2011 U.S. District Judge Roger Vinson (Northern District of Florida) ruled that the ACA’s individual mandate was unconstitutional and struck down parts of the law. That district-court ruling was later superseded by appeals and the 2012 U.S. Supreme Court decision which upheld the mandate under Congress’s taxing power.

claim: Says Marco Rubio endorsed Obamacare for his own family.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Marco Rubio publicly 'endorsed' the Affordable Care Act (Obamacare) on behalf of his own family. Rubio has been a consistent critic of the law, and fact-checkers found claims that he or his family explicitly endorsed or enrolled via Obamacare to be unsubstantiated or misleading. Without a verifiable direct quote or reliable reporting that he endorsed the law for his family, the claim is not supported.

claim: Says "Nicolás Maduro is carrying out a genocide on his people."
rationale: There is no authoritative international legal finding that Nicolás Maduro is committing genocide. Credible bodies and NGOs have documented widespread abuses and possible crimes against humanity in Venezuela, but genocide requires proof of intent to destroy a protected group and has not been legally established in this case.

claim: "I can tell you with certainty (cap and trade) would have a devastating impact on our economy."
rationale: The statement asserts a certain, universally ‘devastating’ economic outcome, but empirical evidence and economic modeling of cap‑and‑trade programs do not support that level of certainty. Analyses by government agencies and academic studies typically project modest macroeconomic costs and show outcomes depend heavily on program design, revenue recycling, and transition measures, so one cannot reliably claim with certainty that cap‑and‑trade would be devastating.

claim: Says he’s the one who gave the nickname "Mad Dog" to former Defense Secretary James Mattis.
rationale: The claim as presented is unverified and incomplete because it does not identify who “he” is, and there is no well-documented single individual universally credited with coining the nickname “Mad Dog” for James Mattis. The nickname has been widely used in media and by colleagues, but reputable sources do not attribute its origin to one clear person claiming credit publicly.

claim: "If we had been on 'Obamacare' and a bureaucrat was trying to tell me when I could get that CAT scan, that would have delayed my treatment."
rationale: The statement presents a counterfactual that is not supported by how the Affordable Care Act works. The ACA did not create a single centralized “bureaucrat” who schedules or approves individual tests; insurance prior-authorization and utilization management are practices used by private and public insurers (and predate the ACA), and timeliness of a CAT scan depends on the specific plan, provider network, and clinical urgency. There is no evidence that simply being covered under the ACA would have automatically caused a delayed scan in the way the claim implies.

claim: "The president came in and campaigned against me 12 times."
rationale: The statement is a specific numeric assertion but lacks any context (which president, which campaign, dates) and no corroborating event record is provided. Without verifiable schedules, news reports, or campaign event lists confirming exactly 12 instances of the president campaigning against this person, the claim cannot be substantiated and should be treated as false in absence of evidence.

claim: "Congress has cut funding, has slashed funding, for veterans' benefits over these last years."
rationale: The broad claim that Congress has cut or “slashed” veterans’ benefits in recent years is not supported by enacted federal budget trends: overall VA discretionary and mandatory benefits spending has generally risen and reached record or near‑record levels in recent budget cycles. While some specific programs or proposed budgets may have seen reductions or policy changes, the aggregate funding for veterans’ compensation, pensions, healthcare and education has increased rather than been slashed.

claim: Says "Rep. Ann Wagner, a three-term incumbent, has never held a town hall in the Second District."
rationale: The claim is false as stated. Ann Wagner has held constituent meetings and town-hall–style events (including telephone town halls and smaller in-district meetings) during her time representing Missouri’s 2nd District, so it is incorrect to say she has "never" held a town hall. The claim likely hinges on a narrow definition of "town hall" (e.g., large in-person forums) rather than the broader range of constituent events she has held.

claim: Says author J.K. Rowling was the first billionaire to fall off Forbes billionaire list because of charitable giving.
rationale: This claim is false. Although media coverage noted J.K. Rowling dropped off Forbes’ billionaire list after large charitable donations, she was not uniquely the first person ever to lose billionaire status because of philanthropy. Earlier philanthropists (for example Chuck Feeney) gave away the bulk of their fortunes and ceased to appear on billionaire rankings, and Forbes list changes can reflect many factors including philanthropy, market moves and taxes.

claim: "Forty years ago, a federal Pell Grant paid for nearly 80% of tuition, fees, room and board at a four-year college."
rationale: The oft‑quoted “nearly 80%” figure refers to the mid‑1970s (around 1975) when the maximum Pell Grant covered roughly three‑quarters of the cost of attending a public four‑year college. Forty years ago (about 1985) Pell grants covered a substantially smaller share because grant maximums did not keep pace with rising tuition and living costs, so the claim misstates the timing and share.

claim: "Texas legislators have filed voucher proposals in every legislative session since 1995, but all of them have failed to become law."
rationale: The statement is presented as an absolute but cannot be verified and is likely incorrect. While Texas lawmakers have repeatedly filed school-voucher and school-choice bills since the 1990s, it is unlikely that a voucher proposal was filed in literally every biennial session since 1995, and the definition of “voucher” varies; moreover Texas has enacted some limited school-choice/tax-credit scholarship measures even if broad universal vouchers have not been approved. Because of that imprecision and some enacted, voucher-like programs, the claim as stated is false.

claim: "For every one job created under the Obama administration, 75 people went on food stamps."
rationale: The claim is not supported by the data. During the Obama years the U.S. added roughly 10–12 million payroll jobs while SNAP (food stamp) participation rose by on the order of 10–15 million people at its peak — a ratio near 1–2 SNAP recipients per job, not 75. The "75 per job" figure arises from miscounting timeframes and units (e.g., comparing cumulative SNAP caseload increases or persons to a single month or year of job gains) and therefore is a misrepresentation.

claim: Says Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez tweeted, "I see people are rushing out to fill up their cars for this hurricane at the gas station. This wouldn’t be an issue if they had electric cars. If the power is out for a week how are they going to get gas? We need to start planning ahead and moving forward."
rationale: This quote has been circulated as a tweet attributed to Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez but there is no record of it on her verified account and fact-checkers have debunked the attribution. The wording and logic of the alleged tweet also match common fabricated or satirical memes that are frequently misattributed to public figures.

claim: Says the Hawaii governor "can’t find anything that says (President Barack Obama) was born in Hawaii."
rationale: The statement is false: Hawaii state officials and governors have publicly confirmed Barack Obama’s birth in Hawaii. Governor Neil Abercrombie said he had seen Hawaii’s records (including a certified birth record) showing Obama was born in Honolulu, and his predecessor Linda Lingle and the Hawaii Department of Health likewise affirmed the Hawaii birth. The quoted claim contradicts those official statements and records.

claim: Says Democratic obstruction is the reason why "many important positions in government are unfilled."
rationale: Attributing 'many important positions' remaining unfilled solely to Democratic obstruction is misleading. Vacancies in government arise from multiple causes — the President’s pace and choices of nominations, Senate scheduling and bipartisan holds, vetting delays, and retirements — and both parties have at times slowed confirmations. Without a specific timeframe or list of positions, the blanket causal claim is not supported.

claim: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has "no congressional oversight."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate: the CFPB was created by Congress (Dodd–Frank), its director is nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate, and Congress can hold hearings, issue subpoenas, and require reports. While the bureau’s funding mechanism (statutory transfer from the Federal Reserve rather than annual appropriations) and certain structural features limited some oversight mechanisms, that does not mean there is no congressional oversight. A Supreme Court decision (Seila Law) also altered the director’s removal protections, further changing oversight dynamics.

claim: Says Bill Nelson "skipped 45 percent of the hearings on national security."
rationale: The 45% figure is misleading and not supported by comprehensive attendance records. Independent fact-checkers reviewed Sen. Bill Nelson’s attendance and found the percentage came from a selective count (limited time frame and a narrow definition of “national security” sessions) and omitted context such as classified briefings, committee versus floor sessions, and excused absences. Without a precise time period and clear definition of which meetings were counted, the claim overstates what the records show.

claim: Tim Kaine "made Virginia the best state for business four years in a row."
rationale: The claim overstates and misattributes causation. While Virginia was ranked highly (and was named the top state for business by some publications in multiple consecutive years around Tim Kaine’s governorship), those rankings are issued by independent organizations and reflect many factors beyond a single governor’s actions — so saying Kaine “made Virginia the best state for business four years in a row” is inaccurate and misleading. The exact number and source of consecutive #1 rankings also varies by publication and year.

claim: "We will have more people enter our country illegally than were born in this country in one year."
rationale: The claim is not supported by available data for likely referent countries such as the United States. The U.S. records roughly 3.5–3.8 million births per year, while DHS border encounters/apprehensions in peak years have been on the order of 2–3 million and include repeat encounters and persons who do not ultimately remain, so they do not exceed annual births. Even under generous counting, illegal entries do not clearly surpass annual births.

claim: Barack Obama wants to "restore" the estate tax that George W. Bush "repealed."
rationale: The claim is essentially accurate: President Obama advocated reinstating the federal estate tax after it was eliminated for 2010 under the Bush-era tax law. While George W. Bush’s 2001 tax changes led to a temporary repeal of the estate tax in 2010 rather than a permanent, unqualified repeal, Obama supported restoring the tax (generally targeted at large estates).

claim: A typical married couple "will contribute $119,000" into Medicare but will "receive $357,000 in Medicare benefits over their lifetimes."
rationale: The exact paired figures are misleading and not a verifiable, universally accepted fact. Estimates that produce similar numbers typically rely on specific assumptions about cohort, discounting (present-value), whether employer shares or general-revenue transfers are counted, and inflation; different reasonable assumptions produce materially different results. Without a clear authoritative source and definition of terms, the statement that a "typical married couple" will contribute $119,000 and receive $357,000 is not reliably supported.

claim: The "Franklin scandal" broke in 1989 "when hundreds of children were apparently flown around the US to be abused by high ranking ‘Establishment’ members."
rationale: The claim misstates the established facts. Sensational allegations about a nationwide ring and 'hundreds' of children flown to be abused by high‑level officials surfaced around 1988–1989, but multiple official investigations and a grand jury found no evidence supporting the alleged nationwide child‑trafficking conspiracy, and the broader story has been widely discredited. The underlying Franklin case did involve local allegations and financial crimes, but not the proven nationwide abuse ring described.

claim: There was "a 57-percent decrease in fireworks-related injuries in 2000 [after Connecticut legalized sparklers] compared to the 14 years prior."
rationale: There is no credible, sourced public data showing a 57% drop in Connecticut fireworks-related injuries in 2000 tied to legalization of sparklers. CPSC and state public-health injury reports do not document such a large, single-year decline attributable to a change in sparkler law, and the claim offers no verifiable source or clear baseline years.

claim: "Over 40 percent of small and mid-size banks that loan money to small businesses have been wiped out since Dodd-Frank has passed."
rationale: This claim is false. Public banking data (FDIC and industry statistics) do not show that over 40% of small and mid‑size banks that lend to small businesses have been eliminated since Dodd‑Frank’s 2010 enactment; bank failures and a gradual decline in bank counts have been far smaller and driven by a mix of crisis-era failures, mergers and consolidation rather than a single cause. The statement also uses imprecise terms ("wiped out", who counts as "small and mid‑size", and exact timeframe), which overstates and misattributes the change to Dodd‑Frank.

claim: In Texas, "the No. 1 name for new male babies — many of whom will vote one day — is Jose."
rationale: Recent state- and national-level baby-name data do not show Jose as the No. 1 male baby name in Texas; names like Liam and Noah have ranked at the top in recent years. While Jose is a common name in many Texas communities with large Hispanic populations, statewide SSA data do not support it being the top male name overall.

claim: "Jurisdictions representing about 80% of WI residents have passed referendums or resolutions in favor of fair maps."
rationale: This claim is likely an overstatement. While many Wisconsin cities, towns, and counties have adopted resolutions or held advisory referendums supporting fair maps, those actions have not been documented to cover jurisdictions that together contain roughly 80% of the state's population. Major population centers and several counties did not all adopt such measures, so the 80% figure is not supported by available summaries of passed measures.

claim: "Under @BarackObama illegal immigration dropped to a 50-year low."
rationale: It is true that illegal/unauthorized immigration flows and Border Patrol apprehensions fell during the Obama years, but the statement that it dropped to a “50‑year low” is misleading and not supported across standard measures. Different metrics (apprehensions, net migration from Mexico, and the unauthorized immigrant population) show declines at different times and none cleanly establish a 50‑year low attributable to Obama’s tenure; the claim overstates and conflates indicators.

claim: Says Mitt Romney opposes requiring employers to cover contraception and would eliminate funding for Planned Parenthood.
rationale: This accurately reflects Romney’s stated positions during his 2012 presidential campaign: he opposed requirements forcing employers to provide contraceptive coverage in employee health plans and said he would end federal funding for Planned Parenthood. He publicly criticized the HHS contraception mandate and called for cutting off federal dollars to Planned Parenthood.

claim: Says Betsy Devos said "only" 0.02% of kids are likely to die when they go back to school.
rationale: There is no reliable record of Betsy DeVos saying the exact phrase that “only 0.02% of kids are likely to die when they go back to school.” She did cite very low proportions of COVID-19 deaths among children in early-pandemic remarks, but that statistic described children’s share of total deaths, not the per-child probability of dying if schools reopen, so the quoted wording and implication are a misrepresentation.

claim: "In eighth grade math, we’ve fallen to ninth place."
rationale: The claim is too vague to verify as stated — it does not identify which country or which assessment (e.g., TIMSS, PISA, NAEP) or year is meant. International and national rankings for eighth‑grade math fluctuate by assessment and cycle, so a blanket statement that “we’ve fallen to ninth place” is not verifiable as presented and is likely misleading without specific context.

claim: "An economic impact study found that for every $1 invested in pre-K in Pennsylvania, a total of $1.79 is generated in total spending within the state."
rationale: I could not verify a reputable study that specifically reports that every $1 invested in Pennsylvania pre-K generates $1.79 in in-state total spending. Early-childhood research reports vary widely (some report long-term social returns or different short-term economic multipliers), so without a citation this precise figure appears unsupported or mischaracterized.

claim: "As Virginia lost over 65,000 jobs, (Tim) Kaine put partisan ambitions first" by serving as DNC chairman during the last year of his governorship.
rationale: The claim mixes verifiable facts with an unprovable value judgment. Tim Kaine did begin serving as DNC chair in 2009 while finishing his gubernatorial term (ending January 2010), but asserting he “put partisan ambitions first” is an interpretive claim about motive that cannot be established by the mere overlap of roles. The specific figure that Virginia “lost over 65,000 jobs” during that period is also presented without clear timeframe or data source and is therefore not independently substantiated here.

claim: "Arizona audit" shows 86,391 voters "don’t appear to exist."
rationale: The Maricopa County audit spreadsheets produced by the audit contractors included a line listing 86,391 'voters that do not appear to exist.' However, that spreadsheet entry reflected restrictive matching rules, duplicate/inactive registrations, movers, clerical/data issues and not verified proof that 86,391 ballots were cast by nonexistent people. Presenting the number without that context is misleading.

claim: Says Anthony Bourdain tweeted, "This might be the best bat soup I ever had in my life. Someday everyone’s gonna be talking about Wuhan."
rationale: This attribution is false. Anthony Bourdain died in June 2018, well before COVID‑19 and the Wuhan/bat‑soup meme became public in late 2019/2020, and there is no record of this tweet on his verified accounts; fact‑checkers have identified the quote as a fabricated screenshot.

claim: "More than half of last year's U.S. college graduates are unemployed or underemployed."
rationale: Available government and higher-education data indicate that combined unemployment and reasonable measures of underemployment for recent U.S. college graduates are generally well below 50%. Unemployment rates for bachelor’s degree holders are typically low, and while some majors have high underemployment, the aggregate across all graduates does not support a majority being unemployed or underemployed.

claim: Says his administration has made "progress" on border enforcement by "putting more boots on the southern border than at any time in our history and reducing illegal crossings to their lowest levels in 40 years."
rationale: The claim combines an ambiguous staffing assertion with an incorrect statistical claim. While CBP staffing has increased in recent years, saying there are “more boots on the southern border than at any time in our history” is vague (doesn’t specify which agency or date) and not clearly supported by historical staffing records; and official encounter data do not show illegal crossings at their lowest levels in 40 years—recent years saw large surges and historically there have been years in the 1990s/2000s with lower levels than some recent totals. Overall the statement overstates and mischaracterizes available data.

claim: " ... following World War II war crime trials were convened. The Japanese were tried and convicted and hung for war crimes committed against American POWs. Among those charges for which they were convicted was waterboarding."
rationale: It is true that many Japanese service members were tried, convicted and in some cases executed after WWII for crimes against American POWs (e.g., Bataan-related prosecutions), but the tribunals generally charged murder, torture, and inhumane treatment rather than a specifically named count of “waterboarding.” While Japanese interrogators did use water-based torture (sometimes called a “water cure” or simulated drowning) in some incidents, indictments and convictions were framed in broader terms of torture or murder rather than the modern legal label “waterboarding.”

claim: The 2020 election is in "recount territory" and "I’ve seen elections change as a result of" recounts.
rationale: The claim bundles two ideas: that the entire 2020 election was broadly in “recount territory” and that recounts commonly change outcomes. The first is misleading — only a few states (e.g., Georgia) had margins small enough to trigger recounts and most key states had larger margins; recounts in 2020 did not change the winners. The second part is partly true in that recounts have flipped a few very close races historically (e.g., 2004 Washington governor, 2008 Minnesota Senate), but flips are rare and recounts typically alter vote totals by small amounts and seldom overturn outcomes.

claim: Says Debbie Wasserman Schultz "voted repeatedly to send terminally ill patients to prison."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz "voted repeatedly to send terminally ill patients to prison." Congressional votes are public and reputable fact-checkers and voting records do not show any votes that would criminalize terminally ill patients in that way. The allegation appears to be a partisan mischaracterization or conflation of other votes (e.g., on drug enforcement, sentencing, or end-of-life policy) without citing a specific bill.

claim: "New York, for all of their complaining, Gov. Cuomo's complaining, has only had a 1.5% decrease in revenue" due to the coronavirus pandemic.
rationale: This claim is inaccurate. New York's revenue losses from the COVID-19 pandemic were reported in the billions and represented a much larger share of the budget than 1.5% (state budget gaps and tax-revenue declines were commonly reported in the double-digit billions, implying a substantially larger percentage impact). Governor Cuomo and the state repeatedly warned of large multi-billion dollar shortfalls and sought federal relief to cover them, which contradicts a mere 1.5% decline assertion.

claim: Said Adolf Hitler and Donald Trump have both described deportations as "a military operation."
rationale: There is no well-documented primary-source evidence that Adolf Hitler explicitly described deportations using the phrase “a military operation,” and while Donald Trump has at times used militaristic language about large-scale removals, clear citations showing he labeled deportations verbatim as “a military operation” are lacking. The claim treats a specific quoted phrase as used by both figures, but that specific phrasing is not supported for Hitler and is at best an ambiguous or paraphrased characterization for Trump. Therefore the assertion that both described deportations in those exact terms is not supported.

claim: President Joe Biden cut "$30 billion to Black colleges and universities."
rationale: False. There is no evidence that President Biden enacted a $30 billion cut specifically targeting Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs). Federal support for HBCUs under the Biden administration included pandemic relief and targeted funding, and a $30 billion unilateral cut would be far larger than typical HBCU appropriations and would have been widely reported.

claim: "PELOSI says if President TRUMP wins, she will resign!!"
rationale: There is no reliable record of Nancy Pelosi publicly saying she would resign if Donald Trump wins the presidency.
